decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c09kjhit. The owner rejected v1, which kept types without a cap of their own. In the owner's words, it threw away the original ask. That ask, after Simon Peyton Jones's work in Haskell, is that a type can limit the effects it may use. v2 makes it the recommendation. It also removes the two costs v1 listed: a third place for promises and a tail rule for generic types.

The one reading. D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 4 says `#FX` above any type means the most that work done in that type's name may do. For an effect type, that work is every function whose row names it. For an ordinary type, option A says the work is its methods, its trait impls in any package, and every closure written inside them.

Generic types need no tail. What a type parameter does belongs to whoever picks it, just as a callback's effects belong to its caller under D-EFF2. So `#FX(IO)` above `Traced<T>` bounds Traced's own code to IO. `Traced<Parser>` does IO plus whatever Parser does, and Parser's part is checked against the caps where `Traced<Parser>` is written. Haskell's monad transformers read the same way: `LoggingT m` adds logging to whatever `m` does.

Why it is sound. Only a type parameter or a function parameter passes effects through, because the caller chose it and sees it. Everything else counts against the cap. A concrete type the methods build and call counts, so no type can launder an effect through another. A trait value in a field counts with its trait's declared row. A function field with a fixed row must fit the cap.

Trait impls in any package. The cap is part of the type's public signature, like a method row. An impl of any trait for the type is checked against it where the impl is written, in whatever package. An inherited default method is checked there too. A `Close` impl is covered, so cleanup cannot reach the network either. Widening a published cap is a semver change, as a row change is under D-EFFECT-OMIT1.

One ladder, not a third place. `#FX` is already the ceiling for a block (spec.md:1825) and, under D-EFFECT-RUNGS1 A, for a module. A type becomes one more rung of the same ladder: block, function, type, module, package. Caps meet, so code obeys every cap above it. A method row may only tighten. `jet explain effects` lists the chain, nearest first.

Cost. The check reads rows the compiler already infers (D-EFFECT-OMIT1). Caps erase before IR, as block caps do today, so generated code is the same with or without them. A generic instance needs no extra check, because each type argument's own work was checked against its own cap. Nothing runs at run time.

Reads with the related ballots. Under D-EFFECT-RUNGS1 A, a type in a capped module obeys both caps. Under RUNGS1 C, the type cap is the only shared ceiling below the package. D-EFFTYPE-USES1 A and D-DECL-TYPES1 rule 4 give `#FX` above an effect type the same reading. D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1 caps whole artifacts and is independent.

Research. Haskell's `ST` type confines mutation, and `runST`'s rank-2 type proves none escapes, at no run-time cost (Launchbury and Peyton Jones, 1994). Monad transformers stack effects so each layer adds its own. Koka and Frank put rows on functions and stay polymorphic in the rest of the row; option A's pass-through reads the same way. Rust has no effect bound on types, only inferred auto traits.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/fx2. model.jet is the shown program in today's syntax, without the other package's impl. `jet check model.jet` is ok, because `#FX` above a struct parses and is ignored today. `jet run -A model.jet` is an internal compiler error in `Parser.display` (card to file), so the snippets are checked, not run. `Parser.Stylesheet`, `http.get` and the `T: #FX(...)` bound are illustrative.

options.name: `#FX` above a type bounds its work
options.detail:
`#FX(...)` above a struct, enum or trait is the ceiling for everything done in the type's name. That is its methods, its trait impls in any package, and every closure written inside them. A method row may only tighten it.

What a type parameter or a function parameter does belongs to the caller, as with `via`. So a generic type needs no tail rule, and `Traced<Parser>` does Traced's work plus Parser's. Above a trait, the cap bounds every impl in any package.
options.technical:
The Prelude `marker FX` sites grow from [.Block] to struct, enum and trait. Its D-MARK-SCOPE1 matrix mode is tighten. The check runs on inferred rows (D-EFFECT-OMIT1). Each method, impl method, inherited default method and lambda body must fit the cap, with E0712 naming it. Calls through a type parameter or a function parameter are excluded (D-EFF2 pass-through). Calls on concrete types are counted.

Trait values count with their trait's declared row (D-EFF3). Function-typed fields with a fixed row must fit. An impl is checked where it is written, in any package. The cap joins the public API snapshot. Caps erase before IR.

options.name: Module caps and rows only
options.detail:
A type gets no cap of its own. Its author moves it into its own module and caps the module, which covers the type, its methods and its helpers. A trait keeps its per-method rows, which already bind every impl.

An impl written in another package sits outside the module, so the cap does not check it. Closures follow their module. Generic types use today's open row tails and `via`.
options.technical: Uses D-EFFECT-RUNGS1=A (module `#FX` cap) and D-EFF3 (trait method rows bind impls). No new placement or grammar. A type with its own promise needs its own module line (`#FX(...) module parse`). Generic methods use `-[via f]>` (D-EFF2) and open tails (D-SHAPE8=A). An impl of the type in another package is checked only against that package's own caps and rows.

options.name: Bounds where the type is used
options.detail:
Types carry no promise. A function that needs one asks for it in a generic bound, and the compiler checks the inferred rows of the type's methods. Rust checks its inferred `Send` and `Sync` the same way.

Authors write nothing, and nothing is promised that no one uses. Each caller who needs the promise repeats the bound. A library change can break those callers, because the library never wrote the promise down.
options.technical: New bound form `T: #FX(...)` on generic parameters, checked against the inferred rows of the type's methods and impls (D-EFFECT-OMIT1). Model: Rust auto traits. No marker sites change.

comparisons.note: `ST s` confines mutation to one type, and runST's rank-2 type proves no reference escapes, with no run-time cost. Source: https://hackage.haskell.org/package/base/docs/Control-Monad-ST.html and Launchbury and Peyton Jones, Lazy Functional State Threads (PLDI 1994).
comparisons.code: runST :: (forall s. ST s a) -> a

comparisons.note: A monad transformer adds its own effect to whatever the inner monad does, the reading option A gives a generic type. Source: https://hackage.haskell.org/package/monad-logger
comparisons.code: newtype LoggingT m a = LoggingT { runLoggingT :: (Loc -> LogSource -> LogLevel -> LogStr -> IO ()) -> m a }

comparisons.note: Rows sit on function types and stay open over the rest of the row, so a higher-order function passes its argument's effects through. Source: https://koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html
comparisons.code: fun map(xs : list<a>, f : a -> e b) : e list<b>

comparisons.note: No effect bounds on types; inferred auto traits such as Send are asked for in bounds (option C). Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/special-types-and-traits.html#auto-traits

recommendation.why: A is the original ask, made safe. One line above a type bounds its methods, its impls anywhere and its closures. It reads like `#FX` on blocks, modules and effect types. Generic types reuse `via`.
gains: A type's promise is written once, on the type, and binds every package.
Generic types need no tail: a parameter's work is the caller's, as with `via`.
One reading of `#FX` from block to package, effect types included.

whyNot.reason: B leaves other packages' impls and a split-out module's helpers outside the promise, and makes authors split modules to state one.
C puts nothing in the library, so every caller repeats the bound and an upgrade can break them silently.

recommendation.tradeoff: A published cap is a promise to users: narrowing it is free, widening it is a breaking change, like a row.

It tried laundering an effect through a concrete type, a trait-value field and an inherited default method, and v2 now counts all three against the cap. It asked whether `Traced<Http>` breaks Traced's `!Net`; v2 checks Http's part where `Traced<Http>` is written.

decisions.title: A library effect says what it may do with the same `#FX` marker
decisions.situation: A library can name its own effect, such as a graph package's queries, so callers can allow or forbid exactly that. Today such a name can only be a leaf under one built-in effect, like `Net.Query`. Worse, its functions cannot actually use the network: the compiler rejects the very calls the name stands for. One rule matters here: a denial such as `!Net` checks what code really reaches, not what its rows claim. The vote decides how a library effect states what it may do. We recommend the same `#FX` marker used on blocks and modules.
decisions.gist: How should a library's own effect say which basic powers it may use?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a kind of power, such as network access. A library may name its own effect, like `graph.Query`, so a caller can allow or forbid just that. The name must say what it may really do. A denial such as `!Net` checks what code really reaches, not what rows claim, so a hidden network call is still caught.
decisions.story: Ana's reports call the `graph` package. Her lead wants one report that may never run a graph query, while another report may. She wants to write `!graph.Query` on that one function and have the compiler hold it.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Folded into the D-EFFECT-LIMITS1 package ballot (card c09kjhit), which the owner rejected. Already ratified: the effect tree with roots and leaves (D-EFFTREE1), leaf declarations (D-EFFECT-DECL1=A), denials hold through calls (D-PROP1), and a new user root is E0119.

Probe findings, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/fx. leaf_wrap2.jet: a function under `-[Net.Query]>` calling `net.tcp_listen` is E0740 "uses the effect `Net`, which its signature doesn't allow". deny_leaf_real.jet: the same for `FS.Notes` over `fs.read` (E0740 on `FS.Read`). So a library leaf is a name with nothing behind it today.

uses_a.jet: `#FX(Net)` above `effect Query` gives E0119 "`Query` isn't a known effect", as expected for new syntax. leaf.jet and deny_net.jet: a denial checks real reach, not the declared row. `-[!Net]>` calling a `-[Net]>` function with an empty body checks clean. db_net.jet: `-[!Net]>` calling a `-[DB]>` function checks clean, since DB is its own root.

Side note for existing cards: in leaf_wrap.jet, `print(port()?)` with a bare `?` checked clean. In leaf_wrap2.jet a bare `?` after a binding is E-ERR-PROPAGATE "A bare `?` has no meaning". The cause is not confirmed.

Reads with the related ballots. D-EFFECT-RUNGS1=A puts `#FX` on module lines with the same "at most" meaning, so blocks, modules and effects share one marker. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 option A needs A here: Core declares `DB` and `Log` as library effects over machine powers. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 and D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1 are independent of this vote.

options.name: `#FX` above the effect
options.detail:
A package declares `effect Query` with `#FX(...)` above it, the same marker that caps a block or a module. Inside the package, a function whose row says `Query` may do what `Query` stands for, here network calls. Callers write `graph.Query`, like any other package item.

A leaf such as `effect Net.Query` keeps working, with the same rule: a leaf may do at most what its root does. So today's leaves become usable rather than changing shape.
options.technical:
Marker site: `#FX` on an `effect` declaration (D-MARK-SCOPE1 matrix, mode tighten). A positive list only; `!` entries are errors there. Package effects resolve as package items (`graph.Query`); unqualified inside the package. A leaf `Root.Leaf` gets the implicit cap `#FX(Root)`, which fixes E0740 on leaf bodies (probe/fx/leaf_wrap2.jet). Denials keep checking real reach (D-PROP1).

Today `$` marks facts and `#` marks rules: Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet writes `effect Net $irreversible`. The cap is a rule checked on bodies, so it is spelled with today's rule sigil.

options.name: Leaves only, made usable
options.detail:
A library effect is a leaf under one built-in effect, as today. The one change: a leaf may use its root, so a `Net.Query` function may make network calls.

A library that needs both the network and files cannot say so with one name. Leaves live under shared roots, so two packages can pick the same leaf name.
options.technical: Semantics only: a body under `-[Root.Leaf]>` may use `Root`. No grammar change. D-EFFECT-DECL1 leaf declarations unchanged. Excludes D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 option A, which needs multi-power library effects.

options.name: A `uses` clause
options.detail:
The declaration lists its powers after a new `uses` keyword. The meaning matches option A; only the spelling differs.

A reader meets one more keyword, and the same "at most" idea is spelled `#FX(...)` on blocks and modules but `uses` here.
options.technical: New contextual keyword `uses` in `effect` declarations. Same semantics as option A.

comparisons.note: User effects are first-class names; what they do is decided by handlers. Source: https://koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html

  fun run-query(text : string) : list<person>

comparisons.note: Abilities are declared by libraries and named in function types. Source: https://www.unison-lang.org/docs/fundamentals/abilities/
Capabilities are ordinary values; a library capability wraps the ones it uses. Source: https://docs.scala-lang.org/scala3/reference/experimental/cc.html

recommendation.why: A reuses the one "at most" marker Jet already has, lets a package own its effect's name, and makes today's leaves usable too. It adds a placement, not a concept.
gains: One rule for blocks, modules and effects.
Unblocks Core's own effects in D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1.

whyNot.reason: B cannot name an effect that needs two powers, and leaf names collide across packages.
C spells the same "at most" idea with a second keyword.

recommendation.tradeoff: Effects gain a marker line above them; a leaf needs none.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: Main. A reuses the at-most marker, so a reader learns no new form; the only risk is reading #FX(Net) as granting Net rather than capping it.

decisions.title: The compiler builds in machine powers; Core declares the rest like a library
decisions.situation: Jet has thirteen built-in effects. Some are things the machine does, such as network, files and the clock. Others are services built on those, such as databases and logging. Because a database is its own built-in effect, forbidding the network does not stop a database call that goes over the network. Packages also cannot define effects the way Core does. The vote decides which effects the compiler builds in. We recommend building in only the machine powers and declaring the rest in Core, the way any package would.
decisions.gist: Which effects should the compiler build in, and which should Core declare like a library?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a kind of power, such as network access. Some powers come from the machine: network, files, clock, randomness. Others are services built on them, like a database. If a service is declared over the machine powers it uses, forbidding the network also stops a database that talks over the network.
decisions.story: Ana's offline report reads from the shop database. She writes `!Net` on it so it never waits on the network. Then the team moves the database to a server, and the report still compiles, because a database call is not a network call to the compiler.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Folded into the D-EFFECT-LIMITS1 package ballot (card c09kjhit), which the owner rejected. Already ratified: the thirteen roots (D-EFF4/5, D-AUTHORITY-ROOTS1), the effect tree (D-EFFTREE1) and leaf declarations (D-EFFECT-DECL1=A). Also settled: the vocabulary is Jet source in Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet (D-META-ONE1=A), and denials hold through calls (D-PROP1).

Probe, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/fx. kernel_today.jet is today's program: `offline_count` under `-[!Net]>` calls a `-[DB]>` function and checks clean. db_net.jet shows the same with a stub body.

Reads with the related ballots. A needs D-EFFTYPE-USES1=A, which lets an effect declare what it may do. It matches D-EXTEND-ARCH1=A: Core uses the same forms packages use. D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1 takes the machine powers as the facts a target profile lists. D-EFFTYPE-GRANT1 grants these names unchanged.

Open detail inside A, not a vote: the exact caps for `Log` and `Secret` follow their Core drivers. A file logger reaches only FS; a collector also reaches Net.

Side note for existing cards: a `DBConnection` has no query method. Even a first program must build a row policy and call `with_policy` to get a `DBScope` (kernel_today.jet; Core/Db/Db.jet:707-715). That is heavy for the beginner path.

options.name: Machine powers built in, services in Core
options.detail:
The compiler builds in what the machine does: network, files, terminal, clock, randomness, environment, processes, foreign code, graphics card and browser host. Core then declares databases, logging and secrets over those, with the same `#FX` line a package uses.

Users keep writing `-[DB]>` and `!DB`. What changes is that `!Net` now catches a database that talks to a server, while a local database file still passes.
options.technical:
Needs D-EFFTYPE-USES1=A. Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet keeps the machine roots (Net, FS, IO, Time, Rand, Env, Exec, FFI, GPU, Browser; deny-only Mem, Panic). Core declares `#FX(Net, FS) effect DB`, `#FX(IO, FS, Net) effect Log` and `#FX(Env, FS, Net) effect Secret`, exported through the Prelude so rows keep bare names. Leaves (DB.Read, DB.Write) move with their parent.

Denials keep checking real reach (D-PROP1), so each driver's real calls decide. A server driver written over `core.net` reaches Net. Core's SQLite driver calls C inside vouched `#Unsafe` gates (Core/Db/Db.jet:1374); those stay invisible to callers, as today. A driver over vouched C names its machine reach on its binding.

options.name: Keep thirteen built-in roots
options.detail:
All thirteen effects stay built in, each its own switch. Forbidding one never forbids another.

A team that wants an offline report must forbid both `Net` and `DB`, even when the database is a local file. A package that builds a service like Core's database cannot give it an effect of the same kind.

decisions.title: Each build's effect limit is read from its target profile; nothing new to write
decisions.situation: Some builds run where the machine lacks things: a web page with no operating system has no files, and a small board may have no memory allocator. Jet already describes each such machine as a target profile with typed facts. Today those facts do not limit what code may do, so a list allocated under a profile with no allocator checks and builds clean. The vote decides where a build's effect limit comes from. We recommend reading it from the profile's facts, with nothing new to write.
decisions.gist: Where should the effect limit for a no-OS web, GPU or board build come from?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a kind of power, such as file access or allocating memory. A target profile lists what a machine has. If the profile says there is no allocator, code built for it must not allocate. Reading the limit from those facts means a machine is described once, and the compiler checks code against it.
decisions.story: Ana's team ships a small price widget built for a web page with no operating system. Its profile says there is no allocator. A helper that builds a list of labels slipped in, the build passed, and the widget failed at load time.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Folded into the D-EFFECT-LIMITS1 package ballot (card c09kjhit), which the owner rejected. Reuses the earlier draft at ballots/out/new/D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1.json, with its fact-to-denial table. Already ratified: typed profile modules selected by `targets:` (D-TARGET-SURFACE1=A), facts as the source of truth (D-FREESTAND-FACTS1=A), and required allocator and panic facts (D-TARGET-ALLOC1=A).

D-FREESTAND-FACTS1 rejected effects as the source of what a machine has. Here effects are only derived from facts, never written, so that decision holds.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/fx. target_today uses Examples/embedded/heap_free_core/package.jet (profile `web.no_os`, `runtime: "core"`). `use core.files` there is E1006 "`core.files` needs `runtime: hosted`". A list allocation checks clean, and `jet build run.jet` exits 0 with a host ELF binary. target_a/run.jet is option A's program and checks clean today.

Side note for existing cards: `jet build --target=web.no_os run.jet` is E2104 "`jet build --target=web.no_os` is not built yet". Plain `jet build` in a `web.no_os` package produced a host ELF binary rather than refusing.

Reads with the related ballots. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1=A keeps the machine powers as compiler roots, which are exactly what profile facts map to. D-EFFECT-RUNGS1 and D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 cap code by where it lives; this ballot caps it by where it runs. The two combine by intersection.

options.name: Read from the profile's facts
options.detail:
The package already selects its profile. Each fact the profile marks absent becomes a denial for that build: no allocator denies allocation, no sockets denies the network, no file system denies files.

A breach is reported at the line, with the call path from the entry and the missing fact. Hover on the profile line, or `jet explain`, lists every derived denial with its fact.
options.technical:
Keeps D-TARGET-SURFACE1=A (typed profile modules selected by `targets:`) and D-FREESTAND-FACTS1=A (facts are the source of truth). Mapping: allocator absent gives `!Mem.Alloc`; sockets `!Net`; file system `!FS`; entropy `!Rand`; browser DOM `!Browser`; GPU `!GPU`; FFI `!FFI`.

Also: no byte sink gives `!IO`; no clocks `!Time`; no sleep `!Time.Wait`. Facts with no effect (startup, linker, regions, MMIO) map to nothing. Each artifact gets its own limit. Shared code that differs per build branches with `comptime if` on profile facts.

options.name: Written by the package
options.detail:
Each target entry in the package file gets a `deny:` list, written by the team. The profile's facts stay separate.

The limit is visible in one line. But the team repeats what the profile already says, and a denial left out is never checked.
options.technical: New `deny:` field on `targets:` entries, checked like `authority.deny` but per artifact. Profile facts are not consulted.

options.name: No effect limit
options.detail:
Keep what exists: `runtime:` refuses imports of whole libraries the machine cannot support. Anything finer, like one allocation, is not checked until link or load.

Nothing new to learn, but the widget story above keeps happening.
options.technical: Status quo. probe/fx/target_today: `use core.files` under `runtime: "core"` is E1006; a list allocation under `web.no_os` checks and builds clean.

comparisons.note: Platform facts are `cfg` values; `no_std` crates fail at link time when they reach for an allocator. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html
Target facts are compile-time values; using a missing feature fails when it is reached. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Targets
Device-code rules are hard-coded one by one in the compiler. Source: https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/

recommendation.why: A turns facts the team already writes into checks, with no new syntax. Each machine is described once, and errors point at the line and the missing fact.
gains: Machine limits are checked at compile time.
No second list to keep in step.

whyNot.reason: B makes teams repeat the profile by hand, and a forgotten line is never checked.
C leaves allocation and similar breaches to fail at load time.

recommendation.tradeoff: The derived limit is not one written line; hover and `jet explain` list it.

decisions.title: `jet add` writes each dependency's grant line; an upgrade that needs more stops with the call path
decisions.situation: Attacks often arrive in an upgrade: a trusted library's new version quietly starts using the network. Jet already has a place in package.jet for what each dependency may do, but nothing writes it, and the compiler refuses any filled-in line today. So a project that allows the network for its own code lets every dependency use it too. The vote decides who writes each dependency's line. We recommend that `jet add` writes it, asking only when the project would gain a power.
decisions.gist: Should `jet add` write what each dependency may do into package.jet, ask first, or leave it?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a kind of power, such as network access. A grant line in package.jet says which powers one dependency may use. If the tool writes that line when you add the dependency, a later version that wants more power stops the build. It names the call that needs the power and offers one command to allow it.
decisions.story: Ana adds a JSON library to her shop. Months later, `jet update` pulls a new version that sends data to a server. Her shop uses the network itself, so nothing in today's package file notices the library's new reach.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Folded into the D-EFFECT-LIMITS1 package ballot (card c09kjhit), which the owner rejected. Reuses the earlier draft at ballots/out/new/D-EFFTYPE-GRANT1.json. Already ratified: per-dependency provenance in the lock and opt-in enforcement (D-EFFBUDGET1=D), the `grants:` field (D-EFFBUDGET1), and the confirmation prompt shape (D-SCRIPT-CONFIRM1=A).

Probe, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/fx/grant_today. A package.jet with `grants: { json: [] }` gives E1221 "`authority.grants` is not supported by the current compiler package-policy boundary". Today's Examples/features/packages/effect_budget writes only an empty `grants: {}`.

Meaning of a grant line. D-EFFBUDGET1 calls a grant a per-dependency escape from `allow`. Under A, the line is that dependency's whole limit, which covers the escape case and also pins a dependency below `allow`. No project has a non-empty line today, so nothing changes meaning.

Why this matters. Upgrade attacks: event-stream (2018) added a payload through a new dependency; ua-parser-js (2021) and xz-utils (2024) shipped malicious releases of trusted packages.

Reads with the related ballots. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1 fixes the names a grant line lists. D-SCRIPT-DESIGNATE1, in the project group, covers what a script grants itself. D-FFI-UNSAFE1 uses the same grant line for a binder's build-time tool.

options.name: `jet add` writes the line
options.detail:
`jet add json` works out what the library uses and writes `json: []` under `grants:`. If that fits what the project already allows, nothing is asked. If it needs a new power, a terminal asks once; without a terminal, the command stops and prints the exact flag to pass.

Each later build and `jet update` checks every granted dependency. A version that reaches further stops with the call path and a one-command fix.
options.technical:
Under `authority.grants`, a listed dependency's limit is its line, replacing `allow` for that dependency. Today non-empty grants are refused (Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/Loader.jet:387-388), so no project changes meaning. Writing grants alone does not turn on `allow` enforcement for the project's own code (D-EFFBUDGET1=D keeps enforcement opt-in).

Prompt shape follows D-SCRIPT-CONFIRM1=A. `--allow` reuses the run flag spelling (`jet run --allow=FS.Read`). Hand-added dependencies without a line keep today's behavior: provenance in the lock. Lines are one per dependency, sorted.

options.name: Ask on every add
options.detail:
Like A, but `jet add` always asks before writing, even when the library needs nothing new.

The question carries no information when the answer is always yes, so people learn to press Enter. Non-interactive use needs a flag on every add.
options.technical: Same grant semantics as A. Adds a confirmation on every `jet add`; `--yes` for scripts.

options.name: Never write
options.detail:
Keep today's rule: the lock records what each dependency uses, and grant lines are written by hand.

The lock shows the change after the fact, if someone reads the diff. Nothing stops the build.
options.technical: Status quo for D-EFFBUDGET1=D provenance; non-empty grants become writable by hand only.

decisions.title: Where does a module's and a package's metadata live, and how do you set it?
decisions.situation: A package and a module each have a body: metadata fields first, then bindings. package.jet and module.jet are bodies with implicit braces; in any other file you write name :: package { ... } or name :: module { ... } and the metadata goes inside the braces. Every example uses the planned binding form, where every named thing is a constant bound with ::. The options differ only in how you read the fields.
decisions.gist: Should a module's metadata fields be read directly, as pricing.category, or only through #module(pricing)?
decisions.lesson: A module groups functions under one name, such as pricing. A package is a project with a package.jet file. Both have metadata: a name, a file, docs, a version and a license. This vote decides how you set and read it.
decisions.story: Mia's shop has a pricing module and an old discount module she wants to retire. Her About screen shows her version, authors and the version of the json package she uses. She marks discount as deprecated so its callers get a warning.
decisions.inWild:
Python: a module keeps its metadata in reserved double-underscore names, such as __name__, __doc__ and __file__.
Rust: Cargo exposes package fields such as CARGO_PKG_VERSION as text, one macro read per field.
Jai: a module is a constant, Basic :: #import "Basic", and module settings are written where it is imported.
decisions.detail:
YOUR RULE

A package in package.jet and a module in module.jet are implicitly wrapped in braces: the whole file is the body. A package or module written in any other file wraps its body in braces, as name :: package { ... } or name :: module { ... }. The metadata and optional fields go in the body, first, followed by the bindings. Both options follow this rule exactly; they differ only in how you read the fields.

THE FORM EVERY EXAMPLE USES

D-DECL-BINDING1=B is ratified: every named thing is a constant bound with ::. A function is total :: fn(text: String) -> Int { ... }, a type is Module :: struct { ... }, and a module bound in a file is discount :: module { ... }. The file-module line, module pricing, stays as that ruling kept it, and finds pricing.jet or pricing/module.jet as today. Lambdas are fn(n) { n + 1 } (D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1=C). None of the proposed forms is built yet, so every proposed example is marked not built.

THE BODY

A package body or module body holds field lines first, then bindings. A field line is name: value, the line form package.jet already uses. A binding is name :: value or name := value.

- package.jet: the file is the package body. Its field lines are today's package.jet lines.

- pricing/module.jet: the file is the module body. category: "billing" at its top sets a field.

- Any other file: discount :: module { category: "billing" ... total :: fn ... } and tool :: package { name: "tool" ... }. The fields go inside the braces, first.

A module's fields are those of the built-in type Module: name, file, doc, package, maturity, category and deprecated. name, file, doc and package are filled by the compiler. maturity, category and deprecated have defaults, so you opt in only to the ones you want. A package's fields are the Package fields package.jet has today, plus authors.

WHAT A MEANS

The fields are the module's own. You read pricing.category, and describe(pricing) passes the module to a function that takes a Module. You read your own package as #package.version and a dependency's as json.package.version.

WHY NOT B, READ THROUGH #module

B writes the bodies and field lines exactly as A, but reads a module's fields only as #module(pricing).category. A module member may then use any name, so nothing is renamed. The cost is a second, longer read form, and a module no longer passes as a Module itself.

THE CLASH RULE IN A, EXACTLY

In every module body, the seven names name, file, doc, package, maturity, category and deprecated are fields. A binding in a module body with one of those names is the generic duplicate-name error, E0105, which lists the module's fields.

Nothing else is touched: locals, parameters, struct fields, methods, types and struct members may use all seven names. Package fields never clash, because they are read through package or #package. The list is closed; your own metadata is an ordinary constant, such as OWNER :: "billing team".

Today 9 module-level items use name or file, out of 59,105, including Core/Files/Path.jet:102 and Core/Sys/Sys.jet:286; jet fix renames them and their callers once.

FIELD LINES

Field lines come first in the body: at the top of package.jet or module.jet, after the /// comment, or right after the opening brace. Each field is written at most once, and the value must have the field's type, so category: 3 is a type error.

Writing a compiler-filled field, such as name: "x", is the generic error for a read-only field. Any other name, such as limit: 5, is the generic error that lists the legal forms: name :: value, name := value, or a field line.

EDGE CASES

- deprecated makes every use from another module warn, as #Deprecated warns today. It never fails the build.

- A module's doc is the /// comment at the top of module.jet, or the one above name :: module { ... }.

- A function that takes Module sees only the seven fields, as a trait value sees only its trait's members.

- A dependency's Package is read-only. json.package.authority shows json's rules; only json's own build applies them.

- Old package.jet files keep working, because every new field has a default.

- Module and Package live in core.meta, not the Prelude. Reading their fields needs no import; naming the type does, as run.jet's use line shows.

- Every field is known while building. Metadata ships in the program only where code reads it.

BEGINNER AND EXPERT

A beginner writes no field lines in a module, because every field has a default, and prints #package.version on an About screen. An expert opts in to category, maturity or deprecated and passes modules to tools that take a Module.

WHAT RUNS TODAY

Probes are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Research/ballots-2026-11-05/modvalue and modvalue3, run with the pinned compiler (jet@0.0.1#006bccd5).

- f01 and f05: a category: "billing" line is an error today, at file top and inside a module. The line form is free.

- f02 and f03: square :: fn(...) and pricing :: module { ... } are not built yet; both are parse errors today.

- f07: a repeated module-level name is E0105, "defined twice".

- m01_today prints 3, standard rules, m01_today and 0.0.0. Only $package.name and $package.version are readable; $package.license is E0107.

- Today module pricing finds pricing.jet, then pricing/module.jet (Compiler/JetDriver Loader.jet:2276-2287).

RATIFIED DECISIONS IT TOUCHES

All code is in D-DECL-BINDING1=B and D-LAMBDA-SHAPE1=C form. Both options use D-ECO-FILEROOT1 for the Package value. B adds #module(m) beside the ratified #package (D-META-HASH1=A). D-MARK-META1=B's law that behavior-free metadata is a #Meta field still holds for functions and types; for packages and modules the metadata is a field of the body. Choice point C2 of Docs/proposals/effect-types-2026-10-29.md is answered: modules are first-class values.

options.name: A module's fields are read directly
options.detail: A package or module body holds its metadata fields first: implicit braces in package.jet and module.jet, explicit braces in any other file. You read pricing.category, and a module passes as a Module. The seven field names are taken in module bodies, so 9 items are renamed once.
options.technical: Sema gives each module the fields of core.meta.Module, filled from the file or binding, owning package, /// comment and the body's field lines. A field line is name: value at the top of a body, before any binding, checked against the field type. A binding in a module body named like a field is E0105. Package is PackageFacts' fields plus authors. #package is that value. All values are known while building.

decisions.title: Effect arguments name a scope, such as a folder, a host or a device, with one covers rule from Core's scope types
decisions.situation:
Ratified D-DECL-TYPES1=A makes an effect a struct whose fields carry constant data, matched by equality. In installment 3 Main proposed one covers rule, so rows, grants and denials share one spelling, such as FS.Read("templates/"). That question is still open with you.

BallotReview3 marked the posted draft NOT CLEAN: an arbitrary covers function has no sound laws, and memory budgets are not scopes. This ballot keeps arguments to scopes and leaves budgets as they are. Keeping equality only is option E.
decisions.gist: Should effect arguments name scopes, a folder, a host or a device, with one covers rule for rows, grants and denials?
decisions.lesson: An effect says what a function may do, such as read files. Today it cannot say which files. An argument narrows it: reading templates/ only. This vote decides whether those arguments are allowed, how a wide permission covers a narrow need, and where the check happens.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A row is the effect list on a function, written -[FS.Read]>. A grant, in package.jet, says what a dependency may do. A denial is a ! entry that forbids an effect.

A scope is what an argument names: a folder, a host or a device. Covers means a wider scope includes a narrower one, as templates/ includes templates/home.html.
decisions.story: Sam adds a template library to a shop. It should read only the templates folder and call only api.example.com. Today Sam can grant it all files and all network, or pass a flag on every run.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. Whether effect arguments may name scopes, how coverage between scopes is defined, and how rows, grants and denials use them. Memory and copy budgets, such as !Mem.Alloc(above: 64), are not scopes; they keep today's aggregate rule, unchanged by every option.

Today, on seed a0_042, re-running G6Lead's probes. e01's !Mem.Alloc(above: N) row runs and prints 1. e04's bare FS.Read row reads logo. e03's FS.Read("assets/") row, e07's !Net("api.example.com") denial and e08's !Mem.Copy(above: 64) give Expected , between effects in the row. e02's constant struct effect, ratified by DECL-TYPES1, fails the same way.

Scoping today is per run and per process. e09 reads logo and secret normally. With jet run --allow=FS.Read:assets it prints logo, then refused. That comes from CLI/Authority.jet and a Linux Landlock rule installed at launch, for the whole process, not per dependency.

Why budgets stay out. BallotReview3's memory probes show a budget adds up: one 40-byte reservation passes !Mem.Alloc(above: 64), and two give E0921. A covers rule treats a repeated need as one, so it would lose the second 40. Budgets therefore keep their own summing rule in Effects/Checks.jet.

The rule under A, part 1: scope types. Core defines three scope kinds, each with fixed laws. fs.Path covers by whole path components after normalization, so templates/ covers templates/home.html but not templates2/. net.Host covers by exact match after lower-casing and IDNA, so api.example.com never covers evilapi.example.com. Every other field covers by equality, as DECL-TYPES1 already says.

Part 2: one covers rule. An effect instance covers another of the same type when every field covers the matching field. A bare type, FS.Read with no argument, covers every instance. Because each field law is fixed by Core, coverage is reflexive, transitive and always terminates; no library code runs to decide it.

Part 3: library effects. A library declares its own effect as a struct whose fields use these scope types, such as Bucket: struct { name: String } with impl Effect. It gets the same covers rule with no extra code. Device arguments use HOST-CAPS1's hardware kinds, so GPU(acme_npu.Kind) names a library-declared kind; the provider work stays ACCEL-LIB1's.

Part 4: rows. A function's row is inferred from what it calls, and arguments come from constant values in the calls. files.read("templates/{name}.html") infers FS.Read("templates/"), its longest constant prefix. A path known only at run time infers bare FS.Read. Core's file and network functions publish which parameter names the scope, and libraries may publish the same.

Part 5: grants. A dependency's inferred row must be covered by its grant in package.jet, checked at build time. A bare need under a narrow grant is allowed only through mediated calls. The file or network function checks the actual path or host against the grant when it runs, and refuses the rest with an error value.

Part 6: denials. A need covered by a denial is a build error. A need that only overlaps one, such as reading all of assets/ with assets/secret/ denied, builds, and the mediated call refuses the denied part at run time. A need disjoint from the denial is unaffected.

Who is checked at run time. A callback runs with the authority of the package that wrote it. A task started by a dependency inherits that dependency's grant. Foreign code and subprocesses are not mediated, so a dependency that uses them needs the FFI or process grant, which covers everything; package.jet shows that.

Engineering away the downsides. The unsound covers function is gone: coverage comes from three fixed laws. The host-suffix attack is gone: hosts match exactly. Budgets keep their summing rule. Inference costs nothing extra to write, because arguments come from constants already in the calls.

What remains. Run-time mediation adds one check per mediated file or network call, only in a dependency whose grant is narrower than its row. Its cost is not measured; the mitigation is that a dependency whose row is statically covered pays nothing.

Census over Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools, Examples and tests. Argued rows in Jet source today are memory budgets, such as !Mem.Alloc(above: N) in 13 rows, and Fail with an error type. No program writes a scoped FS or Net row, so no program changes meaning; grants with arguments are new.

The same program under every option is templ, a library that reads templates/ and calls api.example.com, and a shop that grants it exactly that. Each option shows templ's row.

Beginner path. Write no rows at all: they are inferred, and jet check shows what each dependency may do, folder and host included. Expert path. Write a scope in a grant or a denial, or declare a library effect whose fields use fs.Path or net.Host.

Other options. B allows arguments only in grants and denials, never in rows, checked only at run time, as Deno does. C keeps today's form: arguments only on memory budgets, and scoping by a run flag. D lets each effect define its own covers function in ordinary code. E keeps DECL-TYPES1 as ratified: constant arguments matched by equality only.

B gives up build-time checking of what a dependency may do. C cannot name a folder in a grant. D runs library code to decide coverage, which has no guaranteed laws and may not terminate. E cannot say that templates/ covers templates/home.html, so every file would need its own grant.

decisions.title: A build target is an ordinary Core type that implements Machine, so a package can add a board
decisions.situation:
A target describes the machine a build is for: its instruction set, memory, and services such as a clock or a serial port. Today the compiler holds a fixed table of machines, and a package names one by a string. A board the table lacks cannot be added by a package, and one table board quietly builds code for the wrong chip.

The owner asked for a target to be an ordinary Core type implementing a trait, declared by a library. That changes an earlier ruling, which made targets typed modules; keeping that ruling is option C. We recommend A: a board is a type implementing Machine, with one checked record of facts.

One limit holds under every option: a package can describe a board, but a chip family needs a code generator inside the compiler. Jet has two today, x86-64 and WebAssembly.
decisions.gist: Should a build target be a type implementing Machine, with one typed facts record, so a package can add a board?
decisions.lesson: Programs for small devices must know the machine: how much memory it has, whether it has a clock, how it reports a crash. This vote decides how that machine is described, so a board maker can ship it as an ordinary package instead of waiting for a compiler change.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A target is the machine a build is for. A fact is one thing known about it, such as its pointer size. A service is something the machine provides, such as a clock; its provider is the function that does it.

An emitter is the part of the compiler that writes machine code for one instruction set. A denial forbids an effect for a build.
decisions.story: Kofi's company makes an x86-64 sensor gateway and an Arm sensor board. Today he asks the Jet team to add each to the compiler's table. Under A he publishes acme with both types, and jet check validates every fact. His customers build the gateway today, and the board build stops with a clear message until Jet has an Arm code generator.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How a target is declared and selected, and the one record of facts every option shares. What each fact means stays as ratified in D-FREESTAND-FACTS1, D-TARGET-ALLOC1, D-TARGET-MEMORY1, D-TARGET-LINKER1 and D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1.

Today, with the t6c compiler on dev 76955986d0. Probe pkg_lib selects the profile board.sensor_v1, whose table triple is thumbv7em-none-eabihf, and builds an x86-64 ELF file. Its first bytes are 7f 45 4c 46 and its machine field is 0x3e. The board's facts do not reach code generation. Examples' package files spell profiles in a second vocabulary, web.no_os against the driver's wasm.no-os.

Probe t_web builds with --target web and now prints words Web, as D-BUILD-TOOLCHAIN1=A requires. The seed printed words Linux; that building bug is fixed on dev.

Probes p6 to p8 show the shape A uses already works for user traits. p6 prints a struct's trait constants, thumbv7em-none-eabihf 32 32 32. p7 prints 32 64 with a default constant. p8 leaves a required constant out and gets E0933, MissingTraitConstant.

The rule under A. core.target declares the trait Machine with one required constant, facts, of type MachineFacts. A target is a struct with no fields that implements Machine. Core declares its own machines this way, the host machines and web among them, and a package declares a board the same way.

A package selects a machine by type in targets:, and code reads it as build.target, spelled as D-META-HASH1 ratifies. Hosted single-file programs never name a machine, as D-TARGET-SURFACE1 requires: the host machine is implied.

The record. MachineFacts maps one to one onto the compiler's TargetMachine record today. Required: triple, os, layout, allocator and panic. layout carries pointer and word size, cache line, endianness and atomic width, and is checked against the triple's ABI rather than assumed. os is one of the owner's #6206 list: Linux, MacOS, Windows, Web, Wasm or Freestanding.

The rest default to absent. Machine parts: memory regions, linker input, MMIO, volatile access, startup entry, vectors and placement. Services: the wall and monotonic clocks, zone data, sleep, entropy, scheduler and byte sink read, write and report. Host features: sockets, files, processes, environment, browser DOM, GPU and FFI. Hardware facts, programmers and audit carry over.

Today's HostedDefault arms are gone. Core's host machines state each service explicitly, so no fact is hidden behind a default. This one record is the #6206 c24 capability union, declared once, so no second closed list exists.

Providers. A present service names a provider function, as provider(uart_write). The compiler fills in the rest of D-FREESTAND-FACTS1's contract. Identity is the function's full path, and the digest and provenance come from its package's locked digest. ABI and limits come from the function's signature and declared limits.

A bad provider is today's E3312. A missing allocator is E3303, a missing or host-only service E3311, MMIO E3313, and every other missing fact E3314. Those codes and their texts exist today.

Denials. Each absent service becomes a denial for that build, per D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1. No allocator denies Mem.Alloc; no sockets, Net; no files, FS; no entropy, Rand; no sleep, Time.Wait; no processes, Exec; no environment, Env. Browser is present only on Web.

Partial services are checked per operation, as the compiler does today. A board with a write-only byte sink allows print and refuses a read with E3311 at that line, naming the machine and the missing service. One clock allows only its own reads.

Staging. Each artifact's code and every #if in it see that artifact's build.target. Build code also reads build.target as the target, and reads the machine it runs on as build.host, per D-BUILD-TOOLCHAIN1. A machine is checked when its package is checked, even if no application selects it.

Scope. A package may declare a machine for any triple Jet's layout table knows, Arm and AArch64 included, and jet check validates it. Building a machine whose triple has no emitter stops before code generation. A new registered error beside E3302 names the triple and the emitters Jet has: x86-64 and Wasm today. So pkg_lib's silent x86-64 build becomes that stop.

Census of the cutover on dev, Jet sources only. Six package.jet files in Examples/LowLevel/Embedded name a profile by string. Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Target/TargetMachine.jet builds the machines from literals. The driver's list, the loader, the checker, Jetpack's Targets.jet parser, the embedded battery and Flash.jet read those names. 129 $build reads in 57 files keep working, respelled with HASH1.

Beginner path. Write nothing: a single-file program builds for the host. To build for a board, add one line to package.jet naming the board's type, and errors name the machine and the missing service.

Expert path. Declare a board as a struct implementing Machine with one MachineFacts record. Share a pure function that builds the record when several boards differ in one fact. Check the package with jet check, and every fact is validated before any application selects it.

Downsides of A, and what the design does about them. Each configuration is its own type. A pure facts builder shared by several types keeps each one three lines long, and D is the option that takes configuration as a value.

The trait is named Machine, not the steer's Target. Target already names Core's codegen-family enum (Lang.jet:193) and the declaration every marker expansion receives (Core/Compiler/Compiler.jet:39). Another meaning would collide in every marker body, and probe p4b shows a user trait named Target beside #Target(Web) checks with no warning. A amends D-TARGET-SURFACE1's module wording; option C keeps it.

What remains. No option can add an instruction set from a package: a chip family needs an emitter in the compiler. Under A the board is declared and checked anyway, and the build stop names the missing emitter. Deriving each provider's digest from the lock is compiler work, reusing digests the lock already records.

Other options. B adds a target keyword whose braces hold the same record. C keeps the ratified typed module with a facts field. D takes a value of a type implementing Machine, with facts(self), so boards are configured by fields. E keeps today's compiler table selected by name, as Swift's closed platform list does.

Their best cases. B reads like a declaration of its own and can lower to A's checks. C needs no amendment and checks the module when its package is checked. D configures a board without a type per configuration, at the cost of putting the value into build cache keys. E needs no work.

options.detail: A target is a struct with no fields that implements core.target.Machine, whose one required constant is a MachineFacts record. A package selects it by type.
options.technical: Amends D-TARGET-SURFACE1=A's module wording. MachineFacts maps TargetMachine one to one; triple, os, layout, allocator and panic are required, the rest absent by default. Providers get identity and digest from the lock. Denials per EFFTYPE-TARGET1, per-operation checks for partial services. Any layout-known triple may be declared; building one with no emitter is a registered stop naming the triple.

recommendation.why: A lets a board maker ship a machine as an ordinary package. It adds no keyword and checks every fact before any application selects it.

One MachineFacts record replaces the table and both name lists.
A missing fact is today's E0933, and a missing service names the machine.

losses.loss: A package cannot add an instruction set or a GPU; this holds under every option.
losses.mitigation: The board is still declared and checked, and the build stop names the triple and the emitters Jet has.

losses.loss: Each board configuration is its own type.
losses.mitigation: A shared pure facts builder keeps each type three lines long.

whyNot.reason: B adds a reserved word for what a trait already says.
C keeps machines out of the type system, so generic code cannot take one.
D puts a value into every build cache key and evaluates it to know the machine.
E keeps every board inside the compiler.

recommendation.tradeoff: One trait name, Machine, and one type per board, in return for boards that arrive as packages.

decisions.title: What an entry function does when Jet calls it
decisions.situation: An entry function is code Jet calls for one command, such as `fn dev` for `jet dev` or `fn test` for `jet test`. Today a bare `fn dev()` replaces the program, and a test entry that forgets to start the tests still passes. The vote decides whether an entry only sets values, must take over the work, or sets values and takes over only when asked. We recommend the last, so `jet dev` always runs your program (`fn run`, or the entry of the output you picked) and the tests always run once.
decisions.gist: Should an entry function only set values, take over the work, or set values and take over when asked?
decisions.lesson: An entry function is code Jet calls for one command. Every option makes a bare `fn dev()` an error whose fix shows `fn dev(d: Dev)`. With no `fn dev`, `jet dev` serves an App or web build with live reload, or restarts the program on save. In A and B, `fn build(b: Build)` returns nothing and names its default with `b.default(app)`. C keeps returning a plan.
decisions.story: Mia builds a small web app. She types `jet dev`, clicks the link, and tests in the browser. Later she wants port 8080 every time, so she writes `fn dev(d: Dev) { d.port(8080); d.watch(true) }` in `@dev.jet` or any root file. Her teammate Noor needs golden files unpacked before the tests and a JUnit report written after them. Both needs should fit one entry shape, with no wrapper script and no way to skip the tests by mistake.
decisions.detail:
Scope. This ballot decides the shape of an entry function and states what `jet dev` does with no `fn dev`. Sibling ballots on card c07glrub decide the rest. D-TARGET-ONE1 decides where outputs are declared. D-SETTING-ORDER1 decides setting rows, the one precedence order, and ports. D-ENTRY-NAMES1 decides type names. D-DEV-STATE1 decides kept values across restarts, and D-DEV-SERVICES1 decides local services.

No entry for run and check. `jet run` and `jet check` have no entry function. Their setting rows have two layers, package.jet and flag, which satisfies #4913 (no CLI-only or config-only options). The dev handle is the code form of the dev session's rows.

Settled by the owner on 2026-10-19, not voted. The handle types are `Build`, `Dev` and `Test`. `fn run` is the program, and `fn dev` always runs it. So in every option a bare `fn dev()` or `fn test()` without the handle is a registered error. Its fix shows `fn dev(d: Dev)` or `fn test(t: Test)`. There is no longer a way for dev to replace run.

Shared rule in every option. A direct call to the program's `fn run` inside `fn dev` or `fn test` is a registered error. It would run the program a second time. In option A the fix names `d.run()`.

Where entries run. `fn dev` and `fn test` are ordinary runtime code, compiled on the normal build path at O0, as `fn test(suite: TestSuite)` is today. `Dev` and `Test` are prelude-owned handles, and the session logic lives in the prelude and core library (I9). Only `fn build` runs at compile time. So no new compile-time effect rules apply to dev or test; this ballot does not change D-CTEFFECT1.

Process model. The one process model for the slate is in option A's technical note and holds for every option. D-DEV-STATE1 and D-DEV-SERVICES1 refer to it. Its core: the `jet` tool process holds the `#Persist` store and the local-service supervisor. The compiled `fn dev` session runs the program as its child, and editing program code restarts only the child.

Outputs. One `fn dev` configures the whole dev session for whichever output was picked. `d.output()` returns the picked output's name so code can branch. `t.run()` runs every selected check once. The word output means something a project makes; target means only the platform, as in `#Target(Web)`.

Build entry in options A and B. `fn build(b: Build)` returns nothing. A failing build entry writes `fn build(b: Build) !BuildError`. Jet seals the plan when the entry returns, and `jet inspect build` and `core.build.graph` read the sealed plan. `b.default(app)` names the default output and replaces `return b.plan(default: app)`. Package `defaults:` stays as the data form of the same setting, per D-TARGET-ONE1 and D-SETTING-ORDER1.

Root run first. A root `fn run` still runs first for bare `jet run` and `jet dev`; the default picks only when no root `fn run` exists. This is ratified D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1 and D-DX-ENTRY1, and this ballot does not change it.

Magic default with no `fn dev`, three rows checked in order. First, `fn run` returns `App`: Jet serves it with browser live reload and shows errors in the page. Second, the picked output's platform is web, resolved in the one settings order (`--target=web`, an output's `os: web` in code or data, package `target:`, `#Target(Web)`). Then Jet serves the wasm build with live reload. Third, anything else: Jet restarts the program on save.

Local services that are on in the dev environment start first, and Jet waits until they are ready.

The three rows match today's dispatch order after the `fn dev()` check. The App row is `entry_returns_app` at Source/main.rs:4216. The web row is Source/main.rs:4235, and the restart row is Source/main.rs:4250. So the magic default is today's stock behavior with the replace-the-program path removed.

First run and the ladder. The first `jet dev` prints one line, for example `run.jet returns App → serving http://127.0.0.1:8080 · live reload · customize: jet explain dev`. `jet explain dev` prints the effective `fn dev` for this project as Jet source, which a user can paste into `@dev.jet`. `--show-default` keeps its meaning: ignore the entry, run the stock default, and say so.

Reload boundary. Saving program code restarts the program only, as D-EXEC2=A requires. Saving `fn dev`, code it calls, or the env definition ends the session. Code after `d.run()` runs as cleanup, then Jet enters `fn dev` again. A second Ctrl-C during cleanup stops at once and names the cleanup it skipped.

Today in code. Source/main.rs:4191-4215 runs a top-level `fn dev()` first, and Source/CmdCompile.rs:4605-4612 compiles it as the program's real entry point. The `@dev.jet` template at Source/CmdCompile.rs:5526 says a `fn dev` replaces the stock default. The `@test.jet` template at Source/CmdCompile.rs:5530 writes `fn test(suite: TestSuite) { suite.run() }`. The suite value is crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CommandSuite.rs.

E1254 (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/DiagnosticRows.jet:12055-12068) says project `jet dev` runs `fn dev()` if present, else `fn run()`, and its fix suggests a bare `fn dev()`. Its meaning and fix text change: the fix names `fn run`, and `fn dev(d: Dev)` for settings.

Counts, by search for `^fn dev\s*\(` and `^fn test\s*\(` over tests, Examples and Core on 2026-10-19. There are 32 files with a top-level bare `fn dev()`. Most start `core.web.devserver` by hand or print a marker for a test. There are 6 files with `fn test(suite: TestSuite)`, including Examples/features/devloop/test_override.jet. These counts measure repository sites only, not users.

Amends D-CMD-OVERRIDE1=C: the test entry sets values by default and runs the suite at return unless it calls `t.run()`. A no-parameter override becomes an error instead of a full replacement. The recorded loss, an override that skips work and prints green, is removed because the suite always runs once. `--show-default` keeps its meaning. The handle name `Test` comes from D-ENTRY-NAMES1.

Amends D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1=D: `jet dev` still runs inside env(base + env.dev) and `jet env` still never runs project code. But `jet dev` now runs `fn dev(d: Dev)`, which sets values and wraps the program, and the fallback is the magic default above. E1254 text changes to match.

Under options A and B, amends D-BUILDENTRY1=B: the signature `fn build(b: BuildContext) -> BuildPlan ?` becomes `fn build(b: Build)`, optionally `!BuildError`, with the plan sealed at return. Under A and B, amends D-BUILDTARGET1=A: `return b.plan(default: app)` becomes `b.default(app)`, and `b.plan()` is removed. Option C keeps both as ratified, apart from the owner-settled handle name.

D-JAI-CONFIG1 (open) was rewritten on 2026-10-19 to the slate's terms (outputs, `BuildOptions`, `b.default`, no exact-options rule). Its change calls work until `fn build` returns, which is when every option here seals the plan.

Also amends the owner direction of 2026-07-01 recorded at Source/main.rs:4191, which made `fn dev()` the program's real entry point. Unchanged and relied on: D-EXEC2=A (restart only, no hot swap), D-RUN-WATCH1=A, D-WEBDEFAULT1=A (the web row uses its order), D-JOB-SUBCMD1=C, D-CLAIM-BENCH1=A. Also relied on: D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1 and D-DX-ENTRY1 for root `fn run` first (D-TARGET-ONE1 amends their default spelling and `defaults.dev`). D-DEVMODE1: amended by D-DEV-STATE1 if its option A wins; this ballot adds no further change to it.

Research, right ways. Go 1.15 removed the required `os.Exit` in `TestMain`: if it returns, Go exits with the result of `m.Run` (https://go.dev/doc/go1.15). The lesson is that the tool should finish a closing step users forget. Option A applies the same idea to the start step. pytest yield fixtures put cleanup after `yield`, which is the same split as code after `t.run()`.

Research, more right ways. Zig's `pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void` returns nothing, and the runner acts on the declared graph after it returns (https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/). That is the build shape of options A and B. Vite configures its dev server by values and sends everything else to plugin hooks (https://vite.dev/config/server-options). That is option B, and it needs a hook API for every new need.

Research, wrong ways. A full replacement entry lets dev run code that differs from run. Today's bare `fn dev()` does this, and owner direction now forbids it. A run-it-yourself entry with no default lets a forgotten call skip the work. D-CMD-OVERRIDE1 recorded this as its loss, and Go's pre-1.15 `os.Exit` rule had the same class of mistake. Fixed hook lists were rejected in D-CMD-OVERRIDE1 option D because new needs wait for new hooks.

Cutover. Migrate the 32 bare `fn dev()` files: web ones become `fn run() -> App` or the web platform row, and settings move to `fn dev(d: Dev)`. Migrate the 6 `fn test(suite: TestSuite)` files to `fn test(t: Test)`. Update the four `@*.jet` templates and the Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Host.jet templates. Update E1254 and E3501 text, run_dev_entry, has_dev_entry_fn, and the test override path. Update the spec and every `fn build(...) -> BuildPlan` site. Register new errors under I7.

Review: one fresh combined pass (beginner + adversarial), agent SlateReview, Claude family, 2026-10-19, per owner directive for one review. Repaired: surface shows the build shape, bare `fn dev()` error and magic default; title, B charge, process model, `run()` edge cases, `d.output()`, output wording, root-run rule, trim. Cohesion pass CohesionReview 2026-10-19 repaired: D-JAI-CONFIG1 reference, amendment wording, web default per output, test example, dev environment wording.

options.name: Set values, take over when asked
options.detail:
The entry sets values on its handle. When the entry returns, Jet runs the work exactly once with those values. For `jet dev` the work is the dev session around your program. For `jet test` the work is every selected check.

An entry that needs code around the work calls `d.run()` or `t.run()` once. The work runs at that point instead of at return. A setting call after `run()` is an error. Code after `run()` runs when the work ends: after the suite for tests, and after the first Ctrl-C for a dev session.

Gains: the owner's two-line example works as written, setup and cleanup stay possible, and the suite can never be skipped. Loss: one entry has two shapes, which the error text and `jet explain dev` teach.
options.technical:
`Dev` and `Test` are prelude-owned handles. `fn dev` and `fn test` compile as ordinary runtime code on the normal build path, like `fn test(suite: TestSuite)` today. If no call to `run()` has happened when the entry returns, the runtime makes it. A second `run()` call and a setting call after `run()` stop with a registered error naming the call.

`fn dev` and the program compile into one O0 binary. The `jet` tool process holds the `#Persist` store and the local-service supervisor. It runs the compiled `fn dev` session, which runs the program as its child. Editing program code restarts only the child. Editing `fn dev` or the env definition ends the session and starts it again; the `jet` process stays, so kept values and running services survive. Ctrl-C ends everything.

`d.run()` returns when the session ends and gives no value. An entry that fails before `run()` stops `jet dev` with its error; the program never starts. `t.run()` runs every selected check once and returns the results, so a report can follow it.

One `fn dev` configures the whole dev session for whichever output was picked. `d.output()` returns the picked output's name so code can branch. `fn build(b: Build)` returns nothing, and Jet seals the build plan at return.

options.name: Set values only, with hooks
options.detail:
The entry only sets values, and Jet always runs the work after the entry returns. There is no `run()` call, so hooks are the only way to put code around the work. Option A may also have a `t.before` setting row, but it adds `run()` for code around the work. Setup and cleanup use named hooks that take functions: `t.before(unpack_golden)`, `t.after(remove_golden)`, and `d.before(seed_demo)`. An after-hook receives the results, so a report can be written there.

Gains: every entry reads as a short list of values, and Jet always controls the order. Losses: each new setup need waits for Jet to add a hook, and today's test entries must be rewritten as hooks.
options.technical: `Dev` and `Test` gain hook methods that store function references. The runtime calls before-hooks, runs the work, then calls after-hooks with the results. The hook list is fixed by Jet and grows only by new decisions. The handles still compile as ordinary runtime code, under the same process model as option A. `fn build(b: Build)` returns nothing, and Jet seals the build plan at return.

options.name: Entry takes over, `run()` required
options.detail:
The entry drives the work. It must call `d.run()` or `t.run()` exactly once on every path, and a missing call is an error. `fn build` keeps returning a plan with `return b.plan(default: app)`. This is today's test entry rule, made strict so a forgotten call cannot pass.

Gains: the order of every step is visible in code, and it matches Go's `TestMain`. Losses: the owner's example `fn dev(d: Dev) { d.port(8080); d.watch(true) }` is an error until `d.run()` is added, and every beginner entry carries that extra line.
options.technical: The checker requires exactly one `run()` call on every path through the entry, like a definite-assignment check. The build entry keeps the returned plan value and `return b.plan(default: app)`. `Dev` and `Test` are prelude-owned handles compiled as ordinary runtime code, under the same process model as option A.

comparisons.note: `TestMain` receives the test run as a value and wraps it. Go 1.15 stopped requiring the final `os.Exit` call: if `TestMain` returns, Go exits with the result of `m.Run`. The tool finishes the step users forget. Source: https://go.dev/doc/go1.15.

A yield fixture runs setup before `yield` and cleanup after it, when the tests end. It is the same split as code before and after `t.run()`. Source: https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/fixtures.html.

`build.zig` declares the graph and returns nothing. The build runner then runs the steps the command asked for. This is the shape of `fn build(b: Build)` in options A and B. Source: https://ziglang.org/learn/build-system/.

The dev server takes plain values in a config file. Anything beyond those values goes through plugin hooks such as `configureServer`. This is the shape of option B. Source: https://vite.dev/config/server-options.

recommendation.why: Beginners write only values, and experts add one `run()` call for setup and cleanup. The work always runs once, so tests cannot be skipped.
gains: The owner's example and today's test setup both work.
A forgotten `run()` can no longer skip the tests.

losses.loss: One entry has two shapes: with and without `run()`.
losses.mitigation: A setting after `run()` is an error that states the rule. `jet explain dev` prints the short shape.

whyNot.reason: Each new setup need waits for Jet to add a hook.
It turns the owner's own two-line example into an error and adds a line every beginner must learn.

recommendation.tradeoff: Experts learn one rule about `run()`. Beginners never need it.
