decisions.title: Memory marks live in signatures only; calls carry no & or ^
decisions.situation: Today a Jet call repeats what the called function's signature already says. An argument the function edits carries &, so you write grow(&c). A method that edits its receiver was ratified to need no mark, but the compiler still demands &values.push(3). A take carries ^ in four special cases and not at a last use. You said marks at every call are ugly, tedious and distracting, and that the split rule is hard to teach. We recommend one rule: the signature says what happens, and calls carry no marks.
decisions.gist: Should & and ^ appear only in function signatures, so every call is written plainly?
decisions.lesson: A function's signature already says whether it edits or takes each input. Writing the same mark again at every call repeats that fact about 105,000 times in Jet's code. Under this rule the signature carries the mark, calls look like reads, and the editor shows the marks as faint hints.
decisions.story: Mia writes scores.push(10) and bump(score), with no marks, exactly as she would in Python. Her editor shows a faint & before score. When she declares score :: 0 by mistake, the error says bump edits its input and score is fixed, and offers score := 0.

decisions.detail:
WHAT YOU ASKED

On 2026-11-06 you said marks belong in declarations, that marks at every call are ugly, tedious and distracting, and that a split rule is hard to teach. The full proposal, with counts and examples, is Docs/proposals/2026-11-06-memory-marks-in-signatures.md.

TODAY

D-CALLSITE-MARK1=A keeps & on edited arguments and drops ^ at a last use, except for four kinds of take. D-RECEIVER-MARK1=A drops & on receivers, but that is not built: the compiler still reports E0224. D-COPY-MOVE-SPELL1=A spells an early move x.move(), also not built.

Counts on dev b486d6c09a: 69,758 & marks on arguments, about 29,800 on receivers, 4,222 ^ on arguments, about 1,230 ^ in value positions. Signatures hold 14,246 & and 3,147 ^ marks.

THE RULE UNDER A

A signature says what a function does to each input: fn bump(c: &Counter), fn seal(^self). Every call is plain: bump(score), items.push(3), buf.seal(). A mark stays only where no signature decides. Those places are a write window bound to a name (edit :: &values[2..3]), a match that writes into its subject (if &shape == { … }), and a task that takes a name.

An early move is x.move(), as already ratified, and the ^x value form retires. A part of a list passed to a writing parameter becomes a write window by itself.

WHAT STAYS CHECKED

Safety never depended on the call mark. A call that edits a value needs a changeable value, declared := or received as a & parameter. Two overlapping inputs, one edited, stay an error. A value used after a call took it is an error that names the call, with the fix x.copy() or a reorder. A call never copies on its own.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Seeing changes in plain text. The editor shows & and ^ as faint hints at each call, and the language server underlines a changed argument. In the terminal, jet audit writes lists every call that edits or takes a named value, as jet audit copies lists copies.

2. Teams that want marks in text. #Policy(writes: .Explicit), already ratified for receivers, extends to arguments. It requires the marks everywhere, with a Safe fix that inserts them. No new mechanism is added.

3. A value with cleanup closing at a plain call. The take is in the signature and shown as a hint, and any later use is an error naming the closing call.

4. Errors losing the mark they pointed at. Each memory error quotes the signature line that causes it.

5. The cutover. The compiler knows every mark, so jet fix removes about 105,000 in one commit, with grammars, spec, examples and snapshots.

No loss remains.

EDGE CASES

- values.push(values.len()) stays legal: the length is read before the push writes.
- A function value keeps its marks in its type, fn(&Map), and is called plainly.
- A foreign function keeps its marks in its signature.

WHY NOT B OR C

B keeps today's split, which you called messy: arguments marked, receivers not, and four take cases marked. C marks every call again, which is the 105,000 repeated marks you called tedious.

decisions.title: && marks an input a function takes, and ^ becomes free
decisions.situation: A signature marks an input the function edits with & and one it takes for good with ^. You asked us to study && for taking instead, which would free ^. If marks move to signatures only, the take mark appears about 3,150 times in signatures and in tasks that take a name. Value positions already use x.move(). We recommend &&, because it pairs with &, matches C++'s move parameter, and avoids a dead key.
decisions.gist: Should a signature mark an input it takes with && instead of ^, freeing ^?
decisions.lesson: A function can borrow an input to change it, or take it for good. Jet marks the first with &. Marking the second with && makes the pair one family: & changes it, && keeps it. C++ already writes its move parameter as T&&.
decisions.story: Ravi reads fn close(file: &&GzFile) and guesses right away that close keeps the file, because && looks like a stronger &. On his German keyboard he no longer types ^ followed by a space.

Swift writes consuming, Mojo owned and Hylo sink for the same idea. Source: https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0377-parameter-ownership-modifiers.md
decisions.detail:
WHAT YOU ASKED

On 2026-11-06 you asked us to investigate & for editing and && for moving as prefix marks, judged on frequency, readability and intuitiveness. The full study is section 5 of Docs/proposals/2026-11-06-memory-marks-in-signatures.md.

FREQUENCY

On dev b486d6c09a, signatures hold 14,246 & marks and 3,147 ^ marks, so takes are 18% of signature marks. The rarer mark gets the longer symbol, which matches how often each is typed and read.

CLASHES

&& is also logical and, used 23,545 times. Under D-CALLSITE-MARK2=A the take mark appears only in a parameter type, before self, and after the word task. Logical and always sits between two values. No && appears in any type today, so the parser and the reader never meet both meanings in one place.

If calls keep marks (D-CALLSITE-MARK2 B or C), f(&&x) becomes possible beside a && b. In that case && is a weaker choice, and B or C on this ballot fits better.

READABILITY AND INTUITION

& reads as this function changes it, and && as more than that: it keeps it. C++ programmers already link && with moving. In Rust &&T is a reference to a reference, but Jet has no reference types, so that reading has nothing to attach to. Hover text says takes the value.

TYPING

^ is a dead key on German, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Swiss and Nordic keyboards: it waits for the next key, so ^self needs an extra space. && is one key pressed twice on every common layout.

FREEING ^

With && for takes and x.move() in value positions, ^ has no meaning left. Under D-SIGIL-FREED2 a freed symbol stays an error until a new ballot gives it a job.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Two meanings of &&. Kept apart by position, and the editor colours them differently. A take mark can never start an expression, so a b &&c typo still means and.

2. Two keystrokes. Takes are 18% of marks, and ^ already costs two keystrokes on most non-US keyboards.

3. Rust's double reference. Jet has no storable reference type, so there is nothing to confuse it with.

No loss remains.

EDGE CASES

- task &&job { … } takes job into the task.
- fn(&&Map) is a function type that takes its input.
- A foreign function writes file: &&GzFile, as it writes file: ^GzFile today.
- An early move inside an expression stays x.move().

A taken parameter is marked consuming. Source: SE-0377

gains: One family of marks: & changes, && keeps.
Frees ^ for a later use.
No dead key on European keyboards.

losses.mitigation: The take mark only appears in signatures and after task, never between two values.

C keeps ^ taken and keeps the dead key on many keyboards.

decisions.title: Every declaration is written name: value
decisions.situation: Jet writes a constant as limit :: 100, a function as fn area(…), and a type as struct Point { … }. Package files, struct literals, named arguments and fields already write name: value. You asked for name: value everywhere: fewer characters, a feel closer to Python, a natural configuration language like Lua or Nix, and one shape for every declaration. We recommend writing every declaration that way, with := still marking a value you may change.
decisions.gist: Should every declaration, from constants to functions, types and modules, be written name: value?
decisions.lesson: Jet already writes name: value in package files, struct literals and named arguments. Source files use :: for constants and keywords first for functions and types. Under A every declaration reads the same: the name, a colon, then what it is. A value you may change still uses :=.
decisions.story: Lena opens a Jet file for the first time. limit: 100, area: fn(r: Float) -> Float, Point: struct { x: Int, y: Int }: every line starts with the name she is looking for. Her deploy settings file reads the same, so she never learns a second format.

JavaScript objects and JSON write name: value. Nix and Lua write name = value for settings and functions alike. Source: https://nix.dev/manual/nix/2.24/language/
decisions.detail:
WHAT YOU ASKED

On 2026-11-06 you asked for name: value instead of name :: value, for constants, functions and modules, with example files and every downside designed away. The full proposal with five complete example files is Docs/proposals/2026-11-06-colon-declarations.md.

THE RULE UNDER A

Everything that introduces a name is written name: value; a value you may change is name := value. limit: 100. area: fn(r: Float) -> Float { … }. Point: struct { x: Int, y: Int }. Mode: enum { Fast, Safe }. Shape: trait { area: fn(self) -> Float }. math: module { … }. int_cache: cache<Int>(32). use process: core.process. package: { name: "x" }.

Kind parameters go on the kind word, never on the name: first: fn<T>(xs: [T]) -> T?, Box: struct<T> { value: T }, cache: module<K>(capacity: Int).

Inside the braces after struct, trait, enum or a foreign #Import module, name: Type describes what each value holds. Everywhere else, name: thing makes name that thing. The word before the brace always says which.

WHY

Package files, struct literals, named arguments and fields already write name: value, so source and settings become one language. :: came from Jai's x : Type : value; typed bindings are retired, so the type slot between the colons is gone.

Each of 141,892 :: bindings loses two characters. fn name(…) and name :: fn(…) are two ways to write a function today (891 uses of the second), and A makes them one.

HOW A'S DOWNSIDES ARE DESIGNED AWAY

1. Readers from TypeScript, Python or Rust read x: T as a type. In Jet a declaration has no separate type, so name: thing always declares. Where thing is a type, the familiar reading is right. Where it is a value, limit: 100, a type reading is impossible, so nobody misreads it silently.

2. { a: 1 } as block or record. A brace group whose entries are all name: value is a record. A block that only binds names produces nothing, so no meaningful program changes.

3. x: Int at file level makes an alias, as x :: Int does today. Using it as a number gets a registered error with the fix x: Int{0}.

4. Foreign functions have no body. Inside a foreign module every entry is a signature with its symbol, as today. At file level a bodiless fn(…) is a function type, as on the right of :: today.

5. Searching for a definition. fn area becomes area:, still one search; outlines and go-to-definition read the parser.

6. Headers grow by one character: fn run() is 8, run: fn() is 9. Bindings save two characters each and outnumber headers, and every name starts at the left margin.

7. The cutover. About 225,000 declaration lines change. jet fix rewrites them from the parse tree in one commit, with grammars, registry, spec, examples and snapshots. Meaning does not change, so the run-time tests prove the rewrite.

EDGE CASES

- impl blocks and #Test blocks introduce no name and keep their form.
- An associated type is Output: type in a trait and Output: T in an impl.
- A name: fn binding may call itself, at file level and inside a function.
- String interpolation such as {x:Debug} is unchanged.

WHY NOT B OR C

decisions.title: A test that reads files or env vars, through Jet or through foreign code, is reused while what it read is unchanged
decisions.situation: jet test will keep each passing test row in a result store (#6035) and skip it on rerun while nothing it depends on changed. A test that reads a file or an env var always reruns, because the store cannot see those inputs. Go records the reads its own library makes, but not reads made by C code. The vote decides if Jet records reads, including foreign code's. We recommend yes, with no new flag.
decisions.gist: May a test that reads files or env vars, even through C code, be reused when what it read is unchanged?
decisions.lesson: A result is safe to reuse only if every input is unchanged. Jet's effect rows already say which tests can touch files or env vars. Test builds can note every read, whether Jet code or a C library makes it. The reused row then carries the exact list of what it read.
decisions.story: Ana's package has 300 tests that read fixtures from testdata/. Forty of them open a SQLite fixture through core.db, which is C code underneath. Every `jet test` reruns all 300, though she changed one file. With reads recorded, only the 4 tests that read that file rerun. The rest print `pass (cached)`.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0slmlyv (#6064), split from #6035 as open question Q7 (owner asked to card it, 2026-10-28). Audit/drafts4/BEST-IN-CLASS.md row Result caching marks file and env rows LOSES to Go. The owner rejected v1 because its loss stood: rows that call foreign code never reused. v2 records those reads too.

How foreign reads are seen. An extern whose declared row has no FS or Env reads nothing, so it reuses like pure code. That covers most foreign code, such as math, compression and hashing. For one that may read, the test build routes the C library's file calls through the recorder, as sanitizers intercept calls. So SQLite opening testdata/app.db is recorded like `files.read`.

Why it is sound. On Linux, a syscall filter checks where each file syscall comes from. A file syscall that bypasses the recorder marks the row unseen, and it reruns with the reason shown. On macOS and Windows the recorder sits in the lowest system library, libSystem or ntdll. Neither platform supports raw syscalls, which is why Go moved to libSystem. C code can read `environ` without a call, so an env read by foreign code keys on the whole environment.

What still reruns, and why. Rows with Net, Clock, Random or Process rerun. Their inputs are a server, the time, a seed or a child, none of which the store can hash. That is the meaning of those effects, not a gap in recording. A `.case` row starts processes, so it reruns, as in Go.

Cost. The recorder exists only in test builds; normal and release builds are unchanged. Jet's own reads are recorded at the Core route layer. Foreign reads cost one extra call per open or stat in tests. Hashing reads each recorded file once per run, the same work as Go's test cache.

How it reads with other ballots. `fresh` is an existing jet test flag that PLAN-6035 makes a row: `--fresh`, `fresh: true`, `.fresh(true)`. Under D-TEST-PROFILE1 A, `fresh: true` sits in a package.jet profile; under B it is a `TestProfile` field in test.jet; under C it is the flag. Under D-TEST-MUTFUZZ1, mutant and generated rows never reuse, since each run is new work.

Probes on the dev jet are in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/rd2. `jet check run.jet` is ok, and `jet test` passes both tests, the second through core.db's SQLite. probe/rd2mk builds the fixture database. `jet test --fresh` prints the fresh-run note today. The `(cached)` lines and `--explain-reuse` are proposed; no store exists today (spec.md:3528).

Adversarial pass. Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: BallotDesign (fresh pass). It attacked C code that reads `environ`, makes raw syscalls or maps a file. v2 keys on the whole environment, reruns rows Linux flags, and never stores a file changed mid-run.

options.name: Yes, always, foreign code included
options.detail:
A row whose effect row holds only FS and Env, beyond pure work, is eligible, whether the reads come from Jet or foreign code. While it runs, each read is recorded with a hash of what was returned, including a missing file. The next run reuses the stored pass when every recorded read still matches.

Rows with Net, Clock, Random or Process always rerun. `fresh` (flag, profile field, method) bypasses the store as today.
options.technical:
Adds a read log to the #6035 S4 store entry: (kind, path or name, content hash or absent). Jet reads are recorded in Core Files and Sys at the runtime route layer, under jet test only. Directory listings record a hash of the sorted names. A file that changes during the run is not stored. No new settings row.

Foreign reads: test builds link interceptors for the C library's open, openat, fopen, stat and opendir, as ASan does, at libSystem on macOS and ntdll on Windows. On Linux a seccomp filter compares each file syscall's instruction pointer to the recorder's own call sites; any other caller marks the row unseen. Env read by foreign code keys on the whole environment.

options.name: Opt in per profile
options.detail: The recorder and eligibility rules match A, foreign code included, but they switch on only under a profile, or a run, with `reuse_reads: true`. Stock is false, so a bare `jet test` reruns every file and env test.

options.name: No, always rerun
options.detail: The #6035 store reuses a row only when its effect row holds none of FS, Env, Net, Clock, Random or Process. Fixture tests always run.
options.technical: No change to the #6035 S4 store.

comparisons.note: go test caches results and records the files and env vars read through package os; reads made by cgo code are not recorded. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Test_packages
Bazel reuses a test result when its declared inputs match; undeclared files are absent in the sandbox. Source: https://bazel.build/remote/caching

gains: Fixture-heavy suites rerun in seconds, including database and C-library tests.
No new setting; `fresh` already exists.

whyNot.reason: B adds a row nearly everyone sets, and the plain path stays slow.
C leaves fixture tests slower than Go's for good.

recommendation.tradeoff: A read recorder in test builds buys exact reuse for every file and env test.

decisions.title: Core gets files.sync_filesystem: one durable flush for a whole tree of writes
decisions.gist: How does Jet code make a tree of many new files durable without one disk flush per file?
decisions.lesson: core.files.fsync makes one file durable. Writing a tree of thousands of files and calling fsync on each one costs a journal commit per file. sync_filesystem flushes the whole filesystem that holds a path in one call, so a writer can create every file, flush once, and only then publish the tree with a rename.
decisions.story: Jetpack installs a toolchain of about 1,900 files. Today it calls fsync on every file and directory before it publishes the tree, and a cold install takes 45 minutes on a normal ext4 disk. With sync_filesystem it writes every file, flushes once, and renames the finished tree into place. A crash before the flush still leaves no published tree, and the install takes a few minutes.
decisions.inWild: Linux has syncfs(2), which flushes one filesystem. Go exposes it as unix.Syncfs in golang.org/x/sys, and Rust as nix::unistd::syncfs or rustix::fs::syncfs; neither standard library has it. Python has os.sync(), which flushes every filesystem. Package managers either fsync per file, like dpkg, which sorts its writes so the commits batch, or skip durability, like pip and npm.
decisions.detail:
Option A adds one public function beside fsync in Core/Files/Files.jet: sync_filesystem(path) IOError! -[FS.Write]>. On Linux it calls syncfs(2) on the filesystem that holds path. Elsewhere it calls sync(2), which flushes every filesystem in one call. Where the host has neither, it returns IOError and the caller keeps per-file fsync. Jetpack writes every object, flushes once, and renames the tree into place. A failed flush fails the publish, so a crash never publishes a partial tree.

Option B adds a higher-level fsync_tree(dir) that fsyncs every file under dir from several threads at once, so the journal batches the commits. It adds no new kind of flush, but it still does one fsync per file, and its speed depends on the filesystem's batching.

Option C adds no API and keeps per-file fsync. A cold toolchain install stays at about 45 minutes, and the clean-clone proof (#6096 c65) stays near 2 hours.

options.name: Add sync_filesystem(path)
options.detail: One public Core function: a single flush of the filesystem that holds path (syncfs(2) on Linux, sync(2) elsewhere, IOError where neither exists). The store flushes once before its publish rename.
options.code:
use { files: core.files }

loop object in objects -> files.write(object.path, object.bytes) ?? return Err(err)
files.sync_filesystem(staging) ?? return Err(err)
files.rename(staging, published) ?? return Err(err)

options.name: Add fsync_tree(dir)
options.detail: One public Core function that fsyncs every file and directory under dir in parallel, so the journal can batch the commits. Still one fsync per file.
options.code:
use { files: core.files }

loop object in objects -> files.write(object.path, object.bytes) ?? return Err(err)
files.fsync_tree(staging) ?? return Err(err)
files.rename(staging, published) ?? return Err(err)

options.name: No new API
options.detail: Keep fsync per file. Installs stay slow.

recommendation.why: One call replaces thousands of journal commits, and the write-flush-rename order keeps the same crash guarantee. It maps directly to the operating system's own primitive.
recommendation.tradeoff: The flush also covers unrelated dirty data on the same filesystem, so one call can take longer than a single fsync on a busy disk.

whyNot.reason: It still does one flush per file; batching helps only on some filesystems and adds a thread pool to a file API.
A cold toolchain install stays at 45 minutes and dominates every clean-clone proof.

losses.loss: On hosts without syncfs(2), sync(2) flushes every filesystem, not just one.
losses.mitigation: It is still one call per publish, and the docs say which flush each host uses.

surface.gist: How does Jet code make a tree of many new files durable without one disk flush per file?
surface.lesson: fsync flushes one file. sync_filesystem flushes the whole filesystem holding a path in one call. Write every file, flush once, then publish with a rename.

whyNot.reason: Still one flush per file.
Installs stay at 45 minutes.

recommendation.tradeoff: A wider flush in exchange for one call.

decisions.title: Read and set this program's resource limits, and measure what a run used
decisions.situation: A Jet program can cap a child's CPU time, memory and open files, but it cannot read or set its own limits. It cannot turn off crash core dumps or cap a child's stack. After a run it learns CPU seconds but never the peak memory used. This vote decides how limits and usage appear in Core. We recommend the child-limit names Jet already uses, for this program too, and one usage record.
decisions.gist: How should a program read and set its own resource limits, and learn the CPU time and peak memory a run used?
decisions.lesson: A resource limit is a ceiling the operating system enforces, such as 4 GB of memory or no core dump after a crash. Usage is what a run actually took: CPU time and the most memory it ever held. Under A both use Jet's usual units: Duration for time and Int bytes for memory.
decisions.story: Ana's build tool runs 300 compiler jobs. It turns off core dumps once at start-up with `sys.set_core_file_limit(0, 0)`. After each job it prints `receipt.usage` peak memory in megabytes, so the job that grew to 9 GB is named in the report. The same code reads the same units on Linux and macOS.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: raw numbers per platform; ru_maxrss is KiB on Linux but bytes on macOS.
# https://docs.python.org/3/library/resource.html
import resource
resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_CORE, (0, 0))
print(resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_CHILDREN).ru_maxrss)
// Go: per-child usage on the finished process.
// https://pkg.go.dev/os#ProcessState.SysUsage
usage := cmd.ProcessState.SysUsage().(*syscall.Rusage)
decisions.detail:
Today. ProcessSpec already carries child limits: .cpu_time_limit(Duration), .memory_limit(Int) and .open_file_limit(Int) (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:1915-1932). Memory sizes are Int bytes, as for .output_limit. The spawn path installs these as kernel limits in the child (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/ProcessExecutionLimits.jet:2). It refuses a limit a target cannot enforce.

sys.times() returns CPU seconds for this program and its finished children (Core/Sys/Sys.jet:447). Nothing reads peak memory, nothing reads or sets this program's own limits, and children get no core-file or stack limit. Probe usage_today.jet prints the five times values; no call prints memory.

Who needs it. Tools/agent/cache/safe-jet.sh runs `ulimit -c 0` before every agent probe. release-compiler.mjs and s5-boundary.mjs wrap jobs in `prlimit --core=0 --stack=1073741824`. laneB and laneS read peak memory from the run. Card #5072 criterion 1 asks for get/set of AS, CPU, NOFILE and CORE, and getrusage with max RSS, user and system time.

What A says. Each limit keeps the name its ProcessSpec builder already has. The call sys.memory_limit() reads this program's soft and hard values, and None means unlimited. The call sys.set_memory_limit(soft, hard) sets them, and children inherit them as the OS does.

The same pair exists for cpu_time, open_file, core_file and stack. ProcessSpec gains .core_file_limit and .stack_limit beside its three limits, with the same refusal rule. CPU time is a Duration and every size is Int bytes, the types the builders use today.

One ResourceUsage record carries user time, system time and peak memory. sys.usage(.Self) and sys.usage(.Children) read it for this program. ProcessReceipt.usage carries the exact figure for one child.

Units and portability. Linux reports peak memory in KiB and macOS in bytes. Python exposes the raw field, and its own documentation warns about the difference; psutil exists partly to normalise it. Jet converts once in Core, so peak_memory is bytes everywhere.

Memory is the address-space limit on Linux, the limit ProcessSpec.memory_limit already sets. A target that cannot enforce a limit refuses with an IOError, never a silent no-op, as child limits do today. Windows has no per-process rlimits, so the setters refuse there. Usage works there through GetProcessTimes and the peak working set.

Per-child usage. wait4 already returns the child's rusage on the native runtime (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/HostProcess.jet:172). ProcessReceipt.usage copies numbers the kernel hands back. sys.usage(.Children) is the sum of all waited children, as the OS keeps it. The receipt field is the precise per-job number a pool needs.

Option B mirrors the C interface, as Python's resource module does: integer RLIMIT_* and RUSAGE_* constants, the RLIM_INFINITY sentinel, and the raw ru_* record. Every caller must handle per-platform units and sentinels, which is the mistake Python's documentation has to warn about.

Option C extends children only: the two new ProcessSpec limits and ProcessReceipt.usage, with no call for this program. It is smaller, but a program still cannot turn off its own core dumps or read its own peak memory. safe-jet.sh's `ulimit -c 0` would have no Jet form.

Research. Python resource (docs.python.org/3/library/resource.html) mirrors getrlimit, setrlimit and getrusage and documents the ru_maxrss unit split. Go returns per-child rusage from ProcessState.SysUsage (pkg.go.dev/os#ProcessState.SysUsage) and keeps setrlimit in syscall. Node exposes process.resourceUsage() for itself only, with maxRSS in KiB (nodejs.org/api/process.html#processresourceusage).

Rust std has neither; the rlimit crate wraps the raw calls. psutil normalises memory to bytes across platforms (psutil.readthedocs.io). Lesson: named limits and fixed units avoid the unit bugs, and per-child usage belongs on the finished child, as Go does.

Effects. Reading is -[Env]>, like sys.cpu_count. Setting is -[Exec]>, the effect process.on_signal and process.exit use for changes to the running program.

options.name: The ProcessSpec limit names, for this program too
options.detail: Each limit keeps its ProcessSpec builder name. sys.memory_limit reads and sys.set_memory_limit sets this program's limit, and the same pair exists for the other four; children inherit them. ProcessSpec gains core-file and stack limits beside its existing three. ResourceUsage holds user time, system time and peak memory in bytes. sys.usage reads it for this program or its finished children, and every receipt carries its own child's figure.
options.technical:
```text
// core.sys, this program; None = unlimited
sys.cpu_time_limit() -[Env]> (soft: Duration?, hard: Duration?) IOError!
sys.memory_limit() -[Env]> (soft: Int?, hard: Int?) IOError!       // bytes
sys.open_file_limit() -[Env]> (soft: Int?, hard: Int?) IOError!

sys.core_file_limit() -[Env]> (soft: Int?, hard: Int?) IOError!    // bytes
sys.stack_limit() -[Env]> (soft: Int?, hard: Int?) IOError!        // bytes
sys.set_cpu_time_limit(soft: Duration?, hard: Duration?) -[Exec]> IOError!

sys.set_memory_limit(soft: Int?, hard: Int?) -[Exec]> IOError!
// likewise set_open_file_limit, set_core_file_limit, set_stack_limit
enum UsageOf { Self, Children }

struct ResourceUsage { user: Duration, system: Duration, peak_memory: Int }   // bytes
sys.usage(of: UsageOf{.Self}) -[Env]> ResourceUsage IOError!

ProcessReceipt.usage: ResourceUsage?   // from wait4; None when the OS reports nothing
ProcessSpec.core_file_limit(value: Int) -> ProcessSpec   // bytes
ProcessSpec.stack_limit(value: Int) -> ProcessSpec       // bytes
```

Names and types follow the existing ProcessSpec builders: Duration for time, Int bytes for sizes, as in .memory_limit and .output_limit. The kernel counts CPU time in whole seconds, so a fractional Duration rounds up. Raising a hard limit without privilege is IOError PermissionDenied.

Unenforceable limits refuse with IOError, as child limits do today. Linux: prlimit64 and getrusage/wait4 syscalls (no C library, D-OS-FLOOR1). macOS: libSystem getrlimit/setrlimit/getrusage; memory refuses as for children. Windows: setters refuse; usage from GetProcessTimes and PROCESS_MEMORY_COUNTERS.PeakWorkingSetSize.
options.code:
use core.sys as sys
use core.process as process

fn run() IOError! -[Exec, Env, Time.Wait]> {
    sys.set_core_file_limit(0, 0)                   // no core dumps from here on
    print(sys.open_file_limit().soft ?? -1)         // e.g. 1024
    spec :: process.cmd(["jet", "build"]).stack_limit(1 << 30)
    receipt :: spec.run()
    usage :: receipt.usage ?? return Ok(())
    print("{usage.peak_memory /% 1_000_000} MB, {usage.user} user")
}

options.name: Mirror the C calls
options.detail: Core exposes the C calls with integer RLIMIT_* and RUSAGE_* constants and the raw usage record, as Python's resource module does. Callers convert units and handle the unlimited sentinel themselves.
options.technical: The calls are sys.getrlimit(resource: Int) -> (soft: Int, hard: Int) IOError! and sys.setrlimit(resource: Int, soft: Int, hard: Int) IOError!, with per-target constants. The usage call is sys.getrusage(who: Int) -> RUsage IOError!. It has ru_utime_us, ru_stime_us, ru_maxrss (KiB on Linux, bytes on macOS), and the remaining ru_* fields.

options.name: Children only
options.detail: ProcessSpec gains the core-file and stack limits and ProcessReceipt gains usage. There is no call that reads or sets this program's own limits or reads its own peak memory.
options.technical: ProcessSpec.core_file_limit(value: Int) and ProcessSpec.stack_limit(value: Int) in bytes, and ProcessReceipt.usage: ResourceUsage? as in A. No core.sys additions.

decisions.title: Run many commands at once, at most N at a time, and get every result back in order
decisions.situation: A tool that runs 300 tests or builds has to start many programs, a few at a time. In Jet today that means hand-written tasks, channels and bookkeeping, and the result order, timeouts and clean-up after a crash are easy to get wrong. This vote decides what Core gives for it. We recommend one call that takes the commands and a number, and returns one result per command in the order given.
decisions.gist: How should a program run many commands at most N at a time and collect every result in order?
decisions.lesson: A worker pool runs a list of jobs with at most N running at once; when one finishes, the next starts. Under A this is one Core call. You get one result per command in the order you gave them, and if your program is stopped, the running commands are stopped too.
decisions.story: Ben's checker runs 1,200 example programs with eight at a time. He writes `process.run_all(specs, jobs: 8)` and loops over the results, which come back in his list's order, so his report is the same on every run. When he presses Ctrl+C, the eight running examples stop with his checker and no orphan keeps running.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: a bounded pool; map keeps input order.
# https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(lambda argv: subprocess.run(argv), jobs))
# GNU parallel: -j bounds the jobs, --keep-order keeps input order.
parallel -j 8 --keep-order ./check {} ::: examples/*
decisions.detail:
Today. Tasks run child processes in parallel: probe pool_today.jet runs ten 0.3 s commands across three task.all lanes in about 1.2 s. But task.all takes a fixed written block, so the number of workers is fixed in the source.

A pool of N from a variable list needs dynamic task spawning with a work channel. A Sender cannot be copied (E0102 on `.clone()`), so each worker needs its own result channel. The caller must then rebuild the order by hand. Clean-up when the caller is cancelled or the program is stopped is left to each tool.

Who needs it. The #5072 tool ports: compiler-diff, goldens-census, run-feature-examples, core-module-check, release-compiler, lost-work-audit and the s5 drivers all run bounded pools of child processes. Today they use Node promise pools or `xargs -P`. Card #5072 criterion 2 asks for a bounded pool, N jobs, per-job timeout, collected exit status, deterministic order, and cancellation on parent exit.

What A says. process.run_all(specs, jobs) starts at most `jobs` children at once, starts the next spec when one finishes, and returns one Result per spec in the order given. A nonzero exit is an Ok receipt, as for spec.run(). A child that cannot start is an Err for that spec only; the other specs still run, so every failure is reported in one pass.

Each spec keeps its own timeout, limits and output modes. A per-job timeout is spec.timeout(d), and output can go to its own file through the ratified file output mode (D-CORE-PROCFILE1=A). jobs defaults to the number of CPUs; below 1 is InvalidInput.

Clean-up. Core already puts every child in its own process group. The calling task may be cancelled: a race loser, a closing task.group, or an expired deadline block. The program may be stopped by a signal or an exit. In every case run_all kills each running child's group and reaps it before it returns or the program ends.

On Linux each child is also started with the parent-death signal, so even a parent killed with SIGKILL takes its children. On Windows each child sits in a Job Object that closes with the parent.

Built on tasks. run_all is ordinary Jet in Core, with one task per slot inside a task.group. It follows the task and deadline rules already ratified and adds no runtime machinery beyond the clean-up hooks.

Option B adds only a primitive: process.wait_any(children) returns the index and receipt of the first child to finish. Callers write the scheduling loop, ordering and clean-up themselves; each tool repeats the same 15 lines.

Option C adds a general bounded parallel map to the task language, `task.map(items, limit: 8) { item -> ... }`, for any work, not just commands. It is new syntax across every tier, and command clean-up would still need A's kill rules.

Research. Python's ThreadPoolExecutor.map keeps input order and bounds workers (docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html). GNU parallel's -j and --keep-order are the shell standard (gnu.org/software/parallel). Go's errgroup.SetLimit bounds goroutines but leaves order and process clean-up to the caller (pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sync/errgroup).

Rust futures' buffered(n) keeps order; buffer_unordered does not. xargs -P has no order, so outputs interleave and reports change run to run. Lesson: order must be the default, and clean-up must not depend on the caller.

options.name: One call: run_all
options.detail: Core runs the specs at most `jobs` at a time and returns one Result per spec in input order. A nonzero exit is a receipt; a start failure is an error for that spec only. If the caller is cancelled or the program stops, running children are killed and reaped.
options.technical:
```text
process.run_all(specs: [ProcessSpec], jobs: Int{sys.cpu_count()})
    -[Exec, Time.Wait]> [Result<ProcessReceipt, IOError>] IOError!   // IOError only for jobs < 1
```
Implemented in Core/Process with one task per slot in a task.group. Per-spec timeout, limits and stream modes apply unchanged. Cancellation and exit hooks kill each running child's process group (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the spec's grace) and reap it. Linux children get PR_SET_PDEATHSIG; Windows children join a kill-on-close Job Object. An authority-bound spec keeps its Capture rule.

options.name: A wait-for-any primitive
options.detail: Core adds one call that waits for whichever child finishes first. The caller starts children, keeps the count under N, puts receipts back in order and kills children on cancellation.
options.technical: process.wait_any(children: &[ProcessChild]) -[Time.Wait]> (index: Int, receipt: ProcessReceipt) IOError!; the finished child is removed from the list.

options.name: A bounded map in the task language
options.detail: The task language gains a bounded map with results in input order. Commands run through it like any other work.
options.technical: Grammar: task.map(expr, limit: expr) { binding -> body } returning [T] or failing per D-CONC-FAIL1; parity across parser, sema, TIR, AOT, JIT, interpreter and web. Process kill-on-cancel rules still have to be specified for spec.run().

errgroup bounds goroutines; order and process clean-up are left to the caller. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sync/errgroup

Stopping the tool stops its children.

C adds syntax for a need that today is commands, and still needs A's clean-up rules.

decisions.title: Sort words the way people read them, the same on every machine
decisions.situation: Jet sorts text by its bytes, so `Zulu` comes before `apple` and `éclair` comes after `zebra`. Tools that print sorted names for people, and code moved from JavaScript or Python that used a locale sort, need dictionary order. Asking the operating system gives a different order on each machine. This vote decides what Core gives; we recommend the Unicode standard's default order, which is also English order, fixed in Jet's own tables.
decisions.gist: Should Core sort text in Unicode dictionary order, the same on every machine, and how?
decisions.lesson: Collation is the rule for putting words in dictionary order: ignore case and accents first, then use them to break ties. Unicode publishes one default rule, and English uses it unchanged. Under A Jet ships that rule with its other Unicode tables, so a sort gives the same order everywhere.
decisions.story: Chen's documentation tool lists 400 command flags. With byte order, `Zulu` comes before `apple` and every flag starting with `_` lands in the middle. He writes `&flags.sort_by(text.collate)` and gets `_x, apple, Banana, éclair, zebra, Zulu`, the order a JavaScript `localeCompare` sort gave, on his laptop and in CI.
decisions.detail:
Today. String `<` and sort() compare UTF-8 bytes, which is code point order and exactly LC_COLLATE=C. Probe collate_today.jet prints [Banana, Zulu, _x, apple, zebra, éclair]. Node's localeCompare gives [_x, apple, Banana, éclair, zebra, Zulu]. GNU sort under LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 on the same machine gives [apple, Banana, éclair, _x, zebra, Zulu], because glibc ignores punctuation at the first level. So the host locale and ICU already disagree for English.

Who needs it. Eight #5072 tool ports sort human-facing lists with JavaScript localeCompare: check-agent-doc-flags (ported with an ASCII stand-in), compiler-registries, core-conformance, core-coverage-census, run-feature-examples, test-corpora, native-route-records and classify-native-route-glue. Card #5072 criterion 4 asks for C order for ASCII and a named compare for en_US.

Reconciling ratified law. D-TEXTUNICODE1=A put Unicode algorithms in core.text and said locale collation is an i18n data problem, not v1 core. A keeps that line. It adds only the locale-independent Unicode default order: the Unicode Collation Algorithm with CLDR's root table.

That order is Unicode data, like the normalization and segmentation tables Jet already pins. Per-language rules, such as Swedish putting å after z, stay outside Core. CLDR's English collation has no tailoring, so root order is en and en_US order. C order stays the default `<` and sort().

What A says. text.collate(a, b) returns an Ordering, like `<=>` and every sort_by comparator, so `&names.sort_by(text.collate)` works as written. text.collation_key(value) returns bytes whose plain byte order equals collate.

A key lets the existing sort_by compute one key per item, as Python's strxfrm and ICU sort keys do. Equal keys mean equal text. After the three Unicode levels (letters, accents, case) a final level compares code points, so the order is total and every sort is deterministic.

Data and size. The table comes from CLDR's root allkeys file for Jet's pinned Unicode 17.0.0, vendored beside tests/data/unicode/ucd. The same checksum-verifying generator as the other Unicode assets produces it. Han and unassigned code points use the standard's computed weights, so they need no rows. The table joins a program only when it calls collate or collation_key, as the Unicode names table joins only programs that call text.inspect.

Option B uses the host locale (strcoll and strxfrm under LC_COLLATE). Results differ per machine, as the probe shows, and Jet's Linux builds use no C library (D-OS-FLOOR1=A), so B would have to ship glibc's locale data anyway.

Option C ships every CLDR locale's rules now: text.collate(a, b, locale: "sv"). It answers a wider question than the card asks, adds several megabytes of tailoring data and reverses D-TEXTUNICODE1's i18n line.

Research. ICU and CLDR are the reference implementations used by JavaScript Intl.Collator, Java, Android and Apple platforms (unicode.org/reports/tr10, cldr.unicode.org). Python's locale.strxfrm follows the host locale and differs between Linux and macOS. PostgreSQL moved from glibc to ICU collations after glibc 2.28 changed sort order and silently corrupted indexes (wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Locale_data_changes). Rust's std has no collation; icu_collator is the ICU4X port. Lesson: pin the data to a Unicode version and never read the host's.

options.name: Unicode's default order, pinned
options.detail: Core adds a compare and a sort key in the Unicode default order from Jet's pinned tables. Byte order stays the default `<` and sort(). Other languages' rules stay outside Core.
options.technical:
```text
text.collate(a: String, b: String) -> Ordering   // like <=>
text.collation_key(value: String) -> [U8]        // byte order == collate order
```
UCA (UTS #10) with the CLDR root table for Unicode 17.0.0. Variable weighting is non-ignorable, the CLDR default. Levels 1-3 are followed by an identical level on NFD code points. So collate is Equal only for canonically equivalent text. Implicit weights for Han and unassigned code points are computed. Asset generated by the Unicode table generator from vendored allkeys_CLDR.txt, verified by checksum, linked only when used.
options.code:
use core.text as text

fn run() {
    names := ["zebra", "Banana", "éclair", "apple", "Zulu", "_x"]
    &names.sort_by(text.collate)
    print(names)   // [_x, apple, Banana, éclair, zebra, Zulu]
    print(text.collate("apple", "Banana"))   // Less
    &names.sort_by((n: String) -> text.collation_key(n))   // same order, one key per item
}

options.name: The machine's locale
options.detail: Core asks the operating system to compare under the current LC_COLLATE setting, as C's strcoll and Python's locale module do.
options.technical: text.collate_host(a, b) -[Env]> Ordering and text.collation_key_host(value) -[Env]> [U8] via strcoll/strxfrm on Unix and CompareStringEx on Windows. Linux builds would need glibc locale data, against D-OS-FLOOR1=A.

options.name: Every language now
options.detail: Core ships the per-language rules from CLDR and takes a locale name. English uses the default order.
options.technical: text.collate(a, b, locale: String{"root"}) -> Ordering and text.collation_key(value, locale) with all CLDR tailorings bundled; unknown locale is an error.

comparisons.note: localeCompare and Intl.Collator use ICU; English has no tailoring. Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/Collator
strxfrm follows the host locale, so order differs between systems. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/locale.html#locale.strxfrm
A glibc update changed sort order and broke indexes; ICU collations pin the order. Source: https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Locale_data_changes
ICU4X provides the Unicode collator as a library. Source: https://docs.rs/icu_collator

let c = Collator::try_new(locale, options)?;
names.sort_by(|a, b| c.compare(a, b));

recommendation.why: A gives people's dictionary order with no machine dependence. It is the Unicode standard's own rule, the one JavaScript and ICU use for English, so ported code keeps its output. Byte order stays the default.
gains: Readable order for names and words.
Same order on every machine and every run.
Code moved from JavaScript keeps its output.

whyNot.reason: B makes the order depend on the machine, the failure that broke PostgreSQL indexes.
C ships megabytes of language rules the card does not need.

recommendation.tradeoff: Other languages' rules, such as Swedish å after z, stay in a later i18n package.

decisions.title: Name the "this program" case of sys.usage `.Program`; amends D-CORE-RLIMIT1
decisions.situation: D-CORE-RLIMIT1 (ratified A) gives `sys.usage(of:)` two cases, written `enum UsageOf { Self, Children }`. A probe of that line failed with E0003, and it looked as if `Self` cannot name a case. It can: the error came from the commas, since Jet separates cases with spaces or new lines. The question left is only the word. We recommend `.Program`, because every other line of the ratified ballot already says "this program".
decisions.gist: What should the "this program" case of `sys.usage(of:)` be called?
decisions.lesson: `sys.usage(of:)` reports CPU time and peak memory, either for the running program or for its finished children. The case name is what a reader sees at the call, as in `sys.usage(of: .Program)`. `Self` already has a meaning in Jet: the type an `impl` block is about.
decisions.story: Ana's build tool prints its own peak memory with `sys.usage(of: .Program)` and the children's with `sys.usage(of: .Children)`. A reader new to Jet reads both calls aloud and knows which is which without opening the docs. Nothing else in her code changes between the options.
decisions.detail:
What the probes show. Probes of_self, of_program and of_current in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-3/probes/rlimit write `enum UsageOf { X Children }` and match on `.X`. All three print the same two lines on o0, o1 and o2. Probe kw_type shows the word `Type` works as a case too. The comma form, `enum UsageOf { Program, Children }`, fails with E0003 for every name (probe comma.jet).

So no parser change is needed for any option. ToolsJet's probe usage_of.jet failed because it copied the ratified technical text, which writes commas. Every option below corrects that text to `enum UsageOf { X Children }`, the form Core uses, for example `enum PathPlatform { Unix Windows }` in Core/Files/Runtime/KernelPathComponents.jet:6.

Why the word matters. In Jet, `Self` inside an `impl` block means that block's type. A case named `Self` gives the word a second meaning: inside `impl UsageOf`, `Self.Self` names the case of the type. Probe self_noimpl shows `.Self` and `UsageOf.Self` both work at a call. The parser accepts it; the question is how it reads.

Other names. `.Program` matches the ratified text, which says "this program" for every limit and usage call. `.Current` is shorter, but it does not say current what: program, thread or task. C, Python and Go say `RUSAGE_SELF`, so `.Self` is familiar to C programmers.

Scope. Only the case name and the ratified text change. The calls, units and the rest of D-CORE-RLIMIT1 A stay as ratified. Nothing is built yet, so no code or test moves.

Review. Author: Claude (MemDesign-3 lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this ballot.

decisions.title: Compiler packages read the toolchain's Core sources while building, through a toolchain: path prefix allowed only inside the toolchain tree
decisions.situation:
Jet's compiler needs facts from its own core library's source files, such as the list of effects. Today a script copies those facts into nine compiler files, about 1.2 MB, each stamped with a checksum. Every core edit means running the script again, and 509 commits since October touched those copies.

The compiler cannot read the core files itself while it is built. A build-time file read must name a path below the reading file, and the core library sits beside the compiler, not below it.

We recommend A: a toolchain: prefix names a file from the top of the Jet source tree, and only packages inside that tree may use it. Every other package keeps today's rule.
decisions.gist: Should compiler packages embed the toolchain's Core sources through a toolchain: path prefix allowed only inside the toolchain tree?
decisions.lesson: Jet's compiler needs facts from its own core library's source files. Today a script copies those facts into compiler files, and every core edit means running it again. This vote decides how the compiler can read those files directly while it is built.
decisions.explainer: Words used here. embed_file reads a file while building and makes its text a constant. The toolchain tree is the directory holding Core/ and Compiler/Prelude/. A generated file is one a script writes.
decisions.story: Ivy adds an effect to Effects.jet. Under A, the next compiler build reads the file itself. No regenerate step, no SHA header to refresh, no stale table.
decisions.inWild:
// Rust reaches files above the crate with a path macro:
include_str!(concat!(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"), "/../core/effects.rs"))
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. How a compiler package names a toolchain source at build time. The embed rules of D-CTIO1 and D-CTFIND1 otherwise stay.

Scope, measured on dev c460ba91e5. The generator Tools/agent/CoreSourceRows.jet writes twelve files (CoreSourceRows.jet:2908-2921). Nine are derived tables in compiler and Jetpack packages: 1,240,667 bytes, touched by 509 commits since 2026-10-01. The earlier draft counted only five of them, 279,898 bytes. CoreCallRows.jet alone is 895,709 bytes.

What stays generated under every option. Core/EmbeddedSources.jet, the in-place rows of Core/Compiler/Lang.jet and Compiler/Prelude/Core.jet, and one section of the core-library reference. They are Core or docs, not compiler tables.

Probes with the a0.0.43 compiler. A file beside the reader embeds. A path with .. is E0957 even inside one package, by design. The spellings core: and toolchain: are both E0955 today: A is not built. The ratified #run spelling is E0733, so the code shown uses today's comptime { } block.

Cost, measured. Embedding a 279 KB copy of Core.jet and counting its 116 module rows at build time adds 44 ms and 21 MB to a cold check. A cached check takes about 1 ms more. The whole generator takes 3.09 s and 414 MB today.

Staleness, measured. A cached build notices an edit to the embedded file: the count went 116, then 117 after one added row, then 116 after the revert. The driver records each read's SHA-256 (JetDriver ComptimeInputs.jet:54-57) and the cache keys on it.

A defect found. The spec says every embed records its SHA-256 in .jet/lock (spec.md:539). On a0.0.43 a package that embeds a file builds and runs, and no .jet/lock is written. A's first build criterion is that lock record.

What A does. embed_file and find accept a toolchain: prefix, as in embed_file("toolchain:Compiler/Prelude/Effects.jet"). The rest is a literal path from the toolchain root, with no .. and no absolute form, so E0957's rules still apply after the prefix.

Resolution. The prefix reads the tree the compile already takes Core from: JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT, else the nearest directory above the input that holds Core/ and Compiler/Prelude/ (Request.jet:300). So the tables always describe the Core the new compiler is compiled against. There is no built-in-copy fallback, so the jet binary does not grow.

The gate. The prefix is allowed only in a package whose directory lies inside that tree. Anywhere else it is a new registered error, so Core's file layout never becomes a public interface. When JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT names a different tree, the error names both directories.

Derived rows. A pure copy, such as the effect source, is an embed and runs no code. Row tables are computed by a function over the embedded text, in the package that needs them. The generator keeps only its four non-compiler outputs.

Ratified decisions. A keeps D-CTFIND1 and D-CTFIND2 and adds no ambient name, so D-PRELUDE-LAW1 holds. It fits D-BUILD-COREUNIT1=A: Core stays one compiler-known unit. It amends D-CTIO1 by one sentence: for a package inside the toolchain tree, the project is that tree. The compiler workspace already treats it so, naming ../Examples and ../tests in Compiler/package.jet:43-47.

Peers. Go's embed refuses .. and files outside the module; Zig refuses an embed outside the package path. Rust's include_str! reads any relative path. Go's own compiler keeps a checked-in generated builtin.go, which is D at scale.

Beginner path. Nothing changes; ordinary packages never see the prefix. Expert path. A compiler author embeds the source and derives rows in Jet, with no generator step.

Other options. B adds one workspace grant in Compiler/package.jet, toolchain_reads, listing globs; members inherit it. C gives Core a package.jet and makes it a path dependency. D keeps today's generated files. B still needs A's location check, or any package could write the grant.

decisions.title: Give Core the host's time zone, and let format selectors take a computed number
decisions.situation:
Jet aims for scripts that are no longer than the tools they replace. A trace viewer written for Node has 915 words, and the shortest faithful Jet version has 1000. Most of the gap is a header that shows the time of day.

Node asks the machine for its time zone in one call, while each Jet script must find the zone by hand. A smaller part is that a padded column cannot take its width from the data. Unpadded hours are already decided, so this ballot asks only about the zone and computed widths.
decisions.gist: Should Core tell a program the machine's time zone, and should format selectors accept a computed number?
decisions.lesson: A time zone turns an instant into a wall-clock time. The host zone is the one the machine is set to. A script that shows the time to a person wants it, while a program that must print the same everywhere names its zone.
decisions.explainer:
Today a Jet script finds the host zone itself. It reads the TZ variable, else the system zone link, else it uses UTC. Even with the decided unpadded-hour code, that lookup costs the twin 29 words, and every such script repeats it.

Under A, time.host_zone() returns the machine's zone, and an instant's in_host_zone() shows it there. Both declare that they read the environment and files, as zone(name) already does. The header becomes one interpolation.

The host rule is the one glibc and Go use. An unset TZ means the system setting, and an empty TZ means UTC. A set TZ loses one leading colon, then names a zone, or a zone file when it starts with a slash. Anything that does not resolve gives the zone named UTC.

Under A, every selector number may also be any Int expression: Pad, PadLeft, Fixed, Grouped, Sci, Percent and Hex. A negative number acts as zero. So a column as wide as its longest entry uses the selector, as fixed columns already do.

B adds the zone but keeps literal selector numbers. C adds only host_zone(), so callers write in_zone(time.host_zone()). D adds nothing and leaves the twin at 942 words.
decisions.story: Lee ports a watch-mode trace viewer from Node. Its header shows the wall-clock time, and the Jet version needs a zone lookup by hand to print 6:09:27 AM. Under A the header is one interpolation, and the column sized by the data is one selector.
decisions.detail:
Counts are whitespace-separated words, the gauntlet's source metric. The original viewer has 915. Compact.jet, the twin built from existing forms, has 1000. Projected.jet, with the A spellings, has 908. B gives 912 and C gives 908. The review's variants are in the lane's probes/lc/counts folder.

The no-pad flag is not on this ballot. The ratified one-percent-code ruling already gives every numeric code the GNU flag, so %-I prints 6. With that flag and nothing else, the twin has 942 words, and that is D.

From 942, the host zone saves 30 words and the computed width saves 4. Computed widths alone give 938. So the zone is the part that closes the gap, and the width supplies the slack.

Dev does not have the flag yet. On the t6c compiler, format and strftime copy %-I through as text, and format_checked refuses it. The twin reaches its count only after that ratified work lands, under every option.

Selectors today. {word:Pad(width)} and {x:Fixed(digits)} are refused with 'Expected width inside :Pad( )'. The parser's one number reader serves all seven numbered selectors, so A widens them together. The IR builder already passes the number as an operand of the helper call. A literal stays a constant, so existing output does not change.

The change touches the parser's number reader, the selector's tree node, the source formatter, the tree dump and the IR builder. Every tier runs that IR, so the tiers agree, as the selector ruling requires. The pad helpers already treat a zero or negative width as no padding, and a probe confirms it.

Zones today. zone(name) refuses a leading colon and any absolute path, and knows no POSIX rule string. The twin's hand rule picks the system zone when TZ is empty, but Node, glibc and Go use UTC. A uses UTC there, so the twin matches the original in one more case.

Limits common to every option. A POSIX rule string in TZ gives UTC, where glibc and Node honor it. Day and month names are English, where Node follows the host locale. Selector padding counts characters, not terminal columns.

A Core defect the review found, outside this ballot. zone(name) reads a TZif table but not the rule footer at its end. So New York shows standard time in July 2045, where Node and date show daylight time. The fix needs a POSIX rule reader, and TZ rule strings would then work for free.

Census on dev. Ten lines in eight files pass a computed width to a pad call, mostly package-tool tables. Selector numbers appear on 103 lines in 36 files, all literals. Four lines call in_zone, and one reads the system zone link by hand.

options.detail: Add time.host_zone() -[Env, FS.Read]> Zone and DateTime.in_host_zone() -[Env, FS.Read]> ZonedDateTime. Let every selector number take any Int expression.
options.technical: host_zone() applies the host rule, then zone(name) or a direct zone-file read. in_host_zone() is in_zone(host_zone()). Web asks the browser's Intl zone, and Windows maps its zone setting to the IANA name with the CLDR table. Selector numbers parse as expressions, check as Int and run after the value. The twin projects to 908.

options.detail: Scripts keep the TZ and system-link lookup. With the decided no-pad flag it is a 29-word function. The twin stays at 942 against 915.
options.technical: No API is added. Every script that shows local time repeats the lookup, and the hand rule picks the system zone for an empty TZ, unlike its peers.
options.code:

if name == "" -> name = (files.read_link("/etc/localtime") ?? "").split_once("zoneinfo/")?.after ?? "UTC"

comparisons.note: Date methods use the host zone. toLocaleTimeString also uses the host locale, so its text varies by machine. This is the original's spelling.
time.Local is TZ, else the system zone file, else UTC, and an empty TZ is UTC. That is A's rule. Layouts spell the unpadded hour as 3.
LocalDate and LocalTime are zone-free, as Jet's are, so the host zone is named systemDefault rather than local.
Local::now() reads the host zone. %-I is the GNU no-pad flag Jet has already adopted.
astimezone() with no argument uses the host zone. Format specs take computed widths.

recommendation.why: Showing the clock in the machine's zone is ordinary script work, and every peer does it in one call. Jet already has zones and patterns, and lacks only the host lookup. A computed column width is the normal table case, and the selector path already passes its number at run time.
gains: The twin projects to 908 of 915 words.
One host rule for every script, the same as glibc and Go, including an empty TZ.

The names avoid Local, which Jet's zone-free LocalDate and LocalTime already use.

decisions.title: Build-time reads of walked and data-named files
decisions.situation:
Card #5072 c28 moves five generated Core-declaration tables into build-time code. That code must read files named by a directory walk or by another file's text. On a0.0.43, find returns paths, but embed_file and embed_bytes accept literals only (E0957). A parent import outside a script's authorized root also fails (E0602).

We recommend A: accept build-time String arguments for the existing reads and find, without widening their file authority. E is the smaller change: computed embeds, literal globs. Both cover c28. The ratified toolchain: direction stands; neither proposal works on the seed yet.
decisions.gist: Should existing build-time reads accept computed paths, and should find accept computed globs too?
decisions.lesson: Jet can embed files while compiling. Today their paths must be literals. A table builder needs to read files named by a walk or by another file. This vote picks that read rule. Recording every read in .jet/lock is required but not working on the seed.
decisions.explainer: A build-time read is embed_file or embed_bytes inside #run. find(glob) returns sorted paths. A data-named read gets its path from another file. toolchain: is the ratified prefix for compiler packages reading toolchain sources. Proposed examples use #run; seed probes use comptime. The lock is a required output, not an access grant or a sandbox.
decisions.story: Lee keeps recipes in Markdown files. Under A she writes loop path in find("recipes/*.md") -> embed_file(path). A new file joins the next build's table. The same code works under E, whose glob stays literal. A path outside the existing authority is rejected.
decisions.detail:
A amends D-CTIO1's literal clause and the literal-glob restriction. E changes only the embeds. Neither reopens D-EMBED-TOOLCHAIN1=A. Relative paths remain relative to the embedding file, not the package root. toolchain: keeps its ratified authority check. No absolute path, parent component, symlink escape or ambient file API is enabled.

Independent seed runs confirm E0957 for computed text, bytes and find arguments; sorted results; empty matches; and E0955 for invalid UTF-8 text and symlinks. b.find and b.embed already accept computed String values. The former's literal-only diagnostic is misleading, not an AST literal check.

The traced generator input set has 284 files (19.4 MB), including 42 runtime units and 13 syntax files. Literal-embed adaptations produced matching hashes for CoreCallRows and all twelve views. These are host-only probes, not the five-table package cutover or a cross-target proof. The report records cold-build costs; no option has an end-to-end implementation benchmark.

Implementation is more than deleting sema's literal check. Today's typed host call stores a String and IR emits ConstText. Sema must check a build-time String expression and own the evaluated path-law check. IR lowers checked operations; the rooted host transport remains the security backstop. Preserve the Core-reader authority boundary rather than silently granting Core find.

All options need per-read digests, sorted glob membership including empty results, correct invalidation and watches, and target/toolchain-aware identity. Reusing bytes is a proposed bounded evaluation snapshot, not an existing cache. Key it by root, embedding directory and normalized path. Detect concurrent changes rather than mixing different file versions. Lock diffs show reads after execution; untrusted builds still need external isolation.

The option examples are same-derivation sketches: core_source_rows, pick and core_call_records stand for shared parser work, not new APIs. The complete executable derivation probes use literal embeds because the seed cannot implement any proposed option. The generated baseline stays until the chosen mechanism, shared parser and all cutover proofs pass.

options.name: Computed embeds and globs
options.detail: embed_file, embed_bytes and find accept build-time String values. Apply the existing path law to the value. No new name.
options.technical: Sema checks the argument type, phase and common normalized path law, including evaluated values. Typed calls and IR carry the argument expression instead of ConstText. Evaluation invokes sema-owned validation before rooted transport. E0957 quotes a rejected value; E0955 covers read or UTF-8 failure. Beginner: existing literal embeds. Expert: data-derived paths and globs. The complete record, watch and snapshot contract in the report applies.

options.name: Content globs
options.detail: embed_files(glob) returns [(path: String, text: String)]; embed_files_bytes(glob) returns [(path: String, bytes: [U8])]. Patterns and scalar embeds stay literal-only.
options.technical: Two names need D-PRELUDE-LAW1 admission. Both bulk calls must use the same canonical reader and path law, not duplicate file policy (I8). A static bound is a real review benefit. Data-named reads select from a superset. Invalid UTF-8 fails the text call with E0955; bytes require no UTF-8. Sorted results and empty matches follow find. Beginner: scalar embed, then a content glob. Expert: choose a bounded source set.
options.code:
CORE_CALLS: #run {
    core: embed_file("toolchain:Compiler/Prelude/Core.jet")
    units: embed_files("toolchain:Core/*/Runtime/**/*.jet")
    sources: embed_files("toolchain:Core/**/*.jet")
    owned: loop row in core_source_rows(core) -> pick(sources, "toolchain:{row.path}")
    core_call_records(core, units, owned) ?? panic(err.message)
}

options.name: Computed reads bounded by find
options.detail: Computed embeds must match a literal find already executed in the same evaluation. Literal embeds keep their existing authority.
options.technical: Track normalized matched identities, not bare path spellings. Reject an unmatched computed read with E0957. This adds authority state and call-order dependence, not another reader. Beginner: literal embeds. Expert: run a bounding find before computed reads. The example's Core bound may include files it never uses. Reusing bytes can remove repeated I/O but not the order rule.
options.code:
CORE_CALLS: #run {
    core: embed_file("toolchain:Compiler/Prelude/Core.jet")
    bound: find("toolchain:Core/**/*.jet")
    units: loop path in find("toolchain:Core/*/Runtime/**/*.jet") -> (path: path, text: embed_file(path))
    owned: loop row in core_source_rows(core) -> (path: row.path, text: embed_file("toolchain:{row.path}"))
    core_call_records(core, units, owned) ?? panic(err.message)
}

options.name: Declared input ceiling
options.detail: package.jet declares comptime_inputs globs. Computed reads and walks must stay inside that ceiling; literals retain today's rule. Reading code is A's.
options.technical: A new manifest key contributes to package identity. Reject values outside the ceiling with E0957. The ceiling is distinct from the actual read set and need not change for every new file. Beginner: literal embeds need no field. Expert: choose a narrow ceiling. Costs: another authority surface, manifest maintenance, and wider restrictions if authors use broad roots to avoid maintenance.

options.name: Computed embeds; literal globs
options.detail: embed_file and embed_bytes accept build-time String values. find keeps its literal-only argument. This covers the same c28 program as A.
options.technical: Use A's checked expression, rooted reader and recording contract for embeds without widening find's source restriction. Beginner: existing literal embeds. Expert: data-named embeds work directly; a data-named walk needs a broad literal find and filtering. This is the smallest semantic expansion the traced generator requires. It does not add C's matched-set requirement.

comparisons.note: The implementation resolves a constant-string value and rejects an embed outside the module path. This is a source comparison, not a local Zig execution.
Literal package-relative patterns bound an embed.FS. Computed names read inside it. Patterns exclude parent components and symlinks; empty matches fail. Source comparison only.
A build script is a cached host program. It can derive table literals directly, not only emit include_str! calls. Authors declare invalidation paths. Source comparison only.

recommendation.why: A keeps one value-argument rule across existing operations and matches the computed-value build host. E is equally sufficient for c28 and changes less. Prefer A for consistency, not because these tables prove a need for computed globs. This recommends a direction, not implementation approval.
gains: One argument rule for literal, walked and data-named paths.
No new ambient name.
No superset read is required just to authorize a computed embed.

losses.loss: Shared blocker under A-E: an empty find-only program is cached by jet run and misses its first added member.
losses.mitigation: Reproducer: probes/empty_glob.sh. Record and revalidate empty membership before cache reuse; c25 and the cutover must cover this.

losses.loss: Data-named reads are not visible from source alone before execution.
losses.mitigation: Required lock rows expose the set after a successful build. They are not a pre-execution allowlist; untrusted builds need external isolation.

losses.loss: Wrong computed paths fail during evaluation rather than literal checking.
losses.mitigation: Sema owns language checking; the host independently enforces file authority. Codegen only lowers checked operations.

losses.loss: Ratified literal rules, their tests and explanations change.
losses.mitigation: Update every affected caller and test in one cutover, including positive computed-path and negative computed-escape cases.

losses.loss: Glob tracking, bootstrap authority and target parity remain unproven for the proposed mechanism.
losses.mitigation: Require the report's acceptance matrix before cutover. Do not describe planned fixes as shipped behavior.

whyNot.reason: A real static bound and useful bulk operation, but two names and possible superset reads. Sharing policy can satisfy I8; the toolchain ballot does not ban B.
A real source ceiling, but mutable authority state and a call-order rule.
A useful manifest ceiling, but another policy surface. The ceiling and actual reads are different facts, not duplication by definition.
Equally sufficient and smaller for c28. A avoids differing rules for computed paths and globs; that consistency gain is not a performance claim.

recommendation.tradeoff: Uniform computed arguments, in return for learning the actual read set after execution. E offers a smaller change.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: GPT. Fresh agent: EmbedWalkReview; independent seed probes and matched-output derivations corrected b.find, constant-only IR, repeated reads, lock and I8 claims, and added option E; see the audit for unproven cutover requirements.
