decisions.title: How a Jet tool sends Chrome debugger commands to one page and reads where it paused
decisions.situation: Card #5072 moves repo tooling from Node to Jet. The Jet twin of the source-map check must pause a page at a breakpoint and report the line where it stopped. Jet's browser library can send Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) commands, but only to the browser as a whole, never to one page. Its events keep only a name and a few network facts, so a pause carries no line. The live half of the check therefore cannot move to Jet today. This vote decides how a Jet tool reaches one page's debugger and reads where it paused. We recommend A: a CDP handle for one page, plus named debugger facts on events.
decisions.gist: How should a Jet tool send Chrome debugger commands to one page and read where the page paused?
decisions.lesson: A browser library can hand events to a program as raw protocol data or as a fixed set of named facts. Raw data serves every later need, but carries page content past the library's redaction. Named facts stay small and safe, but each new need is a new accessor.
decisions.explainer:
CDP is Chrome's debugging protocol. A command such as Debugger.enable goes to one target, usually a page, through that page's session. An event such as Debugger.paused comes back with JSON params. A pause lists the call frames, each with a function name and a 0-based line.

Jet's browser library, core.web.browser, speaks WebDriver BiDi to the browser. Chromium's BiDi server passes CDP through a command named goog:cdp.sendCommand. The library's protocol("cdp") handle uses it, but sends no session, so its commands reach the browser rather than a page.

The library turns each event into a BrowserEvent. It keeps the event's kind and named facts: request id, request method, status code, and url_hash. A hash is a fixed-length fingerprint of the text, so the URL itself is not stored. A program can compare a hash with the hash of a string it already knows.

The beginner path is a test that opens a page with page.goto, finds elements with page.get_by_role and clicks them, and reads page.text(). It needs no protocol, and it is the same in every option. The expert path is a tool that needs a CDP feature the library does not wrap. Every option changes only the expert path.
decisions.story: The source-map check serves a built web app and finds the generated app.js line that the source map assigns to a Jet statement. It sets a breakpoint there, loads the page and waits for the pause. It checks that the top frame is render, jet_main or empty. It prints the paused line plus one, and whether Chrome reported app.js.map. Each option writes that live half as one function, live(port, line). The map decoding is plain Jet in every option and is not shown.
decisions.inWild: Puppeteer gives each page its own CDP session with page.createCDPSession(). session.send runs a command, and session.on hands raw event params to the program. Playwright's context.newCDPSession(page) works the same way, on Chromium only. Both pass raw JSON to the program and redact nothing. Selenium 4 sends CDP commands through chromedriver with execute_cdp_cmd and reads no events that way. These outside facts were not re-checked for this ballot.
decisions.detail:
Commands today. BrowserProtocol.send in Core/Web/Browser.jet (line 579) sends goog:cdp.sendCommand with a method and params and no session. The BiDi handle refuses every goog:cdp method (line 573), and so does Browser.subscribe for goog:cdp events (line 216). So no hand-built command can reach a page's debugger. That chromium-bidi takes the page session as a field beside method and params is [INFERENCE] from its schema, not run live.

Events today. __cdp_event_facts (line 1177) keeps only the request id, request method, url_hash and status. A #Test near line 1993 pins that a Debugger.paused event has every fact empty. Docs/spec/architecture.md says the trace never holds payloads and events carry named facts. Command replies are not redacted: send returns the full reply JSON (lines 575 and 580).

Limits today. The event queue holds 256 events and drops the oldest first (C_EVENT_LIMIT, line 1058). The trace holds 8 KiB and also drops the oldest first. Every script the library runs in the page also fires Debugger.scriptParsed, so a long session can push out the event a tool wants.

Hashes today. browser.fact_hash is not public. A probe calling browser.fact_hash("app.js.map") fails with E1004, core.web.browser has no item fact_hash. So no caller can compare url_hash with a known URL today. The hash is 64-bit FNV-1a. It keeps strings out of logs, but anyone who guesses a string can confirm it.

Navigation. page.goto waits for the load to complete (line 339). A breakpoint that fires during the load blocks it, so goto would time out first. Every option navigates with CDP Page.navigate, which returns at once, as the original did.

The original is Tools/web-test/sourcemap.mjs before commit 70532ccd85. It used its own CDP pipe in Tools/canvas-test/driver.mjs, attached to the page with a flattened session. It printed pausedGeneratedLine and scriptParsedMapUrl. It asserted the paused line is within one of the expected line, and the function name is render, jet_main or empty.

Edge cases. A closed page: the page handle in A and B checks page_live (line 1366) before every send and returns closed. A pause left open blocks the page, so each program resumes before it closes. Frames from another site in an iframe run in their own target, which the page session does not reach; this is a stated limit. Sharing the session chromedriver itself uses for the page is [INFERENCE] and is the build card's first live proof.

Migration. No code uses this surface yet. The only caller is the source-map twin under card #5072. Option D restores the deleted Node file.

options.name: A CDP handle for one page, and named debugger facts on events
options.gist: page.protocol("cdp") sends to that page. A pause and a parsed script add named facts to the event; nothing else of the event is kept.
options.detail:
New public items, six in all. BrowserPage.protocol(kind) returns a BrowserProtocol for that page, and accepts only "cdp". "bidi" is refused, because BiDi commands already name their page, and a second BiDi handle would be a second way to send them (I8).

On first use the handle asks chromedriver for the page's session with goog:cdp.getSession. That method joins the protocol allowlist (C_BIDI_2024_11) behind the same CDP check as goog:cdp.sendCommand. Every send then carries the session, which never leaves Core. Its subscribe names this page, so next_event yields only this page's events.

BrowserEvent gains frame_line(), frame_column() and frame_function_hash(), from the top frame of Debugger.paused. It also gains source_map_url_hash() from Debugger.scriptParsed, and url_hash() is filled from that event's url. browser.fact_hash(text) becomes public, so a program can compare any hash fact with a string it knows.

The beginner path does not change. Each further debugger fact, such as scope values or other frames, needs its own ballot.

options.name: A CDP handle for one page, and the raw debugger event
options.gist: page.protocol("cdp") sends to that page. A debugger event carries its raw params as JSON text, which the tool decodes into its own struct.
options.detail:
BrowserPage.protocol("cdp") is the same as in A.

BrowserEvent gains payload(), the event's CDP params as JSON text. It is filled only for Debugger events and is never written to the trace. A payload over 64 KiB arrives empty, and payload_truncated() says so. The cap matters because the queue counts events, not bytes, and a pause with deep scopes can run to tens of KiB.

The tool decodes the text with json.parse and decode into structs it declares with #Rename(.Camel). That decode was probed and runs. Two accessors serve every debugger field, now and later.

The cost is the event rule: events stop being named facts for one protocol domain. A second domain that asks for raw events, such as network bodies, then has no principled refusal.

options.name: The tool speaks CDP itself over a WebSocket
options.gist: No Core change. The tool starts the pinned Chromium, connects with core.net.ws and writes its own small CDP client, as the original did in Node.
options.detail:
The tool finds the pinned Chromium with browser.locked("chromium") and starts it with --remote-debugging-port=0. It reads the port from the DevToolsActivePort file and connects with ws.connect. It then attaches to a page and matches replies to commands by id. The whole program below type-checks today on the dev compiler.

The tool can read every field. But it is a second CDP client beside Core's checked one, and other ported tools would copy it. It skips the protocol check, the trace and the redaction. The public WsConn.recv has no timeout, so a hung browser hangs the tool. The tool must start, poll and stop Chromium itself.

options.name: Defer: keep the live half in Node
options.gist: No new API. Restore sourcemap.mjs for the live half; the Jet twin keeps only the static half.
options.detail:
The deleted Node file comes back beside Tools/web-test/SourceMap.jet. The Jet twin checks the static half: the fetches, the map decoding and the wasm section. Criterion c3 of card #5072 stays open on this ballot.

A stand-in that runs page script, such as reading new Error().stack, is not an option. No page script can see a debugger pause or Chrome's scriptParsed event, so it would print the same line while testing something else.

decisions.title: Shared lifecycle operations without a universal runtime
decisions.gist: Should lifecycle integrations reuse existing operations instead of defining another general runtime?
decisions.lesson: A lifecycle says how work starts, survives an update, and stops. The captured interpreter backend repeats registration work in run, hot_swap and restart. Sharing that setup does not make a task durable or a job merely local. The example shows the distinction between preserving compatible live state and starting a new process; both options must retain it.
decisions.story: Kai adds a long-running integration. Cancellation, waiting, failure reporting, and identity should reuse existing machinery rather than introduce another scheduler or supervisor.
decisions.inWild:
import asyncio
async def work():
    return 42
async def main():
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group:
        task = group.create_task(work())
    print(task.result())
asyncio.run(main())
Source-composed TaskGroup example. Python documents waiting for child tasks at context exit. This does not prove persistent jobs or Jet runtime parity. https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html#task-groups
decisions.detail:
No new type, public method, executor, resource category or I9 exception is authorized. Domain-specific event loops and foreign runtime adapters may remain necessary; reuse means common semantic operations, not pretending all hosts have the same execution model. Durability, cancellation, retry, acknowledgment and capability authority must remain observable. No exactly-once external side-effect guarantee is implied.

Source evidence:

Source/JitBackend.rs:54-69,81-96,120-135

crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Services.rs:6-12,139-165

crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/TaskGroup.rs:470-660

crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Deadline.rs:1

crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Service.rs:10-45,84-118

Captured work:
Prior finding 8 and tactical ambient-registration consolidation.
Shared planned lifecycle, service, UI, job and foreign-runtime operations; retain domain acceptance criteria.

Required evidence before implementation closure:
Run/hot-swap/restart retention and reset transitions.
Cancellation, child failure, teardown and repeated initialization without stale registrations.
Service authority, durable acknowledgment/retry and deadline behavior remain unchanged.

Example status: current snippets are explicitly source-composed or captured source/test expectations. This preparation ran no Jet compiler, provider or UI scenario. Proposed alternatives are design contracts, not implemented behavior. No peer example proves Jet semantics.

Current source boundary: the three repeated paths are methods of InterpreterBackend implementing the JitBackend interface. Compiled-JIT migration, live-value retention and repeated-registration behavior are not proved by that source observation. Any wider reuse must be justified by matching operations, not common names.

Contribution or failure trial (proposed acceptance, not an observed run):

A: Contributor trial: add one required interpreter host binding. Shared setup installs it for run, hot-swap and restart. The existing per-mode reset/retention rules remain separate.

B: Same trial: update three interpreter setup paths. Omitting hot-swap setup must fail the transition check when that binding is needed. This option adds no new runtime.

The concrete consolidation is interpreter registration only. Cranelift run uses reset_one_shot_core_state and try_resident; hot-swap and restart use distinct resident paths. Do not make those paths call interpreter setup.

Compiled hot-swap clears network handles and interrupts while retaining runtime state; fresh run and invocation have other heap/module reset rules. Preserve each transition at its existing owner. No migration success is claimed here.

For other domains, reuse only an already-matching operation such as the existing deadline or task-group primitive. This is not permission to merge Task, durable Job, Stream, service, GUI or foreign event loops.

options.name: Shared operations with explicit policies
options.detail: Factor repeated ambient registration while preserving each mode’s exact state clearing and retention. New services, streams, UI integrations and durable work must use the existing scheduler, task-group, failure, deadline, channel and marshalling owners wherever they perform the same operation. Policy functions remain explicit. Do not automatically create a universal Service, Resource or Async object. A later type-family ballot can unify public artifacts if it preserves their actual guarantees.

options.name: Separate interpreter setup paths
options.detail: Keep the existing InterpreterBackend mode-specific registration/setup paths. Each remains responsible for its own reset, retention and teardown ordering and must prove the transition matrix. This option does not authorize a new executor, scheduler, public resource type or weakened lifecycle contract.

comparisons.note: Source-composed TaskGroup example. Python documents waiting for child tasks at context exit. This does not prove persistent jobs or Jet runtime parity. https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html#task-groups

async def work():
    return 42
async def main():

asyncio.run(main())

recommendation.why: Shared operations remove duplicated machinery while leaving different completion and authority promises checkable.

whyNot.reason: Keeping three copies makes a shared binding change a multi-site edit. Mode-specific reset and retention can remain explicit without duplicating installation.

recommendation.tradeoff: Domain policies remain explicit where their observable promises differ.

decisions.title: How a probe reads whether a Jet HTTP server is ready: both a method and a built-in route, a method only, or a route only
decisions.situation: Card #3078 c16 asks for readiness to be a state a probe can read through drain: not ready, ready, draining and closed. Today the server tracks its phases privately. Its only public signal is the stdout ready line. Nothing tells a draining server from a ready one, and a supervisor or load balancer can't ask. This vote picks the public shape. A gives a method on HTTPServer and a built-in probe route built on it. B gives the method only. C gives the route only. We recommend A.
decisions.gist: Should a server's readiness be read by a method and a built-in probe route, by the method only, or by the route only?
decisions.lesson: A readiness probe asks a running server whether to send it traffic. The answer changes while the program runs. It is no before the server serves and yes while it serves. It turns no again as soon as shutdown starts, while admitted requests still finish.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A probe is a check that a supervisor runs again and again against a program. Kubernetes, load balancers and systemd all run them. A readiness probe decides whether traffic is sent. A liveness probe decides whether the program is restarted.

Draining is the time after shutdown starts. No new work is admitted, and requests in flight get up to a grace period to finish. Binding opens the port; serving starts taking connections from it. Between the two, the kernel queues connections but nobody answers them.
decisions.story:
Ana deploys app.serve() behind a load balancer that checks a path every 5 seconds. Under B she has no server value to ask, because serve never returns. She moves to bind, runs serve in a task, and writes a second admin server whose route calls server.readiness().

Under A and C she points the load balancer at /__jet/ready and writes nothing. On SIGTERM the route answers 503 draining until the requests in flight end. The balancer stops sending traffic before the port closes.

Her colleague Raj also needs the database pool in the answer. Under A he serves a /ready route on a private admin listener. It combines server.readiness() with pool.ready(). The public balancer keeps using /__jet/ready.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides: the public shape of #3078 c16. It builds on c1, not ready before resources are usable, and c2, shutdown stops admission before resources close. It adds no new error code.

Current code, on the #3078 c9 stack, is in Core/Http/Server.jet. __HTTPServerState (:264-273) holds a phase and a stopping flag. Phase 0 is bound, 1 is serving and 2 is finished. serve (:297-359) moves phase 0 to 1 and accepts until stopping is set or its accept is cancelled. It then waits up to the drain budget for live connections (:348-353). Last it sets phase 2 with its report.

shutdown(grace) (:367-375) sets stopping. bind (:554-577) opens the listener with the state at phase 0. None of this is public. A signal-cancelled accept drains without setting stopping (:329-330). So the private state can't yet tell draining from serving there. Every option fixes that by setting stopping when the accept loop ends.

The states, the same for every option:
- NotReady: bound, not yet serving. The kernel queues connections, so a plain TCP probe reads ready too early.
- Ready: serving and accepting.
- Draining: shutdown called, or accept cancelled by a signal, with admitted requests still finishing.
- Closed: serve has reported. Also the state when shutdown runs before serve ever starts.

Bind failure: bind returns Err and no HTTPServer exists. There is no state to read under any option. A probe gets connection refused, which every prober reads as not ready. A settings failure (#3078 c14) exits 78 before bind, with the same result.

Out of scope: resource health after start, such as a pool going bad. c1 is met by building resources before bind (D-VERDICT-3086-1=A). A live resource check is the expert path under A and B.

options.name: Both: HTTPServer.readiness() -> HTTPReadiness, and a built-in GET /__jet/ready route that answers from it
options.gist: No code for the common probe; the state is readable when a program needs more.
options.detail:
The method of B, plus the route of C, which answers from readiness(). It follows C's drain rule. A handler has no accessor for its own server, and A adds none. So a composed probe lives on a private admin listener, or reads a cell the program fills with the server after bind.

Beginner path: as C, nothing to write. Expert path: read the state and combine it with pool.ready(). Serve that on a private admin listener, or through a cell filled after bind.

Gain: both paths, and the route and the method can't disagree because one reads the other. Loss: the surfaces of B and C together.
options.technical: Proposed, not implemented. The work of B, then the work of C with the route handler calling readiness(). Proof: the AppLifecycle golden prints each state as the method reports it. Beside it, it prints what the route answers, through the drain.

options.name: A method only: HTTPServer.readiness() -> HTTPReadiness { NotReady, Ready, Draining, Closed }
options.gist: The program reads the state; any probe route is user code.
options.detail:
One public enum and one public method on HTTPServer. The method reads the private state under its lock, with no I/O. The four cases are as listed in the ballot detail.

Beginner path: app.serve() never returns a server, so a beginner gets nothing here. They must switch to bind, run serve in a task, and write a probe route. A route on the same app can't see its own server, since no handler accessor exists. So the usual answer is a second admin listener, or a cell filled after bind.

Expert path: full control. Combine the state with pool.ready() and serve it on a private admin port that the public balancer never sees.

Gain: the smallest surface, with no reserved path and no change to drain. Loss: probes need user code in every service, the Go pattern. The beginner path is the expert path.
options.technical:
Proposed, not implemented. Add HTTPReadiness: enum { NotReady, Ready, Draining, Closed } to core.http.server, exported in Prelude/Core.rows. Add a readiness(self) -> HTTPReadiness Never! method on HTTPServer. When serve's accept loop ends, it sets stopping before it drains, so a signal stop reads Draining.

Proof: the Examples/Network/AppLifecycle golden prints each state from a probe task. It reads NotReady after bind, Ready after serve starts and Draining during shutdown while a handler holds its lease. It reads Closed after the report. A case covers shutdown before serve, which reads Closed and was never Ready.

options.name: A route only: every served app answers GET /__jet/ready with 200 ready, or 503 draining
options.gist: Probes work with no user code; the state itself stays private.
options.detail:
Every app served with app.serve() or app.bind() answers GET /__jet/ready. The /__jet/ prefix already holds jet dev's /__jet/reload. The answer is 200 with the body ready, or 503 with draining. The route can't show NotReady, because nothing accepts before serve starts. NotReady is visible only through a method (A, B).

During drain, the server keeps accepting connections for the grace period. It stays within the admission limits it already enforces. A connection over those limits is refused as today. It answers /__jet/ready with 503 draining, and any other request with 503 and Connection: close.

Today the listener stops accepting at once and probes get connection refused. A load balancer can't tell that from a crash. Every user path also answers 503 during drain, so a liveness probe must not use a user path. A TCP liveness check keeps passing until Closed.

A user route on /__jet/ready takes the place of the built-in one, but under C it has no state to read. Beginner path: nothing to write; point the probe at /__jet/ready. Expert path: no way to read the state from code, so a custom route that adds the pool can't report draining.

Gain: the probe a deployment needs, with no code, from app.serve() too. Loss: one reserved path, the drain change, a wider overloaded count, and no read from code.
options.technical:
Proposed, not implemented. __app_table adds the route the same way the dev reload route is added (Core/Web/Web.jet:547). The serve accept loop goes on accepting during the drain budget, through the same __admit limits. It answers 503 and closes.

The ShutdownReport counts these as overloaded, not as accepted work. That widens overloaded from over the connection limits to also refused while draining. The spec text for the report changes with it. HTTPServer users who build their own HTTPMux get no route; only web.app does.

Proof: the AppLifecycle golden runs a probe client against /__jet/ready. It prints 200 ready, then 503 draining during the grace period, then connection refused after Closed.

comparisons.note: Readiness is a state that starts false, turns true, and turns false again on shutdown. A failing readiness probe removes the pod from its Service's endpoints. Source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/liveness-readiness-startup-probes/

ApplicationAvailability publishes ReadinessState, the shape of B. Actuator serves it as /actuator/health/readiness, the shape of C. Together they are A. Source: https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/features/spring-application.html#features.spring-application.application-availability
No readiness state. Each service writes its own handler and flips a flag before Server.Shutdown: B's expert path as the only path. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Server.Shutdown
comparisons.code:
var ready atomic.Bool
http.HandleFunc("/ready", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { if !ready.Load() { w.WriteHeader(503) } })

comparisons.note: Type=notify: the service sends READY=1 when it can serve and STOPPING=1 when it drains. The state is pushed, not polled. Source: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/sd_notify.html

recommendation.why: The owner's settings ruling (D-VERDICT-3086-1=A) rejected a design in which every author must remember a step. B repeats that for probes and leaves app.serve(), the beginner path, with no probe. C gives experts no way to add the pool to the answer. A gives both from one state, so they can't disagree.
gains: A deployed app gets a correct readiness probe, including 503 during drain, with no code.
Code can read the same state to compose its own probe.
A draining server answers 503 instead of refusing connections, so a load balancer can tell it from a crashed one.

losses.loss: New public names: the HTTPReadiness enum, its four cases, readiness() and the reserved /__jet/ready path.
losses.mitigation: The path sits under /__jet/, which jet dev already uses, and a user route replaces it.

losses.loss: During the grace period the drain answers new connections 503 with Connection: close instead of refusing them. The report's overloaded count widens to include them.
losses.mitigation: Admission of work still stops at once (c2). The existing admission limits cap these connections. Only the refusal becomes a readable answer, which load balancers need.

losses.loss: During drain every user path answers 503, so an HTTP liveness probe on a user path would restart a draining pod.
losses.mitigation: Point liveness at a TCP check, which passes until Closed; the guide says so.

losses.loss: A handler can't read its own server's state.
losses.mitigation: A composed probe lives on an admin listener or reads a cell filled after bind. A handler accessor would be a separate ballot.

whyNot.reason: Every service writes its own probe, and app.serve() users get none without moving to bind. That is the remember-a-step shape D-VERDICT-3086-1 rejected.
The state stays private, so an expert probe that adds the pool can't report draining, and NotReady is never visible.

recommendation.tradeoff: The no-code probe costs a reserved path and a drain that answers 503 instead of refusing.

reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude Opus. Adversarial model family: Claude Opus. Fresh agent: G6Meta-4. The recommended option holds after five fixes: an admin-listener expert path, a TCP liveness rule, capped drain answers, a method-only NotReady and a full name count.

decisions.title: Whether Jet's web server sends the Date header
decisions.situation: Every web response can carry a Date line saying when the server answered. The web standard requires it from any server with a clock, and caches and clients use it. Jet's server never sends it today, although Jet already formats that exact date style for other headers. You decide whether responses carry Date by default; we recommend yes, read from the program's clock so tests with a fake clock stay exact.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's web server add a Date header to every response by default?
decisions.lesson: A response header is a named line sent before the page. Date says when the response was made. The web standard says a server with a clock must send it. A adds Date to every response from the program's clock, so a test clock gives a fixed value. B keeps today's rule: handlers add it by hand. C adds it only outside tests.
decisions.explainer:
A web response starts with header lines, such as Content-Type, then the body. Date is one header. It records when the server produced the response, in one fixed format called IMF-fixdate.

The standard that defines HTTP says an origin server with a reasonably accurate clock must send Date on its normal responses. Caches use it to compute how old a stored response is. Clients use it to notice clock skew.

Jet's server writes every other framing header itself, but never Date. Jet already formats IMF dates for Last-Modified on static files, so nothing new is needed to produce it.

Option A adds Date to every response the server writes. The time comes from the program's clock, which tests already replace with a fake clock. So a test sees one fixed, predictable Date, while a real server sends the real time. A handler that sets Date itself keeps its own value.

Option B keeps today's behavior and documents that handlers add Date by hand. Option C adds Date only when the server runs outside tests.
decisions.story: Lena puts a small Jet API behind a shared cache. Responses arrive with no Date, so the cache cannot work out their age and stores them by its own guess. Her Go service on the same cache never had this problem, because Go's server adds Date itself.
decisions.detail:
Current state: the server serializer never writes Date. An IMF-fixdate formatter exists and is used only for Last-Modified (claim v3-H2:FknTw9bJsXM-B33). The serializer already owns Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, Trailer and Connection (v3-H2:FknTw9bJsXM-B29). Card #4635 owns the server serve paths.

RFC 9110 section 6.6.1 says an origin server with a clock must generate Date for 2xx, 3xx and 4xx responses, and may for 1xx and 5xx. A recipient cache with no Date must add one on receipt.

Source: ThePrimeagen's From TCP to HTTP course (FknTw9bJsXM), which lists Date among the common response headers used for caching (claims v3-H2:FknTw9bJsXM-B33; web-data-net:C76).

Proven approaches. Go's net/http adds Date unless the handler sets the header to nil. Node's http sets response.sendDate true by default. Rust's hyper adds Date by default and caches the formatted string, refreshing it once a second, so the header costs almost nothing per response. nginx always sends Date.

The known trap is test output that changes every second. Jet removes it the same way it handles all time: the header reads the program's clock service. Test fakes and D-EFFECT-HANDLE1 scoped replacement already control that clock.

options.name: Always send Date from the program's clock
options.detail: The server adds Date to every response it writes, unless the handler already set one. The value comes from the program's clock, so a test with a fake clock sees a fixed date. A real server sends the real time.
options.technical: The serializer reads the clock service once per second at most and reuses the formatted IMF-fixdate text, as hyper does. A handler-set Date passes through. The rule covers the supervised server, the lambda serve path and serve_once, so tests see the same header shape as production.

options.name: Handlers add Date by hand
options.detail: Today's rule stays. The server never adds Date. A handler that needs it formats the time and sets the header itself, and the documentation says so.
options.technical: No serializer change. A public IMF-fixdate helper is documented for handlers.

options.name: Send Date outside tests only
options.detail: The server adds Date when it runs for real and leaves it out under jet test, so test output never contains a time.
options.technical: The serializer checks whether the process runs under the test harness. Production and test responses differ in shape.

comparisons.note: net/http adds Date automatically; a handler can suppress it explicitly.
response.sendDate defaults to true.
Date is added by default and cached once per second.
comparisons.code:

Response::new(body)   // Date added by the server

recommendation.why: A makes Jet's server follow the standard every major server already follows, at almost no cost per response. Reading the program's clock keeps tests exact, which removes the one reason servers ever leave Date out.
recommendation.tradeoff: Raw response bytes in tests now include a Date line set by the test clock.
gains: Caches and clients get the header the standard requires.
Handlers never repeat a date line.
Tests see the same header shape as production.

losses.loss: Existing tests that compare raw response bytes gain one Date line.
losses.mitigation: Under a fake clock the line is fixed, so each expected output is updated once and stays stable; a one-time fixture update covers the corpus.

whyNot.reason: B breaks the standard by default and makes every handler repeat the same line.
C makes test responses differ from real ones, so no test can catch a missing Date.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Check that every 2xx, 3xx and 4xx response from the supervised server, the lambda serve path and serve_once carries one Date line in IMF-fixdate form. Check that a handler-set Date passes through unchanged.

Check that a fake test clock produces a fixed Date, and that the formatted value is reused within one second. Update raw-response fixtures in the corpus once.

decisions.title: A memory limit for each web request
decisions.situation: A web server handles many requests at once. If one request builds a huge list, today it can use all the machine's memory and take every other request down with it. Jet already gives each request a time limit, but not a memory limit. You decide whether each request gets its own memory budget; we recommend a generous default per request, adjustable per route, that ends only the request that goes over.
decisions.gist: Should each web request get its own memory budget, so one runaway request fails alone instead of taking down the server?
decisions.lesson: A budget is a limit on how much memory one request may use. A gives every request a generous default budget, adjustable per route. A request that goes over ends with a server error, and the others keep running. B adds the same budget but leaves it off unless a server sets it. C adds no per-request limit and relies on whole-process limits.
decisions.explainer:
A Jet web server runs each request as its own task. Jet already bounds request time: a deadline cancels a slow request. Memory has no such bound while the program runs. One request that builds a huge value can grow until the operating system kills the whole process, ending every request in flight.

Jet does have a static memory rule, which lets a function promise it allocates at most a fixed number of bytes. That is checked at build time and cannot know how big a user's request will be.

Option A gives every request a running memory budget. Memory the request's task allocates counts against it, and memory it frees counts back. Going over ends that request with a 500 server error and a log record naming the line that crossed the limit. Other requests keep running.

The default is generous, 128 MiB per request, which only runaway requests reach. A route that really needs more, such as an export, sets its own budget. Option B adds the same budget but leaves it off by default. Option C adds nothing and relies on limits for the whole process.
decisions.story: Jun's report endpoint builds the whole year's data in memory when a user picks a wide date range. One such request grows until the operating system kills the server, and 200 other users lose their pages mid-request.
decisions.detail:
Current state: bind and serve take (addr, mux, tls, deadline) and no memory budget (core-library.md:997-998). Request bodies have a shared size limit (core-library.md:984-986; D-CORE-HTTPBODYLIMIT1). D-FOUND-LIFECYCLE1 makes request deadlines a cancellation. D-AUTHORITY-MEM2=A gives a static Mem.Alloc(above: N) denial checked at build time, and D-STACKBOUND1 reports worst-case stack and heap per entry point. Card #4635 owns the serve paths. The v3 A2-langs re-read confirmed the gap (note 2).

Source: Richard Feldman on Roc's NIA platform (DzhIprQan68 17:13-18:33). It gives each request a bounded bump arena, frees everything after the response, and answers 500 when a request exceeds its cap (claims languages-a:R12, R13).

The 2026-10-05 synthesis held this as an evidence gap pending research on response-body escape, streaming and cancellation. This ballot answers those points in the technical text of option A.

Proven approaches. Erlang's max_heap_size kills only the offending process, the model for failing one request alone. Cloudflare Workers and AWS Lambda give each worker or invocation a fixed memory limit. Go and Node have no per-request limit, so one request can exhaust the process.

The known risks are false failures for legitimately large requests and memory that escapes the request. A handles the first with per-route budgets and the second by counting only the request task's live allocations.

options.name: A generous default budget per request, set per route
options.detail: Every request runs with a memory budget, 128 MiB by default. Live memory the request's task allocates counts against it. Going over ends that request with a 500 and a log record naming the allocation site. A route sets its own budget, or .Unbounded. Response bodies being streamed and data handed to shared state stop counting once ownership leaves the request.
options.technical: The request task carries an allocation account in the program allocator (D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1); child tasks inherit it. Crossing the budget raises the existing cancellation on that task, like a deadline, so cleanup runs. The serializer then writes 500 if no response has started, or closes the connection if one has. bind and serve gain limits: .{ request_memory: Bytes }, and mux routes accept memory:.

options.name: The same budget, off unless set
options.detail: The per-request budget exists, but servers have no limit until they set request_memory. Existing servers behave as today.
options.technical: As A, with the default .Unbounded.
options.code: http.serve(":8080", app, limits: .{ request_memory: 128.MiB }) ?? return

options.name: No per-request limit
options.detail: Servers rely on whole-process limits from the operating system or container. One runaway request can still end every request.
options.technical: No change.

// out of memory: the process is killed

comparisons.note: max_heap_size kills only the process that exceeds it.
No per-request memory limit; MaxBytesReader caps only the body.
Each worker isolate has a fixed memory limit.

recommendation.tradeoff: A rare request that legitimately needs more than the default fails until its route sets a larger budget.
gains: One runaway request no longer kills the server.
The failure names the line that crossed the limit.
Large routes opt into larger budgets explicitly.

losses.mitigation: The log record names the route and the bytes needed, and jet dev reports the peak per route, so the budget is set once before deploy.

whyNot.reason: B protects only servers whose authors already know to ask for it.

Check that crossing the budget after the response started closes the connection cleanly. Measure allocator overhead under the strict performance gate.

decisions.title: A field and a method with the same name
decisions.situation: An error object can store its cause in a field and offer a method that returns that cause. Jet currently rejects the shared name in its own encoding library, which prevents the compiler's JSON reader from loading before a user's program runs. The choice is whether fields and methods may share a name, or whether the error must lose its public field or its method. We recommend keeping both operations and letting field access and method calls select the requested operation.
decisions.gist: Can a field and a method share a name, or must the error API choose one?
decisions.lesson: The choice is member declaration and resolution, not error propagation or read-only storage. Shared cause data remains handle-free and typed.
decisions.explainer: Choose whether fields and methods have separate namespaces or share one member namespace. Separate namespaces keep the same name for both operations; access syntax chooses the operation.
decisions.story: Mira checks an encoding error's stored cause and sometimes asks its accessor for an owned cause. Core declares both, so loading the compiler's JSON reader currently rejects Core itself. She needs an ordinary rule, not a special-case exemption for this error.
decisions.inWild: Physically read https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch05-03-method-syntax.html: its Rectangle.width example declares a field and method with the same name. The text says parentheses mean the method; without parentheses Rust means the field. Supplementary exact sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/method-call-expr.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/field-expr.html. No external executable was run.
decisions.detail:
No D-MEMBER-NAMESPACE1 decision existed in canonical live Tower revision75711 or its history. STREAMS431/446 records an undecided question;450 shows this collision already existed on497. Main has now created card4905, c00hgc5h. Current Core/encoding/encoding.jet145 and160 declare public cause storage and a pure cause() accessor. Registration.rs1747-1756 emits E0105 with the message shown here; this implementation is not ratified law.

D-CALLVALUE1=B governs callable values and literal call-member shadowing. Source method_calls.rs7951-7978 currently tries callable fields before resolve_method_sig7989. Choosing A requires paired method-primary resolution, not just deleting a diagnostic. An inaccessible or ill-typed method must report its normal error, never fall through to a field. Existing computed, inherited, trait, generic and operator resolution remains.

Official Rust Book https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch05-03-method-syntax.html was physically read. Its same-named Rectangle.width field/method example distinguishes calls with parentheses from field access. Exact Reference URLs are https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/field-expr.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/method-call-expr.html. No Rust example or proposed Jet program was executed. This short choice changes no Syntax.rs keyword or sigil, invariant, error propagation, read-only-field rule or private Core permission.

options.name: Separate fields and methods
options.detail:
Reject duplicates within fields or within methods, not a field-versus-method pair. A value-position field read keeps its meaning. An ordinary member call chooses the existing method; only absence of a method permits the existing callable-field route. An inaccessible method or wrong arguments report the normal method error, never fall through to a field.

Invoke a callable field explicitly through value.field.call(args). Preserve existing member references, computed fields, inherited and trait methods, operator hooks, visibility, receiver access, effects and provenance. Preserve literal call-member shadowing. EncodingError keeps its public cause field and pure Never accessor. Both compiler paths must migrate their current callable-field-first lookup.

The separate Worker example stores a function that adds one and defines a method that adds ten. Input two produces twelve through the method, or three through step.call. EncodingError.cause is not callable. This example is authored, not executed; its function field and lambda spelling come from existing tests/closures.rs255-259. Same-name coexistence is proposed A.

options.name: Keep the field only
options.detail: One namespace keeps duplicate field/method declarations illegal. Remove EncodingError.cause() and migrate every method caller to its public cause field. The method currently returns a copied value that its caller owns separately. A field read can borrow the stored value instead; use ~err.cause when that separate copy is needed. Preserve cause field name/order/type, constructor literals and handle-free data. No replacement getter or hidden allocation is introduced.

options.name: Keep the method only
options.detail: One namespace remains. Move cause storage to a private differently named field and retain cause()/new()/with_cause(). A public field lets callers read err.cause and construct EncodingError{..., cause: None}. Those operations must change to cause() and the existing constructors when storage becomes private. Compiler records that describe and carry the stored fields must change together, not keep a stale cause field. Migrate every public field read/write/literal constructor and every checked native/Source carrier projection. No alias or field-name-based reporting inference is allowed.
options.code:
print(err.cause() == None)
// Use new()/with_cause(), not EncodingError{..., cause: None}.

comparisons.note: Official Book, physically read: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch05-03-method-syntax.html; its same-named width field/method example explains parentheses. Exact Reference URLs: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/field-expr.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/method-call-expr.html.
comparisons.code:
let field = e.cause;
let owned = e.cause();

recommendation.why: Preserve both existing operations with ordinary resolution rather than changing public error data.
gains: Existing cause access remains
No public field/constructor migration

losses.loss: Callable field overlaps a method name
losses.mitigation: Use value.field.call(args) for the field explicitly.

whyNot.reason: Retires the existing method and changes owned-reader callers.
Changes public data construction and all stored-shape projections.

recommendation.tradeoff: Explicit callable-field invocation makes the overlap teachable without removing data.

decisions.title: General defer: run any statement when a block ends
decisions.situation: Defer schedules work to run when the current block ends, so cleanup sits next to setup, such as logging the time right after a timer starts. Jai lets you defer any statement or block. Jet's rules allow only a deferred resource close, plus a library call, scope.guard, that runs a function at block end; the owner asked for defer when ratifying those rules. The vote decides whether `defer` takes any statement and replaces scope.guard; we recommend yes, keeping close as the one closing word.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's `defer` run any statement at block end, replacing scope.guard, like Jai's defer?
decisions.lesson: A block is code between braces. Defer runs a statement when its block ends, however it ends: normally, by return, by break, or by an error. Today only `defer close(^file)` works, `^` meaning the value is handed over; `scope.guard(() -> ...)` runs a function at block end. A and B reverse the rule against general defer.
decisions.story: Dev ports a Jai job system. Every worker marks a counter, logs its timing and restores a debug flag at the end of the block with defer. In Jet each of those needs a scope.guard value with a throwaway name and a closure.
decisions.detail:
Audit rows refer to Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md. Words used here. Jai is a systems programming language by Jonathan Blow, built for games, with no guardrails by default. `prep { }` runs Jet code while compiling. A `$` word such as `T.$fields` reads a fact the compiler knows. A `#Name` marker attaches a rule to the code below it. `package.jet` is a package's settings file. The main package is the one you build directly.

SEMANTICS UNDER A. `defer stmt` or `defer { block }` registers at that point and runs at every exit of its block: normal end, return, break or next, error exits and stops.

ORDER. Each block keeps one reverse-order list: a binding's automatic cleanup is registered at its declaration, and each defer where it is written. So `f := open(p); defer print(f.name)` prints before f closes.

VALUES. A return value is computed before deferred code runs: `n := 1; defer { n = 2 }; return n` returns 1. Deferred code sees variables as they are at exit.

SAFETY. Ownership is checked in run order: a deferred action may not use a value that an earlier-running action consumed. So `defer f.flush()` written before `defer close(^f)` is an error, because close runs first. A deferred body may not return, break, next or use `?`. A failing call inside must be handled there, so an exit never carries two errors. Each rule has a registered code (I4).

Deferred code's effects join the enclosing function's row, and unsafe operations inside still need `#Unsafe("reason")`.

TIERS AND STOPS. Defers run exactly where automatic cleanup runs, on every profile. Under `--small` (abort on panic), neither runs on a panic, as today, so defer adds no tier difference (I9). During cancellation, deferred code runs like cleanup, with wait points inside shielded. An explicit process stop runs active defers. A host kill does not.

PLACES. Defer is legal in any block, including expression and prep blocks, but not at module scope. Inside a macro (D-JAI-CODE1), a defer in the pasted code runs when that pasted block ends. Attaching work to the caller's block is not proposed.

RESOURCES. `defer close(^x)` stays the one closing word (S63). A lint flags `defer x.release()` on a resource and suggests `close(^x)`, so A does not revive the per-type closing verbs of D-SHAPE-RESOURCE2's rejected option C.

AMENDS. S63's rule 'There is no general deferred statement or block' (E0003) is reversed. scope.guard (`core.mem.scope`) retires in one cutover, with its examples moved to defer. The owner's comment when ratifying D-SHAPE-RESOURCE1 was 'But I want to support defer and have one consistent word for closing any type'.

WORK. A general Defer node replaces the close-only one through the AST, TIR and code generators, and about thirty sema walkers learn it.

EVIDENCE. Jai defer (The Way to Jai. Blow QX46eLqq1ps 00:23:40-00:28:30 and jjCfAg_gtDw 01:32:24, from the mining notes). Blow replaced destructors with defer and macros. Zig and Swift use block-scoped defer. Go's function-scoped defer is a known trap in loops.

decisions.title: A sandboxed app sees its machine's shared class, never the machine itself, with no limit on what it asks
decisions.situation: A portable Jet app is compiled on the machine that runs it, so it can use that machine's matrix units, wide vector instructions or GPU. To pick a fast path, its code reads facts about the hardware, and each fact helps a tracker tell machines apart. The approved rule shows a sandboxed app rounded facts about every device, and each hardware package writes its own rounding. We recommend that a portable app see the facts of a machine class that many machines share, with no limit on what it asks.
decisions.gist: What may a sandboxed app learn about the machine it runs on?
decisions.lesson: A fingerprint is a set of facts that together pick out one machine, so a site can follow a user without cookies. Facts are safe to share when many machines give exactly the same ones. A machine class is such a set: a named bundle of hardware facts that a large crowd of machines all meet. Native programs are trusted and keep full hardware facts under every option.
decisions.story: Dana ships a photo app as one portable file. It asks whether the GPU has matrix units, whether there is 16 GiB of memory, and reads the vector width. On her friend's machine the app takes the fast path. Every answer came from the class her friend's machine belongs to, which thousands of other machines share.
decisions.detail:
Today. `$build.os` and `$build.profile` print Linux and dev on o0, o1 and o2 (probe h6b). Reading `$build.cpu`, `$build.hardware` or `$build.arch` is E0107, "Nothing named `$build` exists here" (probes h1, h2, h6). `jet build --target=portable` and every wasm target are E2104, not built yet. No program reads hardware facts today, so no running program changes under any option.

Ratified law. D-HOST-CAPS1=A gives typed hardware descriptions read through `$build.hardware`, and `requires:` and `uses:` on outputs. Packages add hardware kinds with `satisfies` and `coarse` methods. Its explainer says the host grants which facts a bundle sees, by default only coarse classes, and a coarse projection never overstates.

More ratified law. D-PORTABLE1=A compiles the app on the host from checked portable code. D-PORTABLE2=A says facts never grant powers. D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A and D-CORE-FEATURE-FLOW1=A give every chip path a plain Jet meaning tested equal, so a chip changes speed, not answers.

The gap. The package that defines a hardware kind also writes its `coarse` method. A kind package can return its input unchanged, so a value as precise as a serial number can reach the app. The default also shows every device, and no rule bounds how many facts add up.

Peer evidence. WebGPU says a user agent "must not reveal more than 32 distinguishable configurations or buckets" (W3C WebGPU draft of 27 October 2026, section 2.2). It lets browsers bin hardware limits into buckets (section 2.2.1). Adapter identifiers should be as broad as possible, with details only after user consent (section 2.2.6). A takes the buckets and the consent, but not the fixed count.

Java's Vector API exposes `FloatVector.SPECIES_PREFERRED`, the best vector shape for the current CPU (JEP 529). .NET exposes `Vector.IsHardwareAccelerated` (learn.microsoft.com). Both serve trusted code; neither bounds what untrusted code learns. WebAssembly's relaxed SIMD lets one instruction return different results on different engines, which itself reveals the machine (relaxed-simd Overview, Consistency).

What A means. Jet hosts ship a list of machine classes. A class is a named set of hardware facts, such as a vector width, matrix units and a memory floor. A class enters the list only when a large crowd of machines meets it. In a portable bundle, the host picks the most capable class this machine fully meets. Every `$build.hardware` answer and value the app reads is that class's.

More of A. An app may ask any number of questions and read any value, because all of them together reveal one class and nothing more. No count is fixed: a new class joins the list when enough machines meet it. A fact no class describes answers no, which changes speed only, because every chip path has the same meaning. The user may grant exact facts to one app, such as a benchmark, in the trust store.

What B means. Today's approved rule: a portable app sees the coarse description of every granted device, rounded by each kind's own `coarse` method. What C means. Portable code reads no hardware facts. `requires:` still admits or refuses the app, and Core's automatic chip copies still run, without the app's code seeing which.

Limits under every option. An app can time a loop and guess the chip, as WebGPU section 2.2.3 notes. Classes bound what facts reveal, not what timing reveals. Separate processes, the side-channel hardening D-PORTABLE2 requires for shared processes, and coarse timers are host policy outside this vote. Native outputs are trusted and keep every fact under every option.

Amends. A narrows D-HOST-CAPS1's portable view from each kind's coarse projection to the host's class list. `coarse` stays for descriptions, refusal messages and native code. B amends nothing. C removes hardware facts from portable code. The approved examples spell the branch `prep if`, which is retired; this ballot uses `comptime if`.

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-portable-target-capabilities.md. Review: author Claude (MemDesign-2 lane); no fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

Why no fixed count. A fixed count bounds how many machines a page can tell apart, but it also caps how many hardware facts any app may use. What protects a user is that the crowd sharing their answers is large. A class list keeps every crowd large and lets the list grow with new hardware, so neither the number of questions nor the number of classes needs a cap.

options.name: Shared machine classes, no limit
options.detail:
A portable app reads hardware facts as usual, but every answer and value comes from the machine's class. A class is a named set of facts that a large crowd of machines meets, from a list Jet hosts ship. The host picks the most capable class the machine fully meets.

An app may ask as many questions as it likes, since together they reveal only the class. A fact no class describes answers no, which changes only speed. The user can grant exact facts to one app. Native programs keep every fact.
options.technical: In `form: .Portable` outputs, `$build.hardware` is evaluated against the selected class description, not host observations or a kind's `coarse`. Class selection: the most capable list entry whose every fact the host observed and granted. The class name joins the cache key. The list is host data versioned with the host; an entry needs a published crowd size. A trust-store grant per app hash switches that app to exact facts. `coarse` keeps its role in descriptions, refusals and native builds. Diagnostic code and spelling land under I7.

options.name: Coarse descriptions of every device
options.detail:
A portable app sees the coarse description of every granted device, as the approved rule says. Each hardware kind rounds its own values with its own `coarse` method.

No rule bounds how many facts an app sees in total.
options.technical: No change to D-HOST-CAPS1. `$build.hardware` in portable code exposes the coarse projection of each granted entry, written by each kind's package.

options.name: No hardware facts in portable apps
options.detail:
Portable code cannot read hardware facts. `requires:` still admits or refuses the app at install and launch.

Core's own automatic chip copies still run, chosen by the host without the app's code seeing which one.
options.technical: Amends D-HOST-CAPS1: `$build.hardware` reads are a build error in `form: .Portable` outputs. Requirements and Core multiversioning are unchanged.

comparisons.note: Limits and adapter details are binned; at most 32 distinguishable configurations. Source: W3C WebGPU sections 2.2, 2.2.1, 2.2.6
The Vector API gives any code the preferred vector shape for the CPU. Source: openjdk.org/jeps/529
Any code can ask whether vector hardware is present. Source: learn.microsoft.com, System.Numerics.Vector.IsHardwareAccelerated

recommendation.why: A keeps every fast path an app can name while each user stays in a large crowd, whatever a hardware package's own rounding says. Nothing is capped: apps ask what they need and the class list grows with new hardware. Because every chip path has one meaning, a fact no class describes costs only speed.
gains: No limit on questions or on kinds of machine.
Every user stays inside a large crowd.
Apps may read values, not only yes or no.
A hardware package cannot leak precise values into apps.

whyNot.reason: B trusts every hardware package to round its own values, and nothing keeps the facts an app adds up shared by a crowd.
C stops an app from choosing its own algorithm for the hardware, which A allows without a limit.

recommendation.tradeoff: Brand-new hardware gets its nearest listed class until enough machines share its facts. That costs speed, never answers, and a user can grant one app exact facts.

decisions.title: The same portable app file also runs in a web browser, translated in the page
decisions.situation: Jet's portable app file holds checked Jet code that each machine compiles for itself, which is meant to beat WebAssembly. Browsers run only JavaScript and WebAssembly, so today's approved plan gives the web its own separate build. Then one program ships as two artifacts with two checking paths. We recommend that the same app file also run in a browser, checked and turned into WebAssembly inside the page.
decisions.gist: Should one portable Jet app file run both on a computer and in a browser tab?
decisions.lesson: WebAssembly is the portable code format every browser runs. A host is the program that checks an app file and runs it. Under A, a small Jet host compiled to WebAssembly loads the app file in the page and translates it. In the browser the app runs at WebAssembly speed; outside it, at native speed.
decisions.story: Lee ships a notes app as one file. Colleagues run it from the terminal at native speed. A client opens a link and the same file runs in the browser tab, refused only for the file access a browser page cannot grant.
decisions.detail:
Today. No portable or web output builds. `jet build --target=portable`, `--target=web`, `--target=wasm32-wasip2` and `--target=wasm32-unknown-unknown` all stop with E2104, "is not built yet" (probe w/hello.jet). There is no `.jetapp` code in Compiler/ or Core/. So no shipped program changes under either option.

Ratified law. D-PORTABLE1=A makes the app file versioned, content-hashed portable code that the host verifies and compiles locally. Its text says running in a browser needs a separate adapter. D-PORTABLE2=A adds a machine-code checker for native hosts. D-WASISRV1=A keeps WebAssembly as an export for WASI hosts. D-LEARN-WEB1=A already puts Jet's checker in the page as WebAssembly.

Work in flight. Card #5201 builds a JetIR to JavaScript and WebAssembly back end. Card #5487 (done) runs plugin WebAssembly through JetIR and Jet's own back end, the opposite direction. D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1=A turns a profile's missing facts into denied effects, so a browser profile with no file system denies file access.

Measured cell. The same F32 multiply-add loop, one million values for 400 passes, written in C. Native gcc -O2 took 0.059 s, and 0.044 s with -march=native. Zig's wasm32-wasi build under Wasmtime 48 took 0.122 s with SIMD and 0.324 s without, cold compile included. The machine had load near 90, so treat these as indicative.

The same loop in Jet took 1.72 s at o2 and 2.50 s at o1, minimum of five runs. That native gap is a separate performance finding. So inside a browser the app is bounded by WebAssembly speed. Outside one, local native compilation is what beats WebAssembly.

Peer evidence. Pyodide runs CPython compiled to WebAssembly in the page. Roc's in-browser REPL ships its whole compiler as about 6 MB of WebAssembly (D-LEARN-WEB1 detail). WebAssembly SIMD is fixed at 128 bits, and relaxed SIMD allows engine-dependent results (relaxed-simd Overview, Consistency).

What A means. A Jet host written in Jet, compiled to WebAssembly, loads the app file in the page. It runs the same verifier, compares powers with the page's grants, and translates the checked code to WebAssembly with the same back end as the web export. The browser's engine provides the walls, so the native machine-code checker is not needed there.

More of A. GPU work uses the WebGPU device library. Native-width vector lanes are four F32 values wide in the page. A build may also write a ready-made WebAssembly copy beside the app file, made by the same translator; the page uses it when its hash matches, to skip the in-page translation.

What B means. Today's approved plan. The app file runs only where a Jet host is installed. The web gets a separate `jet build --target=web` from source, with its own artifact.

Amends. A amends D-PORTABLE1's sentence that a browser needs a separate adapter: the adapter becomes the in-page host for the same file. `--target=web` stays as the ready-made copy. B amends nothing.

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-portable-target-capabilities.md. Review: author Claude (MemDesign-2 lane); no fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

options.name: One app file, also in the browser
options.detail:
A small Jet host, compiled to WebAssembly, loads the app file in the page. It checks the file with the same verifier, asks for the page's grants and turns the code into WebAssembly with the same translator as the web build.

A build may also write a ready-made WebAssembly copy beside the app file, which the page uses when its hash matches. Behavior change: an app that needs a power a page cannot grant, such as files, is refused in the browser with the missing fact named.
options.technical:
The host is Jet source built for the browser profile (D-FREESTAND-WASM1), reusing the #5201 back end and the D-PORTABLE1 verifier. Walls come from the WebAssembly engine; D-PORTABLE2's checker applies to native hosts only.

Grants map to page permissions; absent facts deny effects per D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1. `Lanes<F32>` is four wide on SIMD128. Ready-made copies are keyed by app hash and translator version. The loader spelling is illustrative.

The two artifacts are checked by different paths: the host verifier for the app file, and the compiler for the web build.

decisions.title: What a map literal does when two of its keys are equal
decisions.situation: When one map literal writes the same key twice, Jet today keeps the later value and silently drops the earlier one. A beginner course shows the trap: a pasted second level entry quietly replaced the real level. Jet's own JSON reader already refuses a repeated name. You decide what a repeated key in a literal does; we recommend refusing it, at check time for written keys and at run time when computed keys collide.
decisions.gist: When one map literal contains the same key twice, should Jet refuse it or keep one of the values?
decisions.lesson: A map stores values under keys. A map literal writes all its pairs at once, so each key is meant to appear once. Today a repeated key keeps the later value and silently loses the earlier one. A refuses repeated keys: at check time when they are written out, and with a stop naming both entries when computed keys collide. B refuses only written-out repeats. C keeps today's rule and adds a warning.
decisions.explainer:
A map is a collection that stores each value under a key, like a word and its meaning. A map literal is the written form that builds one in a single expression. Each pair in it is an entry.

Today Jet builds the literal one entry at a time. When a later entry has a key that an earlier entry already used, the later value replaces the earlier one. Nothing reports it. The map simply has fewer entries than the literal shows.

Keys can be written out, such as the text "level", or computed, such as a variable. Written-out repeats can be found before the program runs. Computed keys are only known while it runs.

A treats any repeat as a mistake. Written-out repeats are an error when you check the program. Computed keys that turn out equal stop the program with a report naming the key and both entries. When you really mean to replace a value, you write a separate assignment after the literal.

B refuses written-out repeats but keeps the later value for computed keys, as Go does. C keeps today's rule and adds a warning for written-out repeats.
decisions.story: Ana builds a player record whose level comes from a parameter. She pastes an old line that also sets level to 99. Every new player now starts at level 99, the program runs without complaint, and nothing points at the pasted line.
decisions.detail:
Observed 2026-10-05 on the dev candidate jet (built 14:16 from dev 05ea86f65) and on the main checkout's debug jet. A literal with "level" twice prints the later value 99 and checks clean. A literal whose two variable keys are equal prints length 1 and keeps the later value. Probes: p02_dup_map_key.jet and p12_dynamic_dup_key.jet in the batch report.

Jet already refuses repeated names elsewhere. The JSON parse, decode and reader reject a repeated object name with its path and position; the allow_duplicates siblings are the explicit opt-in (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:2170-2174). The owner's 2026-10-05 DataTree ruling makes duplicate object keys a parse error with an explicit opt-in (card #4602, D-DATATREE-RULES1).

Source evidence: a beginner Python course demonstrates repeated level keys in one dictionary literal silently keeping the last value (youtube 4M87qBgpafk, 05:54-05:56). Python's reference states clashes between duplicate keys are not detected and the rightmost value prevails.

options.name: Repeated keys are an error
options.detail: Written-out keys that are equal are a check error. The report points at both entries and offers to delete one. Computed keys that turn out equal while running stop the program with a report naming the key and both entry positions. Intended replacement is written as an assignment after the literal, such as stats["level"] = 99.
options.technical: Sema compares literal, enum-case and constant-folded keys with the key type's equality and reports a registered error at the second entry with a note at the first. Runtime literal construction already locates each key's slot before inserting; a found slot raises a registered stop instead of overwriting. No extra hashing, no extra pass and no allocation are added. The same rule covers every tier and the comptime evaluator. Corpus migration: rewrite any intentional overwrite to an explicit assignment.

options.name: Refuse written-out repeats only
options.detail: Written-out keys that are equal are a check error, as in A. Computed keys that turn out equal keep the later value, as today. This matches Go.
options.technical: Same check-time rule as A. Runtime construction keeps its current overwrite. A computed-key collision still loses an entry silently.

options.name: Keep the later value, warn on written-out repeats
options.detail: Today's rule stays: the later entry wins everywhere. A new warning marks written-out repeats. Warnings show in check and in the editor, not on jet run.
options.technical: Adds one advisory lint. Runtime behavior is unchanged.

comparisons.note: A constant key written twice in a map literal is a compile error. Computed keys overwrite.
The compiler warns on repeated literal keys, and any repeated key in a dictionary literal stops the program.
Duplicate keys are not detected; the rightmost value prevails.

decisions.title: `#Pre` is checked while compiling whenever the values it reads are known; no new mark
decisions.situation: A function states a rule about its arguments with `#Pre(condition, "message")`, checked when the program runs. A call such as `simd_width(6, xs)` can never pass, yet it builds and stops later. The first draft added `##Pre`, a second mark that also made parameters compile-time without saying so. This revision adds nothing to learn. A `#Pre` is decided while compiling whenever the values it reads are known then, the rule you chose for `::` values.
decisions.gist: How should a rule on a function's arguments be checked while compiling, when the call's values are fixed?
decisions.lesson: `#Pre(lanes == 4, "need 4 lanes")` is a rule every call must keep. When a call passes fixed values, such as the number 6, the compiler can work out the answer itself. Under A it does, and a call that can never pass fails to build, on the caller's line, with the author's message.
decisions.story: Ivo calls a library's `simd_width(6, readings)`. Today it builds and ships, then stops on a customer's machine with "need 4 or 8 lanes", a rule the library stated all along. Under A, his build fails on that line with the same message. The library author wrote nothing new.
decisions.detail:
Why the draft was revised. `##Pre` added a second compile-time mark, although D-META-HASH1 A made `#` the one mark. It turned each parameter the rule reads into a compile-time one without a word at the parameter, so each distinct value built its own copy. A run-time value at a call then became an error. That is a hidden cost and behavior change (philosophy principle 8) and a new concept (principle 7).

The rule A uses already exists. D-COMPTIME-WORD1 A, which you ratified, computes every `::` value while compiling whenever it can and falls back to run time otherwise. `comptime` is the one word that requires it. A applies the same rule to `#Pre`: a pure condition over values known while compiling is worked out then. D-PREPOST1 already makes every `#Pre` pure.

What A does at each call. If every value the rule reads is known while compiling, such as a literal, a `::` constant or a `comptime` parameter, the compiler decides the rule. False is a build error on the caller's line, with the message and the values. True means that call carries no run-time check, as a proved check is erased (D-PROVE-SEM1). Otherwise the check runs when the program runs, as today.

If working out the rule runs past the compile-time step budget, the check stays at run time, as a `::` value does; it is never dropped. `#Post` needs nothing new: when a whole call is computed while compiling under D-COMPTIME-WORD1, its `#Post` is checked then too.

Requiring a fixed value. Some functions need the value fixed, for example to pick a vector width. The author writes `comptime lanes: Int`, the ratified spelling (D-COMPTIME-WORD1 A, D-CONSTGEN2 A). Every call then passes a fixed value, so every `#Pre` on it is decided while compiling. The first draft's option B is that case of A, not a separate rule.

Probes on dev, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-3/probes/pre, on o0, o1 and o2. pre.jet calls `width(6, …)` against `#Pre(lanes == 4, …)`: it builds, prints 6, then stops with E3001 on line 8. The first draft's internal compiler error no longer happens. In early.jet the same call sits in a file constant, `BAD :: width(6, …)`. `jet check` passes and the run stops at startup, so early `::` evaluation is not built yet either.

More probes. prepre.jet: `##Pre` is E0003. lead.jet: a `comptime` parameter is E0003, since it is ratified but not built. ctif2.jet: `comptime if` on a plain parameter is E0989. Census (probes/pre/census.mjs): 26 `#Pre` lines, 5 in Examples and 21 in tests; none in Core.

Overlap. Jet has one contract form, `#Pre` and `#Post` (D-PREPOST1); `#Require` was a placeholder name and was archived. Markers, `comptime` and generic recipes (D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1) keep their meaning. A adds no syntax, no error code beyond the build-time form of the existing contract failure, and no rule for parameters.

Review. Author: Claude (MemDesign-3 lane), revising the Main draft after the owner said he was not happy with it. No fresh adversarial pass has run on this revision.
