decisions.title: Require an early marker expression with Jet's existing #run, not a new sigil
decisions.situation: A library sometimes needs a bad argument rejected before the program starts. An ordinary precondition can check a runtime input, so it does not require that early answer. The owner asked for a cohesive way to choose early checking without turning every argument into a generic parameter. Jet already has a request for required early evaluation: #run. Choose whether to reuse that request inside marker expressions or add a general marker-wide mode. We recommend #run on the expression whose answer must be known, with ordinary calls unchanged.
decisions.gist: Should marker expressions use the same #run request as every other required early expression?
decisions.lesson: #Pre says what must be true. #run says when its expression must have an answer: while building. Combining them keeps those meanings instead of inventing another hash. It does not run the whole function early.
decisions.explainer: A required check fails the build when inputs are unavailable or evaluation cannot complete. A number parameter is a compile-time generic value. Distinct generic instances need not imply distinct emitted machine bodies if the compiler can share them safely.
decisions.story: Ola requires a lane count of four or eight before accepting a call, while the list itself remains runtime data. Every option adds [1,2,3,4] to 10. The example tests a contract, not SIMD performance.
decisions.inWild: Zig's comptime expressions and parameters make an early requirement explicit. C++ constant evaluation likewise differs from merely hoping an optimizer folds an expression. These are documented comparisons, not peer performance measurements.
decisions.detail:
Revision 3 answers q3ybwski, q8sdri5o and q1x848xv together. Required early call validation is the job, not duck typing or currying. F writes #Pre(#run { lanes == 4 || lanes == 8 }, "need 4 or 8"). Parentheses belong to Pre; #run owns its braced expression. No new sigil, parameter grammar or build-error operation is needed.

Marker application and code generation happen while building, but a Pre predicate describes each invocation's inputs. Post describes its result. Under F, required evaluation happens at that contract's normal instantiation point. For Pre, substitute checked caller argument facts first, then use the canonical required evaluator. Do not evaluate an unbound parameter once while reading the declaration.

A false early Pre is a build error under D-PRE-COMPILE1=A. Unavailable inputs, invalid operations, refused effects and exhausted budgets are separate errors, never runtime fallback. Ordinary Pre retains its approved early-if-possible behavior. Unread arguments stay runtime values. Requiring a fact does not make the body parameter generic, permit type shaping, or execute the body early.

F's reach is general expression staging. #Post(#run { result > 0 }, "positive") needs an actual permitted early result fact or fails. User-marker delayed predicates use the same #run at their documented instantiation point. #Memo(bound: #run compute_bound()) requires an early bound. #Layout(c, align(#run alignment())) requires an early alignment. Already early expressions gain no power by repeating #run.

Legal sites, schemas and authority do not change. #Unsafe(#run reason()) computes a reason, not an unsafe action. Runtime allocators and callbacks cannot become build-time resources by wrapping them. Non-expression arguments cannot accept value regions. Every expression-bearing marker follows the same rule; other markers are unaffected. Verifying a Kernel or generating declarations does not run their target code.

Forwarding preserves checked requirements and their dependent argument facts. Known literals or pure early expressions discharge them at outer calls. Unknown runtime wrappers cannot hide them. Interfaces, methods, defaults and generic instances retain the same obligation. A plain callable or foreign callback cannot erase unresolved requirements: bind the arguments or preserve a contract-bearing callable type. Recursion keeps canonical budgets.

Beginner path: ordinary #Pre, ordinary parameters and ordinary calls. Expert path: add #run only to the expression requiring an early answer. Use number parameters separately when a value must shape types. Tools show required caller facts on the signature; the body keeps ordinary parameter semantics.

Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/Spellings.jet:26-38 registers current comptime value regions, explicit comptime parameters and $ facts. MathLayout.jet:756-759 owns the requirement word. D-META-SPELL1=A ratifies #run for required regions; D-META-HASH2=A ratifies #build and related filled-in values. A build: fn entry orchestrates a build, not arbitrary early application execution. Facts describe values, not evaluation requests.

Independent t17a a0.0.43 probes, jet run -: comptime { 2 + 2 } prints 4; <comptime N: Int> sum<4> prints 10. #run's value block gets E0733; $build.profile gets E0003. Pre containing a comptime value block is refused, including E0391. Ordinary false Pre prints before, then stops E3005. These prove implementation gaps, not working F syntax.

A is the owner's general ## alternative. It stages all dynamic expressions owned by a marker application, including user markers, at the documented checking point. Post needs early result proof. Runtime-resource or unknown obligations fail; already early markers gain nothing. This adds marker-wide grammar, unlike F's selective expression request. It is not restricted to Pre.

B's early number parameter is sound and useful for type shaping. It changes call organization when only predicate knownness is needed. It is not recommended merely because generic machinery exists. All options share one bounded pure evaluator; no machine-body duplication per count is assumed.

Adversarial verdict: F holds as a cohesive proposal, not current implementation. First try ordinary Pre: it cannot require knownness. Then reuse #run on the deferred expression that needs it. This removes a Pre-only switch. Forwarding and callable-erasure limits remain real and must appear in interfaces and diagnostics. No zero-cost or universal-proof claim is made. Breaking cutovers follow D-LANG-MIGRATE1=A's registered rewrites without retired-syntax teaching.

decisions.title: Carriage return and Unicode escapes in plain strings
decisions.situation: Web, mail and CSV formats end lines with carriage return then newline, but Jet text cannot spell the carriage return, so programs build it from raw byte numbers. Jet's own debug printing already shows text as "a\r\u{1b}", which Jet then refuses to read back. You asked for named terminal codes, easy helpers and a checked terminal-text form instead of raw codes in plain strings, and a companion vote, now ratified, provides exactly that. This vote decides only the plain-text floor beneath it: whether quoted text gains a carriage-return escape and one escape for any Unicode character.
decisions.gist: Add \r and \u{…} to quoted text, add \r only, or keep four escapes and use byte literals?
decisions.lesson: An escape is a backslash code inside quotes that stands for a character you cannot type or see. Jet strings know four: \n newline, \t tab, \" quote and \\ backslash. A carriage return is character 13; web headers end every line with carriage return plus newline. A Unicode escape \u{1F600} names any character by its hexadecimal number.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: write "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n" exactly as in RFCs, tutorials and other languages. Terminal colors and cursor moves do not use raw codes in plain text: the companion terminal vote gives checked ANSI{"[bold red]error:[/] {name}"} text and helpers such as tui.clearLine(). Expert path: write invisible or confusable characters by number, such as "\u{200B}" for a zero-width space, so a reviewer can see them. Byte literals keep their own \x0D form because bytes are not text.

Shared work under every option: E0001 lists the full escape set, the Rust and Jet lexers stay identical, and Debug output prints only escapes that the lexer reads back.
decisions.story: Ana writes a tiny HTTP client over a TCP socket. Every tutorial writes the request as "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n...", and Jet answers E0001. She copies a workaround that builds the two characters from byte numbers, then prints the request with Debug and sees \r again.
decisions.detail:
Suite revision by BallotSuite1, 2026-10-07. Wording only: the companion terminal vote D-TUI-ANSI1 was ratified as A on 2026-10-06, so the situation no longer calls it a proposal. Options and claims are unchanged.

YOUR QUESTION (q4p8lzbr, 2026-10-05)

You asked for three things. First, ANSI escape constants in the TUI Core library, so every terminal code lives in one place. Second, helpers that color text, clear lines, move or reset the cursor and switch to the alternate screen. Third, a strongly typed string literal for terminal codes, so they never mix with plain "" text.

Answer: yes, through the companion ballot D-TUI-ANSI1 on this card. It recommends core.tui constants (tui.ESC, tui.CSI), helpers (tui.moveCursor(row:, col:), tui.clearLine(), tui.altScreen(on:), tui.mouse(on:)) and a checked ANSI{"[bold red]error:[/] {name}"} literal. That literal makes a terminal-text value, not a String. A misspelled style fails the build, inserted user text prints as text, and styles always close. It reuses Jet's existing checked literal heads, such as SQL{…} and HTML{…}, so it adds no new syntax.

What changes in this ballot: it stays the plain-text floor, and it no longer teaches terminal styling through raw codes. Protocol text still needs \r. Debug output, review of invisible characters and core.tui's own source still need \u{…}. Option A's example now shows a zero-width space instead of a hand-written color code, and the beginner path for colors points to the companion. The two votes are independent: D-TUI-ANSI1's checked literal works under every option here.

CODE FACTS

These code facts were checked on 2026-10-05 against dev 91a438ce4 and release jet dev-05ea86f65.

Law: spec.md:62-63 and S20 allow four escapes. Any other escape is E0001. D-BOUND-RAW1 and D-RAWSTR1 reaffirm the four-entry table. Byte-head literals already accept \xNN (Compiler/JetLexer/Source/Lexer/Payload.jet:551-572): [U8]{"GET / HTTP/1.1\x0D\x0A..."} produced 27 bytes with byte 14 = 13 in a probe.

Exercised: "{head}\r\n..." fails E0001 three times (probe status_line.jet, first version).

Workarounds in the tree: Examples/features/net/http_parse_body_limits.jet:32 `crlf :: String.from_bytes([U8]{13, 10}) ?? panic("CRLF")`; Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/Loader.jet:211,263,571 and Pipeline.jet:2503 `String.from_bytes([U8]{U8{13}}) ?? ""`; Examples/features/net/http_server_trailers.jet:26-29 pushes bytes 13 and 10 per line. 105 tracked .jet files compare or push byte 13.

Debug round trip: the evaluator renderer (Compiler/JetEval/Source/Formatting/Values.jet:157-181) and the default-run runtime both follow Rust's {:?}. A probe ($JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/mine/legwork/adversary2/debug_rt.jet) printed the text a, CR, NUL, ESC, {b}, ', e plus U+0301 as "a\r\0\u{1b}{b}'e\u{301}". None of \r, \0 or \u{…} lex today. Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Emit/Context.jet:476-520 only spells Rust source literals, so it is not a Debug renderer.

Ratified example drift: D-HTTP-BYTES-FORM1's code writes "POST / HTTP/1.1\r\n...", which does not compile today (handled on card #4428 independently of this vote).

No decision was found that rejected \r or \u{...} on purpose; S20 is the original four-entry choice.

Fresh review reconciliation, 2026-10-05. D-BOUND-RAW1's line that plain strings keep the four-entry table only states its own scope, so A amends it together with S20. Once #3881 [#4204] rejects raw direction marks inside literals, \u{202E} becomes their legitimate visible spelling, as rustc's lint already suggests.

Java decodes \u escapes before lexing, so a comment containing \u000a ends early; that design is a known failure. A avoids it because Jet decodes escapes only inside quoted text. In interpolated text the lexer reads \u{ as an escape before a brace can open a hole, so "\u{1b}" never names a binding 1b.

Adversarial pass, 2026-10-05, same release; probes in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/mine/legwork/adversary2/. Braces: the probe above prints {b} unchanged, and pasting "a{b}" back would interpolate b. So the round-trip promise covers escapes only. Doubling braces in Debug was rejected because it would make every JSON value in Debug output harder to read, and Rust prints them plainly too.

char_quote.jet: '\'' is E0001 today, although the char-literal E0001 text lists \' as an escape. So no apostrophe Char can be written, yet the evaluator's Debug prints one as '\''. A adds \' to character literals so that Char Debug output reads back too.

One table, Syntax::ESCAPES (crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/math_layout.rs:456), feeds plain strings, character literals, [U8] byte-head bodies and the module evaluator (crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Eval.rs:2608). Adding r there gives byte literals \r as well, as in Rust's b"\r"; \u{…} is handled outside that table and stays text-only.

options.name: Add \r and \u{…}
options.detail:
Quoted text and character literals gain \r (character 13) and \u{H}. H is one to six hexadecimal digits naming any Unicode scalar. Surrogates (D800-DFFF), values above 10FFFF, empty braces and seven digits are E0001 at the exact span. Character literals also accept \', which today's error text already lists but the lexer rejects. Byte literals gain \r through the shared table, keep \xNN for other bytes, and do not gain \u.

Debug prints only \n \t \r \" \' \\ and \u{…}, so every escape it prints reads back as the same text. Braces still print as themselves, as in Rust, so pasted Debug text containing { needs {{. jet fmt rewrites \u{a}, \u{9} and \u{d} to \n, \t and \r, and writes other hex in lowercase without leading zeros. Each character keeps one spelling in formatted code.
options.technical:
Both lexers change. Rust paths: crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Strings.rs:195-210,550-561 and Scan.rs:1014-1030. Self-hosted path: Compiler/JetLexer/Source/Lexer/Payload.jet:574-590. Syntax::ESCAPES gains r=13, the char-literal path gains \', and a braced scalar escape is added for text and Char only. Validation uses the scalar rule of D-CHAR-SCALAR1 Char.from_u32: 0..=0x10FFFF minus 0xD800..=0xDFFF.

Triple-quoted strings follow automatically, since spec.md:73-74 gives them the ordinary escape rules. Raw backtick strings and typed text heads are unchanged (D-RAWSTR1, D-BOUND-RAW1). The module evaluator's literal decoder (crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Eval.rs:2608) learns \u{…} too.

The evaluator renderer (JetEval Values.jet:157-181) and the runtime Debug formatter for default run and AOT print NUL as \u{0} instead of \0. Everything else they print already lexes under A. E0001 why-text lists the six text escapes, and the char-literal text matches its real set. jet fmt canonicalization is a formatter rule, not a new diagnostic.

decisions.title: Terminal colors, cursor moves and screen clearing in core.tui
decisions.situation: Terminal programs color words and move the cursor by printing hidden control codes. Jet has no named list of these codes, and its one styling call silently prints plain text when a color is misspelled. Text from users can also carry its own codes, which rewrite the screen when printed. This vote decides how Core spells colors, cursor moves and clearing; I recommend a checked terminal-text form that refuses typos and makes user text harmless.
decisions.gist: How should Jet programs color terminal text and move the cursor?
decisions.lesson: A terminal reads hidden codes inside printed text: one code turns words red, another clears a line. Jet already has checked text forms, such as `SQL{"…"}` and `HTML{"…"}`, which check their contents when the program is built and make inserted values safe. Terminal codes have no such form today, so they are unchecked plain text.
decisions.explainer: Beginner path: write `ANSI{"[bold red]error:[/] {name}"}` and print it; a misspelled style fails the build, and `name` prints as text even if it hides codes. Expert path: `tui.moveCursor(row:, col:)`, `tui.clearLine()`, `tui.altScreen(on:)` and `tui.mouse(on:)` return the same checked value, and `tui.ESC` and `tui.CSI` reach codes the table lacks. Shared work under every option: plain strings keep whatever escapes the carriage-return ballot grants, and full-screen apps keep `tui.run` with `TUIStyle`.
decisions.story: Omar writes a deploy tool that prints red errors next to server names typed by users. A misspelled color printed plain text for a week. A server name holding hidden codes once cleared his whole screen.
decisions.inWild:
# Python rich (rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/markup.html)
from rich.markup import escape
console.print(f"[bold red]error:[/] no user {escape(name)}")
# forget escape() and `name` can inject its own markup
decisions.detail:
Origin. Owner question q4p8lzbr on D-STR-ESCAPE1 asked for terminal escape constants and helpers in the TUI library, controlled by a strongly typed string literal. D-STR-ESCAPE1 stays the lexer floor (`\r`, `\u{…}` in plain strings). This companion ballot owns the terminal vocabulary. Both outcomes of D-STR-ESCAPE1 work with every option here.

Jet today. Core/tui/tui.jet:30-41 has `TUIColorProfile` and `TUIColor` (`ANSI16`, `ANSI256`, `RGB`), and `TUIStyle` with `style_text`. Core/term/term.jet:101 `term.style(style, text)` calls the host. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Term.rs:273-288 accepts one of ten single words and returns the text unstyled for anything else, so `"bold red"` and `"redd"` both print plain.

More of today. Core/term/term.jet:103-178 `style_force` parses a different multi-word table, so the two tiers disagree. Term.rs:245-262 already applies NO_COLOR, FORCE_COLOR and the is-a-terminal test. No cursor, erase, alternate-screen or mouse codes exist. Eight `term.style` calls sit in six tracked .jet files. Two files build the escape byte with `String.from_bytes([U8]{27})`.

Rust. crossterm (docs.rs/crossterm 0.29) exposes typed commands: `cursor::MoveTo`, `terminal::Clear`, `EnterAlternateScreen`, `EnableMouseCapture`, queued onto a writer. owo-colors adds zero-allocation methods such as `"x".red()`. It honors NO_COLOR, FORCE_COLOR and terminal detection only through `if_supports_color` and an optional feature.

Go. lipgloss builds style values (`NewStyle().Bold(true).Foreground(Color("205"))`) and renders text through them. It downsamples true color to 256, 16 or no color for the detected terminal. Styles are values, but each colored word needs its own render call.

Python. rich uses bracket markup, `[bold red]alert![/]`, inside strings, and raises MarkupError on mismatched tags. Its own docs warn that interpolated text can inject tags and require `rich.markup.escape`. That check runs at run time, and forgetting `escape` is silent.

Node. chalk chains styles (`chalk.red.bold("x")`) and drops codes when color is unsupported. chalk-template is a tagged template, `` chalkTemplate`{red ${x}}` ``. It escapes braces in inserted values but not control codes, and its docs say raw template input must be escaped by the caller.

Known failure. Terminal escape injection is a recorded bug class: CVE-2021-25743 says kubectl did not neutralize escape and control sequences in data printed to a terminal (CWE-150). The code table follows the common reference, fnky's ANSI Escape Sequences gist (gist.github.com/fnky/458719343aabd01cfb17a3a4f7296797).

What the evidence says. Typed values with automatic terminal detection (lipgloss, chalk) prevent codes leaking into files. Markup (rich, chalk-template) reads best for mixed inline styles. Every surveyed library leaves inserted text unescaped by default or behind an extra call. Option A combines the readable markup, build-time checking, terminal detection, and inserted text that is made harmless by default.

How A fits Jet. D-TEXTHEAD-TYPE1=A lets a library declare checked text as a String-backed type with a `CheckedText` impl, so `ANSI` needs no compiler change. D-UNIFYLIT1=A and D-REGEX-LIT1=D fix the `Type{"…"}` head form. D-TEXT-CONTROL1=A supplies the control-character test used for inserted text.

Names. The helpers use the camelCase spelling from the owner's question. Under the ratified D-CASE-LAW1=A they would read `move_cursor` and `clear_line`; D-CASE-LAW2 is open and decides which spelling ships.

decisions.title: When printed text leaves the program
decisions.situation: When a program prints, the text can go straight to the screen or file, or wait in a small holding area and leave in larger batches. Today Jet sends every print immediately, even into a file or pipe, so printing a million lines makes a million system calls and stdout.flush() does nothing. You decide when printed text leaves the program; we recommend sending it at each line on a terminal and in batches into files and pipes.
decisions.gist: Should printed text leave the program at every print, at every line, or in batches when it goes to a file?
decisions.lesson: A buffer is a holding area for output. Writing it out is called flushing. Today every print flushes at once, even into a file. A flushes each line on a terminal and batches output into files and pipes, and it always flushes before the program waits, reads input, starts a child or exits. B flushes every line everywhere. C keeps today's flush on every print.
decisions.explainer:
Programs print a little at a time. Sending each piece to the operating system costs a system call, which is slow compared with copying text into memory. Most languages keep a small buffer and send it in batches, then flush it at sensible moments.

Today Jet flushes after every print on every stream. On a terminal that is harmless. Into a file or a pipe it multiplies system calls, and the stream's flush method has no work left to do.

Option A follows the rule C and Python have used for decades. On a terminal, text leaves at each line ending, so a person sees whole lines at once. Into a file or pipe, text leaves in batches.

A also flushes before every moment where waiting text could confuse anyone. That includes before the program reads input, sleeps or waits on the network, starts a child process, writes to stderr, stops with an error, or exits. stderr itself keeps flushing on every write, so error text is never held back.

Option B flushes at every line everywhere, as Rust does. Option C keeps today's rule and documents flush as having nothing to do.
decisions.story: Dev writes a log converter that prints two million lines into a file with jet run convert.jet > out.txt. It takes far longer than the same loop in Python or C. The time goes to two million separate writes, and calling stdout.flush() at the end changes nothing.
decisions.inWild:
/* C: stdout is line buffered on a terminal and fully buffered otherwise.
   https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/stdin.html */
for (int i = 0; i < 2000000; i++) printf("%d\n", i);   // few write calls into a file

# Python: the same rule; stderr is line buffered (3.9+)
# https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.stdout
decisions.detail:
Current state: every non-empty stdout and stderr write flushes, even into files and pipes. The flush flag passed down is dead, so stdout.flush() is a no-op in practice (cpp-craft F3b; Term.rs:152-177; FSIoEnvOsTesting.rs:279-326). The native image runtime also prints text and newline as two writes (card #4013). D-COREIO1=A gives core.io ownership of the standard streams and flush, and says nothing about the default policy.

Card #4634 asks to measure, then fix. The measurement belongs to that card. The default itself is an owner choice because every program observes it in output order, crash output and speed.

Sources: The Cherno, 31 nooby C++ habits (i_wDa2AS_8w 00:43), where std::endl flushing every line is the first habit to drop (claims cpp-craft:I02, R02).

Proven approaches. C stdio buffers stdout by line on a terminal and fully otherwise, and leaves stderr unbuffered (POSIX stdin(3)). Python uses the same split, and since 3.9 makes stderr line buffered. Rust's stdout is a LineWriter everywhere, so output into pipes still pays one write per line unless the program wraps it in a BufWriter. Go's os.Stdout is unbuffered, so heavy output needs bufio by hand.

Known failure of plain buffering: a prompt without a newline stays hidden before input, and buffered output can be lost when a program aborts. Option A removes both. It flushes before input and blocking waits, and the stop path flushes before printing its report.

options.name: Lines on a terminal, batches into files and pipes
options.detail: On a terminal, stdout flushes at each line ending. Into a file or pipe it flushes when its buffer fills. Every stream also flushes before the program reads input, sleeps or waits, starts a child process, writes to stderr, stops with an error, or exits. stderr flushes every write. stdout.flush() forces a flush at any time.
options.technical: core.io keeps one buffer per standard stream in the shared runtime, chosen once from the TTY fact (D-CORE-TERMSTDIN1). The scheduler's blocking points, process spawn, the stop and panic report path and process exit call one flush hook. Every tier shares the rule through the one-runtime law (D-EXEC1). The image runtime's two-write print becomes one buffered write.

options.name: Flush at every line everywhere
options.detail: stdout flushes at each line ending on a terminal and into files and pipes. stderr flushes every write. Output that prints many short lines still makes one system call per line.
options.technical: One line-buffered writer for stdout on every target, as Rust's LineWriter. No TTY check. Large line-oriented output into files keeps most of today's system-call count.
options.code:
loop i in 0..1_999_999 { print(i) }
// jet run convert.jet > out.txt: one write per line

options.name: Keep flushing every print
options.detail: Today's rule stays. Every write leaves at once on every stream. stdout.flush() is documented as having nothing to do. Programs that need speed wrap the stream in their own buffer.
options.technical: No runtime change. Documentation records flush as a no-op for the standard streams.

comparisons.note: stdout is line buffered on a terminal and fully buffered into files and pipes; stderr is unbuffered.
The same terminal versus file split; stderr is line buffered since 3.9.
comparisons.code:
# https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.stdout
print(i)                  # batched into a file
print(i, flush=True)      # force

comparisons.note: stdout is line buffered everywhere, which keeps one write per line into pipes.

recommendation.why: A gives people whole lines on a terminal and gives files and pipes batched writes, the split C and Python proved over decades. Flushing before every wait, child, error report and exit removes the classic hidden-prompt and lost-output failures.
recommendation.tradeoff: Two programs writing into the same pipe may see their lines grouped differently than today.
gains: Large output into files stops paying one system call per print.
stdout.flush() does real work again.
Prompts and crash reports still appear in order.

losses.loss: Output written into a shared pipe by a parent and a child can group differently than today.
losses.mitigation: Every stream flushes before a child process starts and before waiting on it, so parent output written before the spawn always comes first.

whyNot.reason: B keeps one system call per line into files, which is most of today's cost for line-oriented output.
C keeps the cost and leaves a flush method that never does anything.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Measure on card #4634 first: system-call counts with strace and matched timings for one and two million printed lines into a file, a pipe and a terminal.

Check that a prompt written without a newline appears before read_line returns. Check that output printed before a stop, a panic, a child spawn and exit appears in order in a captured pipe, on every tier.

Check that stderr writes are never delayed. Check that stdout.flush() empties the buffer, and that the image runtime prints one write per print call.

surface.lesson: Flushing sends held output to the screen or file. Today every print flushes at once, even into a file. A flushes per line on a terminal and in batches into files, and always before waiting, input or exit. B flushes every line everywhere. C keeps today's rule.

options.name: Every print, as today
options.gist: Nothing is held back; flush has nothing to do.
gains: No behavior changes.
losses: Large output stays slow.
flush stays a method that does nothing.

proposed.code:

// one write per print

recommendation.why: A uses the terminal-versus-file rule that C and Python proved. It flushes before every wait, child, error report and exit, so nothing goes missing.
gains: Fast output into files and pipes.
flush works again.

losses.loss: Parent and child lines in one pipe may group differently.
losses.mitigation: Streams flush before a child starts and before waiting on it.

whyNot.reason: B keeps one system call per line into files.
C keeps the cost and a flush that does nothing.

designAway.loss: Output written into a shared pipe by a parent and a child can group differently than today.
attempts: Flush on every write into pipes only. Rejected: pipes are where the large outputs go.
Flush at every point where another process or person could observe order: before spawn, wait, input, stderr writes, stops and exit. Kept.

designAway.loss: A long-running program writing a log file shows lines late to someone watching it.
attempts: Flush on a timer. Rejected: a hidden timer adds a thread and makes output timing nondeterministic.
Flush whenever the program blocks waiting for time, input or the network. Kept: an idle program has flushed everything it printed.

decisions.title: A busy task still stops on time and lets others run
decisions.situation: Jet runs many small tasks on a few processor threads, and a task stops or gives way only when it waits, such as on a timer or the network. A loop that never waits keeps its thread, so a deadline cannot stop a runaway handler, a cancelled race loser holds up the winner, and busy tasks can starve the server. You decide whether each loop turn also becomes a place where cancellation, deadlines and fair turns can land. We recommend one cheap check per loop turn, switched on only after a speed gate shows no slowdown.
decisions.gist: Should cancellation, deadlines and fair turns reach a task that is busy in a loop and never waits?
decisions.lesson: A task is a small piece of work that runs alongside others; Jet runs many tasks on a few processor threads. A wait point is where a task already pauses, such as sleep, a channel receive or network input. Today cancellation, deadlines and turn-taking happen only at wait points, so a loop that never waits runs to its end no matter what. The choice is whether a loop's turn back to its top also becomes a safe stopping place.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. A task is a small job, such as handling one web request. Jet runs thousands of tasks on a few processor threads, one per processor core, and switches between tasks when one of them waits.

A wait point is a place where a task already stops for a moment: a sleep, a channel receive, a network read, or waiting for another task. Today those are the only places where Jet can cancel a task, report a missed deadline, or let another task have the thread.

A busy loop is a loop that computes without waiting, such as adding up a billion numbers. Under today's rule it keeps its thread until it finishes. If a deadline passes, nothing notices. If the task lost a race, the race still waits for it.

A time slice is a short turn, such as ten milliseconds. Fair sharing means a task that used its whole slice gives the thread to waiting tasks and then continues later.

The check proposed in A is one memory read and one branch at the bottom of a loop. Loops that count over a known range check once per block of iterations, not every time, the way Java's optimizing compiler has done since Java 10.
decisions.story: Ravi runs a Jet API with a one-second request deadline. One customer uploads a pathological input, and a parsing loop in his handler runs for twenty minutes. The deadline never fires, the request never ends, and on deploy the server cannot drain, so it is killed without cleanup. A second such request leaves only the other cores for every other customer.
decisions.detail:
Code facts come from source reading of the checkout at the time of drafting. Nothing here was executed.

Law today. core.tasks is cooperative: "the scheduler does not turn a blocking computation into preemptive parallelism" (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:2609-2611). The scheduler is M:N with no async coloring (Docs/spec/spec.md:2302-2306, D-ASYNCRT1=A, which chose Go's goroutine model). Cancellation unwinds only at wait points (spec.md:2107-2111, D-CANCELMODEL1=C).

D-FOUND-LIFECYCLE1=A states the consequence as its tradeoff: "a CPU-bound handler notices its deadline at its next wait point". D-TASK-PAUSE-TIER1=E kept pause at wait points by default. It also ratified an optional strong mode, mode: .CheckLoops, with portable back-edge checks on every engine.

Runtime today. The shared scheduler runs one work-stealing worker per core and has no time-slice preemption (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Scheduler.rs:3669-3805). task.all, task.race and task.any cancel losers and then drain them (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/TaskGroup.rs:485-498). A drain blocks on the child's result (Scheduler.rs:3956-3959).

So a cancelled child that never reaches a wait point is joined only when it ends by itself. The race result, a parent deadline and E3003 all wait for it (Scheduler.rs:4032-4056).

Inside Jet already. Sandbox plugins, build plugins and compiler extensions enable Wasmtime epoch interruption (Prelude/Plugin.rs:240-243 and 1372-1406, BuildPlugin.rs:26-28, CompilerExtension.rs:90-93). They stop a guest that passes its time limit, two seconds per call by default (D-CORE-PLUGINLIMITS1=A). Epoch interruption is a counter check at loop back-edges and function entries.

The REPL interpreter already polls before each instruction, so Ctrl-C returns within 100 ms (spec.md:3363-3366, D-FE-REPL-INTERRUPT1=A). The only Jet code a runaway loop can hold forever is ordinary compiled Jet code.

What this does not cover. Foreign C and C++ calls already run on worker threads (Docs/spec/reference/mixed-repo.md:101-102). A deadline that passes during one is delivered when it returns, in every option. Memory per request is a separate question.
Prior owner ruling. D-TASK-PAUSE-TIER1 rejected its option C because forced checks on every pause tax the default fast path. This ballot keeps that ruling for pause.

This ballot asks a different question. Should cancellation, deadlines and fair turns use the back-edge sites that the ratified strong pause (.CheckLoops) already requires on every engine? Option A turns its default on only after the hot-loop speed gate shows no measurable slowdown. Counted loops check once per block. Loops that already wait need no check. If the gate fails, the sites stay opt-in and the D-FOUND-LIFECYCLE1=A tradeoff stands.

Independent of the vote, strong pause is ratified but unbuilt. pause(mode: .CheckLoops) is rejected with E0764, and no engine calls the Prelude loop pause hook. Building that shared back-edge check is repair work on the owning card whichever option wins.

Merged sources (2026-10-05 mining). RntfkL8lUY4: BEAM promises a greedy green thread never blocks the scheduler, and a bad regex must not either. IxQ586TS8Gw 45:46-48:32: in Riot, a while-true actor bricks a cooperative scheduler, so the speaker wants compiler-inserted yields. The same talk records the dissent that preemptive scheduling beats polite yields.

options.name: Loops are stop points
options.detail:
Every engine checks one per-thread attention flag where a loop returns to its top and on entry to a function that can call itself. The check is one load and one branch. A loop over a known range checks once per block of iterations instead of every time.

When the flag is set, the task does what it would do at a wait point. A pending cancellation or blown deadline unwinds with Drop cleanup, a strong pause stops, and a task past its time slice gives its thread to waiting tasks and continues later. #Shield keeps deferring cancellation and deadlines exactly as today.

Beginners write nothing new: deadlines and races just work for busy code. The default is switched on only after the hot-loop speed gate shows no measurable slowdown; until then today's rule stays, so no program gets slower.
options.technical:
Amends D-CANCELMODEL1=C: delivery points become wait points plus loop back-edges and recursive entries. Amends the stated tradeoff of D-FOUND-LIFECYCLE1=A. Under D-TASK-PAUSE-TIER1=E the .CheckLoops sites become the default sites for cancel, deadline and fairness; pause may keep its wait-point default.

The mechanism follows Wasmtime epoch interruption, which Jet already uses for plugins. A timer thread raises a worker's attention word when its task has run past the slice while runnable work waits. cancel() and an expired #Context deadline raise the target task's word directly.

Counted loops are strip-mined as in HotSpot C2 loop strip mining (JDK-8186027, Java 10): the inner block runs check-free and the outer loop checks. Checks are elided in loops whose body already reaches a wait point or a checked call on every iteration. One Prelude delivery function serves every engine, and the interpreter keeps its per-instruction poll.

Safety argument: the unwind lands only between iterations. That is a statement boundary where an index or arithmetic panic can already unwind today. Shared-state critical sections keep #Shield.

options.name: Fair turns only
options.detail:
The runtime interrupts a task that used its whole time slice with an operating-system signal and runs other tasks, then resumes it later. Loops get no added check, so tight loops run at full speed. This is how Go solved starvation in Go 1.14.

Cancellation and deadlines still land only at wait points. A busy race loser still keeps the race waiting, and a runaway handler still ignores its deadline and blocks a clean shutdown.
options.technical: Signal-driven preemption needs the runtime to suspend a task at an arbitrary instruction and switch stacks from a signal handler. Runtime locks and allocation need no-preempt regions. Go's design (proposal 24543) also needed safe-point metadata for its garbage collector. Jet's ownership model needs less of that, but each engine still needs its own signal and context-switch path, and Windows needs SuspendThread. Unwinding at an arbitrary instruction is not safe, so this cannot deliver cancellation.

options.name: Keep waits as the only stop points, and warn
options.detail:
The rule stays as today. The compiler adds a warning for a loop that never waits inside task or request-handler code, and the docs teach calling tasks.yield_now() in long loops.

There is no runtime cost. Every author and every library must remember the call, including text parsing, sorting and decoding loops the author never wrote.
options.technical: A lint over loop bodies with no reachable wait point, scoped to task bodies and handlers. Library loops are reached through calls, so the lint either floods or misses them. Tokio documents the same rule and states it will not detect blocking tasks (tokio.rs/blog/2020-04-preemption).

comparisons.note: Go first used cooperative turns, and tight loops could hang the scheduler for five years. A loop check cost a 7.8% geomean slowdown in 2017 tests. Go 1.14 then switched to signal preemption, but cancellation by context stayed cooperative.

The BEAM preempts every process on a reduction budget, so a hot loop or a slow regular expression cannot block a scheduler. Native code must return within about a millisecond or run on dirty schedulers.
comparisons.code:
%% https://www.erlang.org/doc/apps/erts/erl_nif.html#long-running-nifs
loop(N) -> loop(N + 1).   % other processes keep running; exit(Pid, kill) stops it

comparisons.note: Epoch interruption loads one counter and compares it at loop back-edges and function entries. It measured about twice as fast as fuel counting, and one mechanism can yield, trap or call back. Jet's plugin host already uses it.

recommendation.why: A makes deadlines, races, cancellation and fair sharing work for busy code with no new syntax. It uses the check Jet already runs for plugins and already ratified for strong pause. The speed gate means no program gets slower to get it.
gains: A request deadline stops a runaway handler and a clean shutdown can drain it.
task.race returns when the winner finishes, not when the slowest loser does.
Busy requests share the processor, so one heavy input cannot stall the server.

losses.loss: Loops that never wait run one extra check, which the Go team measured as costly in its tightest loops.
losses.mitigation: Counted loops check once per block and loops that already wait need no check. The default turns on only after the hot-loop speed gate shows no measurable slowdown.

losses.loss: Cancellation can now land between two loop turns, not only at a wait.
losses.mitigation: It lands only at a whole-turn boundary where a panic can already unwind today, Drop cleanup still runs, and #Shield still keeps critical sections whole.

whyNot.reason: B stops starvation but leaves deadlines, races and shutdown waiting on busy code, and it needs a separate signal and stack-switch path on every engine.
C makes every author and library remember a manual call, and the warning cannot see loops inside library code.

recommendation.tradeoff: A asks Jet to build a strip-mined loop check that passes the hot-loop speed gate. In return, every Jet task honours its deadline, cancellation and fair share whether or not it waits.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Build the gate first. Take the hot-loop gauntlet cells from card #2254 plus a counted sum, a while loop over a linked structure, recursive Fibonacci, a regex scan and a JSON decode of a large input. Run each as a paired program with the check on and off in the same release profile, and compare against Rust. The default turns on only where every cell stays within the strict performance gate.

Then check behaviour on every engine. A task.race between an immediate value and a busy loop returns the value within one slice. A #Context deadline of 20 ms around a busy loop reports E3003 within one slice and runs Drop cleanup. A cancelled busy task inside #Shield finishes the shielded block first.

Eight busy tasks plus one sleeping task on a two-core machine still wake the sleeper within a few slices. SIGTERM during a busy handler drains within the serve deadline. Strong pause keeps working. A loop that already waits on every turn shows no added check in the generated code.

surface.gist: Should deadlines, cancellation and fair turns reach a task that is busy in a loop and never waits?
surface.lesson: Jet runs many small tasks on a few processor threads. Today a task stops or gives way only when it waits, such as sleeping or reading the network. A loop that never waits keeps its thread until it ends, so deadlines, races and shutdown wait for it. A makes each loop turn a safe stopping place.

current.note: Today the race waits for the busy loser to finish by itself.

wild.note: Since Go 1.14 a busy loop no longer blocks other goroutines.

options.name: Loops are stop points
options.gist: Each loop turn checks one cheap flag for cancellation, deadlines and fair turns.
gains: Deadlines and races work for busy code.
Busy requests share the processor fairly.
No new syntax; plugins already work this way.
losses: One cheap check in loops that never wait.
Cancellation may land between loop turns.

proposed.code:

print(answer)   // 42 at once; the loser stops at its next loop turn

options.name: Fair turns only
options.gist: The runtime interrupts long turns so others run, but stopping still waits for a wait point.
gains: No added check in any loop.
Busy tasks no longer starve others.
losses: Deadlines and races still wait for busy code.
Needs a separate interrupt path on every engine.

proposed.code:
answer :: (task.race { cached(), slow_count(50_000_000_000) }) ?? 0
print(answer)   // others keep running, but 42 waits for slow_count

options.name: Keep waits only, and warn
options.gist: The rule stays; a warning asks authors to yield by hand inside long loops.
gains: No runtime cost at all.
losses: Every author and library must remember to yield.
The warning cannot see loops inside libraries.

recommendation.why: A makes deadlines, races, cancellation and fair sharing work for busy code with no new syntax, using the check Jet already runs for plugins.
gains: Runaway handlers stop at their deadline.
Races return when the winner finishes.
One heavy request cannot stall the server.

losses.loss: One cheap check in loops that never wait.
losses.mitigation: Counted loops check once per block, and it ships only after the speed gate shows no slowdown.

losses.loss: Cancellation may land between two loop turns.
losses.mitigation: Only at a whole-turn boundary where panics already unwind; cleanup runs and #Shield still protects.

whyNot.reason: B ends starvation but deadlines, races and shutdown still wait for busy code.
C relies on every author remembering, and cannot see library loops.

recommendation.tradeoff: Building a gated loop check buys deadlines, cancellation and fair turns that reach every task.

decisions.title: Cancelling a task that has a task group open: cancel the group's children too, let them finish first, or keep today's lost cancel
decisions.situation: A task group is a block that starts several tasks and waits for all of them at its closing brace. Today, cancelling a task that is waiting at such a brace does not reach the tasks inside the group. Those children run to their end, and then the cancelled task carries on as if nothing happened, so its join reports success and the cancel is lost. A child that waits forever, such as a server loop, makes that cancel hang for good. This matters for anyone who stops a job made of parallel parts: a crawler, a fan-out request, a test that times out. You are asked what a cancel does to the children of a group the cancelled task has open. We recommend that it cancels them, waits for their cleanup, and then the task stops as cancelled.
decisions.gist: What should cancelling a task do to the tasks inside a group that task has open?
decisions.lesson: A task group waits for every task it started before its block ends. When the task that opened the group is cancelled, the children can be cancelled with it. They can instead be left to finish before the cancel lands. Or they can be left alone as today, where the cancel is lost.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A task is work that runs alongside the rest of the program. A task group is a block, written task.group name { ... }, that starts child tasks and waits for all of them at its closing brace.

Cancel asks a task to stop. The task notices at its next wait, such as a sleep, a channel read, a network read or waiting for another task. It then unwinds: it leaves its functions and runs its cleanup on the way out. Join waits for a task and gives back its result, or a failure such as Cancelled.
decisions.story:
Mia's command-line tool fetches twenty pages in a task group, inside a job task. When the user presses Ctrl-C, or her two-second time limit runs out, she cancels the job. Today the twenty fetches keep going to the end. Then the job prints that all pages were fetched, and its join says it succeeded.

Under A the fetches stop at their next network wait, close their connections, and the job's join reports Cancelled within moments. Under B the job waits for all twenty fetches, then reports Cancelled. Under C nothing changes.
decisions.detail:
What this ballot decides. What happens to the children of a task.group block when the task that opened the block is cancelled while the block is open.

What the rules say today. spec.md, Task completion and cancellation: cancellation lands at wait points, and task join is one of them (D-CANCELMODEL1=C). spec.md, Structured tasks and combinators: the group owns and joins every child created in its body (D-CONC-SPAWN1=D). task.all cancels remaining children on a failure, and task.race and task.any cancel the losers.

D-NURSERY1=A says work created inside the scope must finish, be cancelled, or report an error before the scope exits, without choosing which. No ratified rule says whether cancelling the opener reaches the group's children. process.on_signal cancels every live task, which is a separate path.

What the code does today. Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/TaskGroup.jet task_group_close cancels the group's children only when the closing task's deadline has expired (status 2). Otherwise it calls task_drain on each child, and task_drain (Task.jet) is a plain futex wait with no cancellation check. So the closing brace is not a stop point for the opener.

The combinators already cancel their children when the waiting task is cancelled: task_selection_wait_check delivers the cancel and task_selection_drain(handles, count, true) cancels every child.

Seed run. Seed b14, at --optimize=none. A parent task opens a group whose one child sleeps 3 s. run cancels the parent after 100 ms and joins it. Output: child finished its sleep, then parent closed its group, then parent joined Ok, and the join took at least 2 s. The cancel was lost, and the parent's code after the group ran.

Relation to other ballots. D-TASK-SLICE1=A makes loop turns stop points, so under option A a busy child also stops promptly. D-EXIT-TASKS1 covers detached tasks at process exit. Detached tasks are not group children and are untouched here.

options.name: Cancel flows down to the group's children
options.detail:
Cancelling a task also cancels every child of each task group it has open, and their own groups' children, all the way down. Each child stops at its next wait and runs its cleanup. The group's closing brace still waits for all of them, so no child outlives its group. Then the cancelled task itself unwinds, and its join reports Cancelled.

A child that must finish a step it started puts that step in #Shield, which already delays a cancel until the step is done. This is what task.all, task.race and task.any already do with their children, and what a group already does when its deadline passes.

The cost of A. A child stopped in the middle of a step that is not in #Shield leaves that step half done: a file half written, a request half sent. Its cleanup still runs, so the file is closed and the connection dropped, but the half-done work is not undone. Steps that must not stop halfway go in #Shield.
options.technical:
The cancel of a task walks the groups it has open and cancels each unfinished child (scheduler_control_cancel), recursively. This is what task_group_close already does under an expired deadline. A task records its open groups, so a cancel that arrives while it is already parked at the closing brace still reaches them.

task_group_close cancels the children when the closer is cancelled and not shielded, waits for all of them, then delivers the pending cancel so the closer unwinds as Cancelled. A closer inside #Shield keeps today's behaviour until the shield ends. spec.md gains one sentence in Task completion and cancellation and one in Structured tasks and combinators.

Cost. A cancel walks only the unfinished descendants in open groups: one step per such task, paid once per cancel. Each group's child list is read under that group's own lock, and the cancels are sent after the lock is released, as the deadline path already does. A task that is never cancelled pays one list push and one pop per task.group block, to record the open group.

options.name: Children finish first, then the cancel lands
options.detail:
The group's children are not cancelled. They run to their own end, the closing brace waits for them as it does today, and then the cancelled task unwinds and its join reports Cancelled. The cancel is no longer lost, but it takes as long as the slowest child. A child that waits forever, such as a server's accept loop, makes the cancel hang, so the author must stop such children by hand through a channel or a flag.

B keeps the ratified rule that waiting for a task is a stop point; it only delays the cancel.
options.technical: task_group_close keeps task_drain without cancelling children, then delivers the closer's pending cancel. Group children differ from task.all, task.race and task.any children, which are cancelled. B does not amend D-CANCELMODEL1=C: the cancel still lands at the closing brace, which is a task join, only after the children end.

options.name: Keep today's behaviour
options.detail: The group's closing brace is not a stop point. The children run to their end, and then the cancelled task carries on with the code after the group as if it had never been cancelled. Its join reports success. A child that waits forever hangs the cancel. Choosing C amends a ratified rule: today waiting for a task is a place where a cancel lands, and C makes the group's closing brace an exception.
options.technical: No change to task_group_close or task_drain. spec.md must then name the group's closing brace as an exception to task join being a wait point. C amends the ratified D-CANCELMODEL1=C, which lists task join among the wait points where a cancel lands.

comparisons.note: Cancelling a task cancels every child task in its task groups; children check at their next await.
comparisons.code: job.cancel()   // the group's addTask children are cancelled too

comparisons.note: Cancelling a parent Job cancels all of its children, and the parent completes only after they finish unwinding.
comparisons.code:

job.cancel()

comparisons.note: Cancelling a scope cancels everything inside it, including every task in a nursery opened there.
comparisons.code:
with trio.move_on_after(2):
    async with trio.open_nursery() as n:
        n.start_soon(fetch, "a")
        n.start_soon(fetch, "b")

comparisons.note: Cancellation is explicit. A context's cancel reaches every context derived from it (pkg.go.dev/context: "When a Context is canceled, all Contexts derived from it are also canceled"). But a goroutine sees it only if it was passed that context and checks Done(). A goroutine that was not passed it runs on. This is the strongest case for B or C: nothing stops without being told in the code. Go also has no group that must outlive its children, so a forgotten goroutine is a leak, not a hang.
comparisons.code:
ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(parent)
go fetch(ctx, "a")   // stops only if fetch checks ctx.Done()
go fetch(ctx, "b")
cancel()

comparisons.note: StructuredTaskScope (JEP 453, preview; docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/StructuredTaskScope.html). shutdown() interrupts every unfinished subtask, and join() and close() wait for all of them. An owner interrupted while waiting in join() gets InterruptedException, and closing the scope then shuts it down, so the subtasks are interrupted and awaited, as in A.

recommendation.why: A cancel means the whole job stops, children included, and nothing outlives its group. It matches how Jet's own task.all, task.race and task.any already treat their children, and how Swift, Kotlin and Trio treat groups.
gains: A cancelled job stops promptly, with every child's cleanup run.
The cancel is never lost: the join reports Cancelled.
A child that waits forever no longer hangs a cancel.
Groups and task.all, task.race and task.any follow one rule.

losses.loss: A child's unfinished work is cut short when its group's opener is cancelled.
losses.mitigation: Work that must outlive the job is started with detach() instead, so it is not a group child.

losses.loss: A child stopped mid-step outside #Shield leaves that step half done, such as a half-written file or a half-sent request.
losses.mitigation: Steps that must not stop halfway go in #Shield, which already delays a cancel until the step ends. Cleanup still runs either way, so files close and connections drop.

losses.loss: Each cancel walks the unfinished tasks in open groups.
losses.mitigation: The walk is one step per unfinished descendant, paid once per cancel, with each group's lock held only to copy its list. Tasks never cancelled pay one push and pop per group.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the cancel but makes it wait for the slowest child, and a child that waits forever hangs it. It also gives groups a different rule from task.all, task.race and task.any. Go's explicit style favours B, but Go has no group that must wait for its children, so it never hangs.
C silently loses the cancel and reports success for a job that was asked to stop. It also amends the ratified rule that waiting for a task is a stop point.

recommendation.tradeoff: A child's in-progress work stops with its job, and #Shield keeps the steps that must finish.

decisions.title: Const generics: a compile-time Int as a type parameter
decisions.gist: May a compile-time number be a type parameter, and how is it spelled?
decisions.lesson: A generic type takes a type parameter: `Pair<T>`. Some types need a number: a 64-byte packet, a 3x3 matrix. Today a constant can size an array field, but `Packet<64>` cannot be written, so each size is a separate struct. A slice does not help: the size must live in the type so a 64-byte frame cannot pass as a 32-byte one. This ballot asks whether a compile-time `Int` may be a type parameter (option D: no) and how to spell it. Running code never builds a type.
decisions.story: Omar writes firmware. His radio frames come in 32, 64, and 128 bytes. He wants one `Packet` type and one `checksum` function. Today he copies the struct three times. With `Packet<@N: Int>` he writes it once, and passing a `Packet<64>` where a `Packet<32>` is expected is a compile error at the call.

options.name: Compile-time sigil: struct Packet<@N: Int>
options.detail:
A value parameter is written with the `@` that S57 gives compile-time names: `struct Packet<@N: Int> { data: [U8#@N] }`, used as `Packet<64>` or `Packet<@lanes>`. Type parameters like `T` are also compile-time, so here `@` marks 'value, not type'; that widens the sigil's meaning. It cannot be misread as a trait bound (`<T: Add>`, which constrains T to implement Add). Inside the body `@N` shadows any outer `@N` constant.

Only `Int` for now; the `: Int` is written so later kinds (`Bool`, `U32`) fit the same slot. Any Int is legal; a negative or zero size fails only where it sizes an array, as `[U8#0]` does today. A bare argument is a literal or `@name`; anything else takes parentheses, `Packet<(@lanes * 16)>`, like `[Float#(@lanes * 2)]`. Inside a generic body arguments are a bare `@N` or fully closed; `Packet<(@N * 2)>` is rejected, so type equality never needs algebra.

`Packet<64>` and `Packet<(@lanes * 16)>` are the same type. One compiled copy per distinct value, like `<T>`. At a call site the value is inferred from the argument, or written explicitly (D-GENERIC-CALL1=A). Value and type parameters mix in declaration order with optional defaults: `Matrix<T, @R: Int, @C: Int = @R>`. `impl<@N: Int> Wire for Packet<@N>` and `impl Wire for Packet<64>` overlap; the existing coherence rule rejects that.

Narrow amendment to S26: a compile-time Int may parameterize an existing type constructor. `Meta.Const` (D-META-GATE1) governs declaring `<@N: Int>`; instantiating a dependency's `Packet<64>` is always allowed.
options.technical: Generic parameter list accepts `@name: Int`. Arguments: literal, `@const`, or a parenthesized comptime Int expression; a bound value parameter may appear only bare. Sema instantiates per distinct value; `[T#@N]` sizes resolve after instantiation and reject non-positive sizes there. A runtime value in the slot is a teaching diagnostic.

options.name: Plain name: struct Packet<N: Int>
options.detail: Rust and Swift shape without a keyword; uniform with the unsigiled `T`. `<N: Int>` looks exactly like a trait bound `<T: Add>` until the reader knows `Int` is not a trait, and the body writes `N`, unlike every other compile-time constant in Jet. The parser cannot tell the kind without name resolution, which Jet's parser does not do today.
options.technical: Disambiguate by resolving the bound: if it names a type rather than a trait, the parameter is a value. Requires name resolution before the parameter kind is known.
options.code:
struct Packet<N: Int> { data: [U8#N] }     // reads like a trait bound <T: Add>
p :: Packet<64>{data: [U8#64]{}}

options.name: Keyword: struct Packet<const N: Int>
options.detail: Rust's spelling, recognized at once by Rust readers, and the body stays unsigiled like `T`. It reserves `const` for one position (I7 has no contextual keywords) when `@` already carries the meaning.
options.technical: Reserve `const` (I7). Parameter kind is known at the parser without name resolution.
options.code:
struct Packet<const N: Int> { data: [U8#N] }   // new reserved word
p :: Packet<64>{data: [U8#64]{}}

options.name: No const generics: keep per-size types
options.detail: Keep S26 as written. Sizes stay array facts (`[U8#64]`); one struct per size by hand, or a generated sibling file per size from `fn build`. Zero grammar change and no monomorphization by value. Cost: `checksum` is written once per size, and a shared field or method cannot be generic over the count.
options.technical: Status quo. Alternatives considered and refused here. A trait with an associated constant (`struct Packet<S: Size>`, typenum style) needs one marker type per size and cannot infer from a literal. A `#N` size parameter reuses the array-size marker but keys the whole feature to arrays.

comparisons.note: A keyword marks a value parameter; only integers, bool, char today.
comparisons.code: struct Packet<const N: usize> { data: [u8; N] }

comparisons.note: Types are values; a function takes a comptime size and returns a struct type. Jet refuses this route.
comparisons.code: fn Packet(comptime n: usize) type { return struct { data: [n]u8 }; }

comparisons.note: Non-type template parameters have existed since the start; the type is written before the name.
comparisons.code: template <std::size_t N> struct Packet { std::array<uint8_t, N> data; };

comparisons.note: Value generics use a plain `let N: Int` marker; only Int today.

recommendation.why: `@` already marks a compile-time name in Jet, so `<@N: Int>` needs no new word and cannot be read as a trait bound; the sigil's meaning widens to 'value, not type'. Inside the body `@N` looks like every other constant. The amendment to S26 stays narrow: a number parameterizes an existing type, no type is computed, and arithmetic over bound parameters is refused so equality stays by value.

whyNot.reason: It reads as a trait bound until the reader knows Int is not a trait, and the parser needs name resolution to know the parameter kind.
Familiar to Rust readers, but it reserves a word for one position when `@` already carries the meaning.
One function per size forever; generated sibling files hide the count in a build step instead of the type.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet takes on monomorphization by value and a second kind of generic parameter. Only Int is allowed, which covers sizes and counts and keeps the type checker away from arbitrary values.

losses.loss: A second kind of generic parameter to learn.
losses.mitigation: A number and a type cannot share one parameter kind without types-as-values.

losses.loss: Only Int values for now.
losses.mitigation: A scope choice: sizes and counts are the shipped need; `Bool` or `U32` can follow in the same slot.

losses.loss: No arithmetic over a bound parameter in a type argument.
losses.mitigation: Deciding `Packet<(@N * 2)>` equals `Packet<(2 * @N)>` needs symbolic algebra.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: completion-beginner-constgen1. Skill: rli5. A stateless fresh reader flagged the unexplained `[U8#@N]`, the trait-bound comparison, and call-site inference; all repaired in option A.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: Anthropic. Fresh agent: completion-adversarial-constgen1. Verdict 'recommendation holds', with material gaps: no status-quo option, arithmetic over bound parameters, parse ambiguity of bare expressions, negative and zero sizes, and `@` shadowing. Repaired by adding option D (with the associated-constant and `#N` alternatives refused there), a bare-or-parenthesized argument rule, closed-or-bare arguments in generic bodies, size checks at the array, and the shadowing rule.

decisions.title: Should a reusable type choice be an alias body or an ordinary type-returning function?
decisions.situation: Should a reusable type choice be an alias body or an ordinary type-returning function? A library wants small storage inline and larger storage in a growing list. Mia uses both and prints their counts, 2 then 3. An ordinary alias names one shape but does not express this checked choice. We recommend extending aliases with the existing required early evaluator and trait bounds, without creating a wrapper type.
decisions.gist: Should a reusable type choice be an alias body or an ordinary type-returning function?
decisions.lesson: An alias is another name for an existing type. A bound requires that chosen type to implement a trait. The choice happens while building; the resulting value has no runtime selection wrapper.
decisions.story: Mia stores two numbers inline and three in a growing list. Both recipes hide that storage choice and print 2, then 3.
decisions.inWild: Illustrative early type-returning function, the broader alternative here.
decisions.detail:
origin/dev:Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Declarations/Types.jet:51-85 classifies transparent generic aliases. origin/dev:Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/Spellings.jet:27-32 supplies early evaluation and number parameters. Both options reuse those generic identities and the ordinary trait checker.

D-ALIAS-GENERIC1=A authorizes generic aliases; D-META-SPELL1=A supplies #run for required early work. D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1 is archived; the later alias decision preserves angle-bracket generics and does not approve either computed form. A proposes `Name<parameters>: Bound #run { type-expression }`. B proposes `#run name: fn(parameters) -> Type<Bound>` and constant calls in type positions. Both run the same canonical early evaluator, never an alias-specific interpreter.

The shared Inline and Heap implementations below are deliberately retained. A generic-implementation failure in the shared baseline must not be hidden by changing the workload. The proposed result retains exact Inline<2> identity: passing it where that type is required needs no conversion. B preserves the same identity through its type-valued result. No fresh nominal identity, allocation or emitted runtime branch is authorized.

Beginners use the recipe as an ordinary type. Experts supply bounds and explicit value parameters. Check every reachable return type against Store, including an unused choice; generic branches need sufficient declared constraints rather than an invented universal proof. Refuse non-types, runtime conditions, invalid capacities and cycles with their declaration path. Conditions may use permitted pure early constants, not ambient host state. Keep ordinary evaluation budgets and diagnostics.

A keeps the new capability at aliases. B is a real stronger option: reusable type values and type-returning functions beyond alias selection. It is not intrinsically a second evaluator, slower or less safe. Both introduce public syntax and therefore remain an owner gate. Explicit concrete constructors remain available under either choice; removing the already requested recipe is not a same-capability alternative.

Fresh review, 2026-11-11. Kept the full shared workload and its generic-implementation failure; corrected archived authority and retained general type functions as a fair stronger alternative.
